The traffic signs are designed and positioned as complementary means and tools for planning and determining traffic arrangements in road systems. In theory, traffic arrangements in a perfect road network could function well even without traffic signs, relying instead on conventional means of goodwill, politeness, or mutual yielding of the right of way, while adopting the behavioral rules established in T.A. 64. In practice, there exists a given road network (with its limitations) intended to serve a broad and diverse population of drivers, who, in situations of congestion, pressure, and other constraints, lose the aforementioned conventional means, leading to potential "misunderstandings" or "different interpretations," which can cause disruptions, accidents, reduced capacity, and more. To ensure that everything operates smoothly, clear, simple, uniform, and unequivocal "communication" or "sign language" or "rules and regulations" are required—dictated and mandated by law—through which arrangements and rules for smooth and safe traffic will be established.

D. In general, it is preferable to place traffic signs using the "do" method. In this method, traffic arrangements are determined by the signs, which "instruct" or "guide" or "direct" or "indicate" in a "positive" message, the actions that the driver can and is allowed to perform. This simplifies decision-making and makes it easier for the driver to continue driving.  
In contrast, placement using the "do not" method through signs that prohibit with a "negative" message certain movements and actions imposes on the driver the obligation to examine the prohibitions and find the movements that remain permitted and which of them are also suitable for him. Under driving conditions with pressure from other drivers, various errors and risks may develop.

The main characteristics of the signs on the board are:  
2.1: Division into sections  
The board is composed of 10 sections, based on topic division.  
In each of them, the signs related to the topic of that section are gathered.  
Section 1 – Warning and Alert – includes the signs on this topic,  
which aim to provide the driver with relevant information about the situation ahead.  
The idea is that the information will be presented "in time," so that the driver has the  
technical-physiological ability to perceive, understand, and respond correctly and in a timely manner.  
Section 2 – Instructions – includes the signs where the message is in a  
mandatory format (in command), without leaving the driver discretion and/or choice regarding how  
to respond. This arises from the particularly severe consequences that may  
result from non-compliance with the instruction on the sign. For example: driving in the wrong direction...  
Section 3 – Right of Way – where the signs concerning granting  
the right of way in various places and situations are gathered.  
Section 4 – Prohibitions and Restrictions – includes the signs that contain  
"prohibition" or "do not do." For example: entry prohibitions, overtaking prohibitions,  
turning or driving above the permitted speed.  
Section 5 – Public Transport – includes the signs and markings  
related to public transport and priority arrangements.

Part 5 – Public Transportation – includes the signs and markings related to public transportation and its priority arrangements. For example: bus lanes, light rail lanes, bus stations, local train stations, taxi stands, etc.  
Part 6 – Information and Guidance – details the guidance signs for navigation purposes on urban and intercity road networks, parking arrangements, and announcements.  
Part 7 – Traffic Lights and Lane Control – includes the group of "sophisticated" signs that operate remotely and/or emit light of various types. These also exchange messages, change, and are "interesting". Apparently, this way they also attract attention and achieve a better compliance level.

2.3: Validity  
(a) The validity of mandatory traffic signs can take four different forms.  
(1) Until the next intersection  
(2) Until canceled by another sign along the section  
(3) Until the end of the marking that accompanies it  
(4) Until canceled by another sign in a different location, not necessarily in the same section (also known as a "zone" sign).  
(b) The impact of jurisdictional boundaries between traffic authorities on the validity of the sign.  
(1) A jurisdictional boundary between traffic authorities exists in various combinations between adjacent local authorities, as well as between local authorities and other entities, government companies, licensees, and corporations that are local traffic authorities.  
(2) Signs placed according to Regulation 17 of the Traffic Regulations are not required to have the consent of the local traffic authority or prior consultation with a police officer, and therefore they are valid at their placement location on both sides of the jurisdictional boundary – regardless of it.  
(3) Signs placed according to Regulation 18 of the Traffic Regulations are based on the decision of the local traffic authority (after the consultations detailed in the regulation) and are valid only within the jurisdiction of the relevant local traffic authority. If there is an intention for the sign's instruction to apply further, beyond the jurisdictional boundary – coordination between authorities is required.

Traffic arrangements are determined with a clear intention to ease the burden on drivers, in addition to other trends such as safety, capacity, traffic flow, etc. Uniform and simple arrangements allow for a quick understanding of the permitted and prohibited traffic directions, as well as the ability to decide and execute them well. Therefore, "correct" traffic arrangements are evaluated – among other things – by the degree of their assimilation among drivers with a minimal number of errors. Basic conditions for this are, of course, uniformity and simplicity, which combine the familiar and known with the accessible and understandable.

(Hereinafter: "crossings" or "railway crossings").  
Although in most crossings there will be a grade separation between the track and the road, as far as can be anticipated, there will still be at-grade crossings for a long time. For this reason, the importance of the subject remains.  
In an effort to improve the level of crossings and the traffic arrangements at them, "Guidelines for the Planning of Railway Crossings" were prepared and published in March 2006. (Reference M.M. 20 in the list of references in the guidelines here).  
Additionally, "Guidelines for the Planning of Pedestrian Crossings at Railway Crossings" were published in December 2010. (Reference M.M. 35 in the list of references in the guidelines here).  
There, one can find details and elaboration on the various planning details.

It is commonly assumed that the influence area of a railway level crossing on the traffic of vehicles on the road crossing the tracks reaches about 300 meters on a two-lane non-urban road. On such a road, the maximum permitted speed (M.M.) is usually 90 km/h (which is about 12 minutes of travel in such a section). There, the signs 130 and 129 are also placed to alert the driver of the approach to the crossing. 

At crossings with roads of lower speed and capacity, the influence area also shortens according to the road, its geometric structure, field of vision, stopping distances, etc. See diagrams No. 1, 2 (from M.M. 20) below.

Attention is drawn to the manner of distributing the authorities between the local traffic authority of the road and the local traffic authority of the railway:  
The local traffic authority of the road – applies to the entire road network within its jurisdiction, except for areas for which another local traffic authority has been appointed. 
The local traffic authority of the railway – applies to the entire right-of-way strip of the railway as defined in the national outline plan for railways (TAMA/23), and additionally also to the section of the road that crosses the railway at a common level – with a length of up to 100 meters on both sides of the railway, subject to defined conditions (see the notice in the records) and also in diagrams No. 6, 7, 8 below. 
Traffic arrangement plans for the road must be prepared in conjunction for each travel route on both sides of the railway, under the responsibility of the local traffic authority of Israel Railways, in full coordination with the local traffic authority/authorities of the roads on both sides of the railway, so that a continuous traffic arrangement is achieved, see diagram No. 6.

All travel routes on both sides of the track are the responsibility of the local signage authority of Israel Railways, in full coordination with the local signage authority/authorities of the roads on both sides of the track, so that a continuous flow of traffic arrangements is achieved, see diagram No. 6 for defining planning boundaries.

Regulation 64 of the Traffic Regulations 5721–1961  
Section 9: Right of Way  
(64)(a) If there is no sign indicating the right of way at an intersection or a stop before approaching the intersection in the direction of travel of the vehicle, the following provisions shall apply:  
(1) When several vehicles approach an intersection from different directions, the driver of a vehicle shall give the right of way to vehicles coming from the right.  
(2) A driver approaching an intersection or located at an intersection and about to turn left or make a U-turn to the left shall give the right of way to vehicles coming straight ahead and located at the intersection or close to it, without detracting from what is stated in paragraph (1).  
(3) A driver exiting from an unpaved road and about to enter or cross a paved road shall give the right of way to vehicles approaching on the paved road.  
(b) A driver exiting from a yard, from a driveway to a house, from a gas station, from a service station, from a parking place for vehicles, or from any place that is not a road, and is about to enter or cross a road -  
(1) shall slow down and, if necessary, stop to allow pedestrians to cross safely before entering the sidewalk or the shoulder of the road.  
(2) shall slow down and give the right of way to vehicles approaching on that road before entering the road.  
(c)

(1) He shall slow down and, if necessary, stop to allow pedestrians to cross safely before he gets onto the sidewalk or the shoulder of the road.  
(2) He shall slow down and yield to vehicles approaching on the same road before entering the road.  
(c) A driver approaching an intersection or a road merge where a sign indicates yielding to traffic on the crossing road shall slow down and, if necessary, stop his vehicle to yield to another vehicle approaching or entering the intersection or road merge from another road.  
(d) A driver approaching an intersection where a sign indicates a stop requirement shall stop at a place where he can see the traffic on the crossing road, and if a stop line is marked - before the stop line, and shall yield to another vehicle approaching or entering the intersection from another road.  
(e) A driver approaching an intersection where traffic is regulated by a traffic light shall obey the signals of the traffic light and shall not enter the intersection until a green light appears. If the traffic light shows a flashing yellow light - the driver shall slow down and, if necessary, stop his vehicle to allow a pedestrian to complete crossing safely and yield to another vehicle entering the intersection from another road, or to a vehicle approaching the intersection.

1. Meaning of the traffic signs  
They indicate the beginning and end of a road where the right of way is granted to vehicles traveling on it. This notification/declaration regarding the granting of the right of way on the road - explicitly and through special signage - gives vehicles the legal option to take the right of way while disregarding the rules for granting right of way detailed in Regulation 64. As is known, Regulation 64 establishes rules whose common denominator is granting the right of way and not taking it.  
2. Justifications for placement  
Due to the contradiction between the provisions of these traffic signs and the provisions of Regulation 64, they are not placed in Israel. Their mere presence in the "traffic sign board" stems - therefore - from the need to maintain consistency between the Israeli traffic sign board and the European traffic sign board - according to the "Vienna Convention." In any case, the decision to place these traffic signs on the roads of Israel will likely involve a fundamental and special discussion. (Also, see M.M. 34).

The beginning and end of an area where educational institutions for children of preschool, elementary school, and middle school ages are located. (See M.M. 68 in the new guidelines).  
The roads as well as the paths for bicycles and pedestrians in this area are characterized by the fact that children cross these paths to get to school or back home. 1. Meaning of the markings  
The division and marking of the roadway into lanes are basic means for guiding and assisting the driver in navigating the "asphalt space," which has varying sizes and different directions of travel. This also allows for quick navigation and selection of the appropriate lane for their destination/direction of travel, thereby simplifying and reducing the variability in driving styles among different drivers and the need for frequent and confusing lane changes, which can sometimes lead to potential misunderstandings.  
For the marking to be effective and easily understood by the driver, it must be in a uniform language, simple, continuous, and hierarchical, while dividing between the different lanes and directions of travel according to their order of priority/importance, as follows:  
(a) Division that separates movements in opposite directions and delineates the internal roadway area – markings 801, 803, 805, 806.  
(b) Division that delineates the external roadway area – marking 807.  
(c) Division that separates movements of branching or weaving in the same direction – marking 808 (short and long rectangles).  
(d) Division that separates movements in the same direction (the basic division into lanes) – markings 801, 802, 804, 809.  
Maintaining marking according to a fixed and consistent hierarchy and method will lead over time.

Short and long rectangles  
(d) A division that separates movements in the same direction (the basic division into lanes) – markings 801, 802, 804, 809.  
Maintaining markings according to a fixed and consistent hierarchy and system will lead over time to faster recognition and understanding of the way the roadway is divided and improve the driver's orientation in the "asphalt space."  
For example, here are situations for establishing hierarchy through markings:  
(*) A double solid line (803) will be between lanes in opposite directions (even when there is a separation between them, as on a separated road), and will not be between lanes in the same direction for the purpose of any emphasis.  
(*) Long rectangles (808) will come after a marked traffic island (815) and will separate between those continuing in the main lanes and those turning in the outgoing lanes. Long rectangles will not be marked between the outgoing lanes themselves.

1. Meaning of the traffic signs – at work sites  
The beginning and end of a work site on the road.  
They warn of work being carried out at the site (on the road and its surroundings), when workers, materials, and tools are present in the area, involving changes and/or narrowing and/or widening of the roadway or lane, to the extent of creating an obstruction to traffic flow and safety.  
In general, the marking on the road will be in orange. The marking that differs from the regular marking (in white) is intended to illustrate to the driver that the "driving environment" is different from usual, and to prompt better alertness and attention.  
Note that sign 902 at the end of the section does not cancel the restrictions and prohibitions within it.  
2. Justifications for placement – at work sites  
A. When workers, materials, or tools are exposed to vehicles moving on the road.  
B. Part of the road is blocked to traffic.  
C. The designation of travel lanes is different from the regular designation.

Traffic islands (in various shapes), marked on the road in orange: It is forbidden to cross, stop, or park on them.

1. Meaning of the marking – at work sites  
A. Marked traffic island - in place of a built island - within the roadway that is "outside the area" for vehicles, for any purpose, including: driving, crossing, parking, and stopping.  
B. Vehicle travel will be along the sides of the marked area - as above - according to the traffic arrangements established on site.  
2. Justifications for marking – at work sites  
A. Establishing traffic arrangements at sections and intersections which require:  
- Defining marked separation areas between traffic lanes and paths.  
- Creating a continuous driving flow in a manner that can be immediately perceived by drivers, allowing them to easily adapt to this continuity.  
- Defining a hierarchy between different roads.  
- Establishing arrangements for right and/or left turns.  
B. In general, it is preferable that various types of traffic islands be physically constructed and delineated by curbstones. In such a case, they are clear and compel the driver to act accordingly. (See in this context marking 815 regarding built traffic islands). However, in places where it is not possible to construct the island for various reasons, such as: the island area being too small, lack of lighting during dark hours, difficulties for large vehicle movement, drainage obstruction, etc., or at work sites where it may be required for a defined and short period, it can be painted.

It is possible to build a traffic island for various reasons, such as: the area of the island is too small, lack of lighting during dark hours, difficulties for large vehicle movement, interference with drainage, etc., or at work sites where it may be required for a defined and short period, it can be painted, as detailed here.  
Attention is drawn to the fact that a built traffic island is preferable for various reasons over a marked traffic island, for example: the compliance level of drivers with a built traffic island is better, it can serve as a refuge for crossing pedestrians, a marked traffic island requires much more maintenance and it is not possible to place any signage on it.

1. Meaning of the signs – at work sites  
A barrier for vehicles on the road before places where various activities/work are being carried out, disrupting free movement.  
2. Justifications for placement – at work sites  
Before places where activities are being carried out, such as:  
- Road works.  
- Construction or infrastructure works.  
- Maintenance and repair activities.  
- Road marking.  
- Accident.  
- Blockage by the police for security and enforcement reasons.  
3. Guidelines for placement – at work sites  
A. The pole or horizontal arm will allow for blocking the passage for vehicles.  
B. The pole will be made of a forgiving and brittle material that will not cause damage to a vehicle that hits it – intentionally or accidentally.  
This pole is not intended to serve as a substitute for safety barriers or energy absorbers.  
C. Care should be taken to ensure good visibility of the poles and proper light reflection during dark hours.  
D. If the road is completely blocked in both directions, or if travel is only permitted in the opposite direction, a sign 401 or 402 should be placed on the barrier along with signs 205 - 204, as appropriate.  
E. If the road is partially blocked, and entry is permitted in a specific manner only, signs 213 or 215 - 214 should be placed on the barrier.

A. A large and very prominent warning device against the general landscape. This feature is achieved from the relatively large dimensions of flashing lights with strong light intensity – even against the sun. 1. Meaning of the sign – at work sites  
Indicates the existence of a stopping bay in case of emergency at a work site, at the distance specified in sign 916, which is applicable to road sections that do not have standard shoulders where one can stop in emergencies and distress.  
2. Justifications for placement at work sites  
A. In general, emergency stopping bays will be installed on non-urban roads (speed, main, and regional), on the right side of the road, when the right shoulder is 3.0 m or less. The assumption is that a shoulder of this width does not allow for safe stopping.  
B. Emergency bays will be constructed at distances of about 2.0 km, as long as there is no exit from the road, or other options or places where stopping can be performed.  
C. For this matter, as well as the various dimensions of the bay, see in the "Guidelines for Road Design, – Volume 1, Part 3.3, Table 3.2, in the section discussing the issue of shoulder width on the road, according to the number of lanes in the cross-section. (M.M. 59).

16A (a) The National Traffic Inspector may, for the purpose of  
conducting a trial, in consultation with the licensing authority and a police officer, decide to grant an exemption to the trial conductor or their representative from the provisions of one or more regulations in Chapter Two of Part B of these regulations under conditions or without conditions, as appropriate.  
(b) In making a decision under subsection (a), the National Traffic Inspector shall consider the possible impacts of conducting the trial on traffic, including the following considerations:  
(1) ensuring the safety of road users during the trial, including trial participants.  
(2) minimizing disruption to traffic flow on roads that may result from conducting the trial.  
(3) providing a response to emergency events that may occur during the trial.

By virtue of its authority under sections 68 and 88 of the Local Councils Regulations (Judea and Samaria), 1981, the Ariel Local Council enacts this bylaw:
Chapter A: Interpretation
Definitions
(Amendment 1989)
1. In this bylaw, the words and terms listed below shall have the meanings assigned to them unless expressly stated otherwise.
"Garbage" - food and kitchen scraps, peels, paper, bottles, glass shards, boxes, containers, cartons, various packaging, junk; cans, pieces of wood, planks, rags, factory waste, ash, cigarette butts, waste of all kinds, and anything that may cause uncleanliness or disorder or may pose a health risk, excluding trash and construction waste.
"Plant waste" - a picked, uprooted plant, or a fallen plant, including branches, leaves, grass, and the like.
"Sewage pit" - any structure or facility above or below ground, intended for the collection or storage of sewage, waste, or any other liquid waste, as well as any type of decay pit, infiltration pit, sewage, drainage channel for sewage, inspection chambers, or pipe for transporting sewage.
"Building" - any structure or fence, whether built of stone or constructed of concrete, mortar, iron, wood, or any other material, whether permanent or temporary, or any part thereof, generally.

"Yob" - a conduit for the transport of sewage, inspection chambers, or a pipe for the transport of sewage water.  
"Building" - any structure or fence, whether constructed of stone or concrete, mortar, iron, wood, or any other material, whether permanent or temporary, or any part thereof, including sanitation facilities and including a facility used for selling goods.  
"Animal" - any animal including a pet kept in a cage inside the house, and including dogs and cats.  
"Owner of a place of entertainment" - one or more of the following:  
1. The owner of a place of entertainment.  
2. The holder of a place of entertainment.  
3. A person managing a place of entertainment.  
4. A license holder for operating a place of entertainment.  
5. A person under whose supervision, oversight, or management entertainment takes place.  
"Property owner" - one or more of the following:  
1. The registered owner of the property, or someone entitled to be registered as the owner of the property in the registration records.  
2. The recipient of the authorization according to a decree regarding the registration of certain real estate (Judea and Samaria), to use the property.

In the years 2009 to 2011, the Ministry of Transportation and the Ministry of Housing launched five guideline books for street planning in cities, available in both digital and print editions. Since the distribution of these guideline books, they have served as a basis for multidisciplinary planning of streets in many new neighborhoods, for the rehabilitation of existing streets, and for the planning of streets and bike paths in master plans. The experience accumulated over nearly a decade since the launch has led the Ministry of Transportation to conduct a critical assessment of the guidelines to identify issues that require updating, refreshing, and emphasizing topics that have not been implemented, in relation to the manner of implementation thus far.

In recent years, a policy prioritizing the development of soft mobility infrastructure (pedestrians and bicycles) and the development of public transportation infrastructure, at the expense of private vehicles, has been promoted in most advanced countries around the world. A similar development has occurred in Israel over the past decade, which included the promotion of numerous public transportation, bicycle, and pedestrian projects, at the expense of the traffic areas of private vehicles and their parking spaces.

Private vehicles and their parking spaces. In the field of public transportation, projects for road and rail mass transit lines are being promoted, and in a few years, several new mass transit lines will operate in various metropolitan areas. Furthermore, hundreds of kilometers of exclusive public transportation lanes are planned and being constructed. There is also significant momentum in the construction of bicycle traffic routes: in the last decade, spatial plans for bike paths have been promoted, such as "Dan Bicycles" in the Dan region and "Metropen" in the Haifa metropolitan area. Additionally, the National Transportation Infrastructure Company is advancing the development of bike paths along the national road system. Hundreds of bicycle route plans are also being promoted in cities and towns. The accelerated development of transportation systems has revealed the need to update guidelines, with a strong emphasis placed on updating the guidelines related to planning solutions for bicycles in street and intersection areas. Updates to standards and regulations concerning the accessibility of urban infrastructure necessitated adjustments in the guidelines. Consequently, the Ministry of Transportation decided to promote an initiative to update the five guideline books and prepare a new edition.

The Ministry of Transportation established a broad steering committee that included professionals from various fields. The committee held nine meetings between the years 2016-2018, during which updates to the background materials and recommendations for changes and updates were presented. Final drafts of the chapters and sections were published extensively on the websites of the Ministries of Transportation and Housing in the summer of 2019. These were completely replaced in this edition, following the approval of the committee members and the Ministry of Transportation.

The innovations in the drafts mainly included:
- A new introduction to the planning methodology was integrated, along with updates to street templates following the updates in the street space book that were included in other books.
- All cross-section sections were redone, and the chapter on solutions at intersections and junctions was updated (in coordination with the bicycle traffic book).
- The guidelines for public transportation stations were updated, and a section was added regarding the types of suitable paving stones for different street segments in the pedestrian traffic book.

All of these included the replacement and updating of dozens of diagrams in the various books. In the second phase, which is now concluding, all updates were integrated into the digital edition of the five books, and they are hereby presented to you. Each page in this edition contains a note indicating whether it has been updated. Additionally, at the beginning of each book, there is a list of updates.

Streets in cities constitute, from the perspective of the Ministry of Construction and Housing, an additional and central layer in a series of planning guidelines that the ministry has been leading in recent years in the field of sustainable development and environmentally friendly planning. The street is the main component in the planning of the urban fabric. The street space is the central field of activity in urban existence, where pedestrians, cyclists, private vehicle drivers, public transportation, and various uses that define the street coexist. All these elements merge together in a wide range of activities and interactions that are the essence of life in the city. The quality of the street is the main factor determining urban quality of life. 

The planning of street space and its functions was primarily aimed at addressing the needs of private vehicles and the convenience of their drivers, while the other components and users were mainly reflected from the perspective of these needs, according to the guidelines for planning urban streets and intersections that have existed since 1983. The new guidelines in the "Green Series" in general, and the guidelines for planning streets in cities in particular, aim to balance the needs of the various users of street space, from a perspective on all the functions of the street, where most human activity occurs in the urban fabric.

"The Green Line" in general, and the guidelines for street planning in cities in particular, aim to balance the needs of the various users of the street space, with a view to all the roles of the street, where most human activity occurs in the urban fabric. 

As with the existing guidelines, the preparation of these new guidelines was a joint effort by the Ministry of Transportation and the Ministry of Construction and Housing. The new guidelines were prepared by a multidisciplinary team that included all relevant planning fields: architecture and urban planning, traffic and transportation, roads, landscape planning and development, drainage, infrastructure planning, environmental quality, and more. 

The final product of the guidelines is a result of finding the "wise balance" between sometimes conflicting interests, between different disciplines and worldviews. We believe that these guidelines will lead to the planning of new urban fabrics and the upgrading of existing urban fabrics to be better and more friendly to all "residents" of the street who use it, while achieving the right balance between a variety of street activities, traffic flow, and safety.

The years of the State of Israel, along with various trends of population dispersion and concentration, have led to the current distribution, in which 70% of the population is concentrated in four metropolitan areas that are not as densely populated as most metropolitan areas in the world. Alongside them, there are urban and rural settlements in the periphery of the country. Despite all this, the State of Israel ranks high among countries where most of the population lives in cities, and thus the street, which is the artery of life, culture, and the economy of the city, occupies a central and irreplaceable space in the daily existence of most citizens of the state. 

In light of this, and due to the special importance given to the street among all those engaged in the fields of engineering, behavioral sciences, and the humanities, an innovative system of guidelines for street planning was prepared about a decade ago. This system replaced the previous guidelines and connected the best knowledge in Israel with the best global knowledge accumulated in the fields of urban construction and architecture, combined with the transportation sector. This was done after the government's policies for land conservation and mixed-use, prioritization of public transportation, safety, and quality of life were also integrated into the books.

The urban structure, which combines residential, employment, education, culture, and commercial uses, inherently generates significant movement of diverse populations for various purposes and between different locations. The Ministry of Transportation's policy generally states that walking is the preferred means of transportation that should be encouraged as much as possible as an alternative to motorized travel, followed by a preference for public transportation and cycling. 

First and foremost, we are pedestrians before we are drivers, and therefore a whole book in the series is dedicated to guidelines for pedestrian movement in Israel, emphasizing safety aspects, as the number of accidents involving pedestrians is still high, necessitating efforts for their prevention. 

Cycling, as an alternative to car travel, has gained significant momentum in Israel over the past decade, aligning with sustainability. This policy states that the use of bicycles as a complementary and alternative means to private vehicles and public transportation is worthy of encouragement, evidenced by the increasing investment in bicycle infrastructure in Israel, alongside the understanding that investment in the safety of cyclists as vulnerable road users is essential.

Looping the Ministry of Transportation's policy for private vehicles and public transportation is worthy of encouragement, as evidenced by the increasing investment in bicycle infrastructure in Israel, alongside the understanding that safety for cyclists as vulnerable road users must be prioritized. The update of the guidelines was requested in light of the intensive use by planners and authorities, which led to the accumulation of requests, comments, recommendations, and insights for updates and additions to the guideline books. Additionally, there has been significant progress in paving infrastructure for cyclists. In light of all the above, an updated edition of the guidelines for street planning in cities is presented to you. Special thanks to all those involved in this work, to the steering committee, to the writing team of the guidelines, and to the Senior Transport Planning Division that promoted this important update. This document before you is the first and basic part of a set of guidelines for planning vehicle traffic in city streets, which will be published in the coming year in a joint package, which also includes the "Guidelines for Planning" and "Guidelines for Planning Pedestrian Traffic," "Guidelines for Planning Urban Intersections," "Bicycle Traffic in Cities."  
This set of guidelines is also part of a new series of guidelines published by the Ministry of Transportation - "The Green Series."  
This series is intended for multidisciplinary planning teams that will address the planning issue from various professional aspects.  
Guidelines for Integrated Street Planning in Residential Areas were published in this series until today, "Guidelines for Planning Roundabouts," and "Guidelines for Planning and Implementing Speed Bumps," both published in 2002.

Introduction  
Five guideline books for street planning in cities have been launched. From 2009 to 2011, the guidelines served as a basis for planning streets in many new neighborhoods, for the rehabilitation of existing streets, and for the planning of streets and bike paths in master plans. The experience accumulated from the launch date until today has led the Ministry of Transportation (and through it, the planning team) to conduct a critical assessment of the guidelines to identify issues that require updating, as well as to refresh the emphasis on topics that have not been fully integrated, in relation to the implementation so far.  
The main changes required pertain to the book dealing with bicycle traffic, and most of the implications of the current update are dedicated to this. However, it is important to take advantage of the current update edition to emphasize several principles that have been reflected in the guidelines, but whose integration has not been fully realized. The oversight is particularly pronounced when we examine the changes in the world regarding the overwhelming preference for soft mobility, primarily walking and cycling, and the reduction of private vehicle traffic spaces in the urban landscape of New York, London, Paris, Copenhagen, and even in several cities in Israel. The first chapter of the updates, presented to you here, focuses on emphasizing the principles and lessons of the years.

Purpose of the Guidelines for Street Planning in Cities
A. Objective
The basic purpose of the planning guidelines is to create a guiding framework for conducting an orderly, systematic, and clear planning process, through which the policy for developing public space can be implemented as proposed in the guideline books.
The main objective guiding the guideline book before you is to enhance and improve the public space in the city, thereby contributing to shaping the city as a place that is good to live in and as a means to promote the national goal of encouraging settlement in cities.
B. Goals
To achieve the main objective, two primary goals have been defined:
Creating safer, more efficient, accessible, and human-centered streets. •  
A new allocation of public space among the various movements in the city - while prioritizing • 
“soft movements” (pedestrians and bicycles) and public transportation at the expense of private vehicle movements.

Coordinated, multidisciplinary planning that is attentive to all street users. The guidelines are a multidisciplinary document that provides policymakers with tools for decision-making regarding the planning, establishment, and maintenance of the street space as a whole. The guidelines present the needs of different users, the policy behind the allocation of infrastructure for them, and the perception and various planning components required for them.  
These guidelines are based on the most updated guidelines and findings from countries that have already accumulated experience in developing urban space according to the new perception, while adapting them to local conditions - the legal framework and transportation planning policy in Israel.

C. Guidelines for bicycle traffic planning in cities
The book explains the rules and guidelines for integrating bicycle traffic into the urban street network of various types, so that they can move comfortably and safely alongside other street users. 
The guidelines are based on the assumption that bicycles are a mode of transportation that should be able to reach anywhere from anywhere, especially in the city but also outside of it. Therefore, the guidelines include measures for fully integrating bicycles within the urban framework and the city's transportation system. 
Bicycles are a mode of transportation, and therefore they should move separately as much as possible from pedestrians, and the level of separation from other vehicles is determined based on safety considerations. The guidelines define three levels of separation for bicycle traffic (without separation) - Level A: minimal separation - in a separate lane, Level B: bicycles on the existing road, and Level C: maximum separation - in a separate path. 
Accordingly, the guideline book includes tools for selecting and planning the most suitable arrangement for bicycles on road segments and at intersections. The book also presents the necessary traffic signs for each arrangement and establishes the standards for bicycle parking in various uses.

3.3.2 Street Movements  
The street serves as a venue for the movement of five main types of users: pedestrians, cyclists, public transportation, private vehicles, and service vehicles, as detailed below.  
A. Pedestrian Movement  
Pedestrian movement is the basic and essential component of the street and can even be the sole component (unlike an urban road). Pedestrian movement occurs along the street and must be continuous, comfortable, free of obstacles and detours, and accessible for individuals with mobility limitations. Pedestrian movement is intended to connect buildings and uses along the street and its active frontages, and therefore, complete accessibility to entrances of homes and active frontages must be maintained.  
The intensity of pedestrian movement is generally a derivative of the volume of uses along the street and their characteristics, of traffic-attracting focal points, of important locations along the street, and of the street's significance, ranking, and urban status. The greater the intensity of pedestrian movement, the more space should be allocated on the street for this movement.  
B. Bicycle Movement  
Bicycle movement is considered, along with pedestrian movement, as the "soft fabric" of the urban traffic system. The current policy is to nurture and encourage bicycle movement.

And more, yes, a wider area should be allocated on the street for this traffic.  
B. Bicycle Traffic  
Bicycle traffic is considered, along with pedestrian traffic, as the 'soft fabric' of the urban traffic system. The current policy is to nurture and encourage bicycle traffic and to prefer it over private vehicle traffic, due to its being more environmentally friendly (noise, air pollution) and its lower consumption of space within the public realm.  
The baseline for planning bicycle networks:  
Bicycles move from anywhere to anywhere in the city, whether within the roadway - in conjunction with motor vehicles or in separate lanes, and whether on special paths.  
Bicycles are vehicles, and therefore they always move separately from pedestrians. Therefore, it is necessary to avoid as much as possible allocating bicycle lanes on sidewalks - and even more so while narrowing pedestrian traffic lanes.  
Bicycles are separated from motor vehicles in direct relation to the speed and intensity of traffic. A preliminary "rule of thumb":  
30 km/h - bicycles move together with all motor vehicles on local streets at a speed of up to 50 km/h, it is appropriate to allocate a separate traffic lane for bicycles within the roadway on collector streets and streets with a speed of 50 km/h.  
On busy collector streets and roads, a separate lane should be allocated as much as possible.

In local streets with a speed limit of up to 30 km/h, it is appropriate to allocate a separate traffic lane for bicycles in collector streets and streets with a speed limit of up to 50 km/h. In high-traffic collector streets and roads, a bicycle path separated from other traffic by physical means should be allocated as much as possible. It should be emphasized that when creating a system for bicycle traffic, it is essential to allocate lanes and paths in urban roads and busy collector streets, where the fast movement of motor vehicles poses a safety threat to cyclists.

C. Public Transportation Movement
Public transportation movement includes all means of transport that carry large numbers of passengers in the city at once, such as: bus, light rail, metro, etc. (and additionally taxis that serve as an alternative to private vehicle movement). The significant differences between the components of public transportation - their dimensions, their movement characteristics, and how they interface with the street - require separate consideration for each of them. It is advisable that street planning be based on an understanding of the existing or intended public transportation components that will move along the planned street, as well as their physical and movement variables.
The assumption is that the inclusion of mass transit means in the street (such as an elevated or underground urban train) will be carried out in a special planning process based on a complete understanding of the required planning variables. Therefore, in the planning of a 'regular' street, the bus serves as the conventional public transportation component, which influences the distribution of the space in which it is intended to move.

C. Bicycle parking 
In order to promote bicycle movement, reasonable conditions must be provided for the cyclist, one of the most important of which is a place to park the bicycle as safely and protected as possible. In active streets such as those with commercial frontages, it is advisable to provide cyclists with bicycle parking spaces also within the area.

Bicycles have reasonable conditions, and one of the most important of these is a place to park the bicycles as safely and protected as possible. In active streets, such as those with commercial frontages, it is advisable to provide cyclists with bicycle parking spaces within the street area. Bicycle parking areas can be integrated either within the private vehicle parking spaces or within the sidewalk areas in active edge strips and street activity areas, or within auxiliary strips. Bicycle parking areas should not be allocated within the traffic lanes of pedestrians and motor vehicles. It is important to remember that a lack of solutions for bicycle parking along the street leads to unregulated parking, which poses functional, safety, and visual obstacles to the overall activity in the street. 

The extent of bicycle parking and its distribution along the street will be adjusted to the expected demand and will be installed in a way that encourages bicycle use. For further details on this matter, see the guidelines book for bicycle traffic planning.

Position strips (static strips)  
The static strips are designated areas intended to accommodate activities and uses that occur along the street but do not constitute movement along it, such as the placement of stationary objects - traffic signs and signals, lighting poles, barriers, street furniture, etc., vehicle parking, space for activities along an active commercial front, and so on. The strips for stationary objects can also be shared by multiple uses and activities, provided that the shared use is reasonable and efficient, for example, using a shared strip for a tree-lined avenue, lighting poles, and street furniture.  
Special spaces  
Special spaces are areas required at various sections of the street or adjacent to it, often at street intersections, for local activities or uses that are not continuous, such as a bus station, waiting space for pedestrians at crosswalks, a resting corner or other pedestrian activities, a loading and unloading area for a commercial front, space for gathering, storing, and recycling waste, and so on. Special spaces can also, under certain conditions, be shared by multiple users or be part of strips.

Rest or other activities of pedestrians, loading and unloading area for commercial fronts, space for concentration, storage, and recycling of waste, and similar. Special spaces can also, under certain conditions, be shared by several users or be part of parking strips, such as the location of bus stops within a parking zone (ear), or use of the loading and unloading area for incidental pedestrian activities and similar.

Street Portrait - The Program for the Street
Due to its importance, complexity, and the variety of roles of the street, its planning requires a fundamental thinking process to formulate a program. The purpose of the program is to determine who and what is expected to use the street, the "strength" and scope of activity of each of the users, and to define the relationship between them. 

Establishing the program for the street is a condition for making decisions that balance the different functions of the street and for setting priorities among them. The process of preparing the program is called formulating the "Street Portrait." 

The Street Portrait is a concise characterization of the planned activity in the street and its basic functions. The purpose of the 'portrait' is to allow street planners to consider the full range of considerations in the planning of the street, to intelligently address the different needs of the users in the street, and to propose solutions for the special needs of each street.

And of its basic functions. The purpose of the 'portrait' - to allow street planners to consider the full range of considerations in the design of the street, in a reasoned manner between the different needs of the users of the street, and to propose solutions to balance the special needs of each street. For the purpose of a uniform and systematic procedure in street planning in cities, a portrait will be developed for each street or segment of a street that is under planning. A street portrait will be formulated for both new streets - with reference to the concept of the street and its relative position in the planned space - and for existing streets undergoing redesign. This will be done with regard to their current functions and conditions, and with regard to their future roles and characteristics - as planned.

C. Traffic Volume in Streets  
Defining the function of the street according to the proposed classification or its sub-classifications does not explicitly dictate the volume of traffic within it. In particular, there is no fundamental restriction on the volume of traffic in collector streets intended for the passage of traffic between parts of the city. To facilitate the movement of large volumes of traffic, traffic lanes must be allocated as required within existing planning constraints; however, care must be taken to ensure clear accessibility to the side, the safety and well-being of pedestrians according to the activity on the side of that street, and to minimize environmental hazards.  
D. Traffic Function and Urban Function  
It should be emphasized that there is not necessarily a correlation between the traffic function of the street and its urban roles, and in many cases, there is even a contradiction. For example - the essence of maximizing motor traffic efficiency and the absence of urban activity along it. In contrast, a street with relatively low traffic volume can host vibrant urban activity along its length, be a local street, and even serve as a main street from an urban perspective. E. Designated speed for motor traffic  
The speed of motor traffic on the street is one of the essential factors determining the character of the street and influencing the nature of the activities within it. High speed optimizes traffic flow but may hinder urban activity on the street. Low speed allows for comfortable and safe street activity but burdens traffic efficiency.

A. Pedestrian Traffic
The intensity of pedestrian traffic is generally derived from the extent of uses along the street and their characteristics, from traffic-attracting focal points, from important points along the street, and from the street's significance, ranking, and urban status.
B. Bicycle Traffic
Bicycles are considered, along with pedestrians, as the 'soft fabric' of the urban traffic system. Bicycle traffic is separated from motor vehicle traffic in direct relation to the speed and intensity of the traffic. 
A primary "rule of thumb" (for precise details see "Guidelines for Bicycle Traffic Planning"):
At speeds of up to 30 km/h, bicycles move together with motor vehicles on local streets in the same lane.
At speeds of 30-50 km/h on collector streets, it is advisable to allocate a separate lane for bicycles.
On heavily trafficked collector streets and roads, a separated bicycle path should be allocated as much as possible, physically separated from motor vehicle traffic.

The street template is a fundamental description of the street's configuration in its planned form, as a response to the street's portrait.  
The street template represents an optimal balance between the needs of the users in the street and a final determination of the space allocated to each user.  
From Portrait to Template  
Introduction  
After the street portrait has been characterized, the planning team has a value program for the street. The consolidated portrait includes the needs of the street and its urban and traffic roles, the users who will operate in the street and their relationships, structural and visual principles, and the definition of the basic infrastructure system. The portrait also includes the anchors of the portrait - rigid physical or planning dictates that serve as starting points for determining the street template.  
Determining the final template of the street - translating the values of the portrait into final quantities and dimensions, requires delving into the planning guidelines of each of the street components, as detailed in the relevant guideline books - guidelines for pedestrian movement, guidelines for bicycle movement, guidelines for motor vehicle movement, public transportation guidelines, and so on, as well as existing guidelines for solutions for specific streets such as traffic calming areas and integrated streets, as described in the diagram.  
Collecting the required measurements for each of the

Bicycle traffic guidelines, motor vehicle traffic guidelines, public transportation guidelines, and similar, as well as existing guidelines for solutions for specific streets, such as in traffic calming areas and mixed-use streets, as described in the diagram. Collecting the required dimensions for each of the uses is a condition for creating the street template, but the total dimensions obtained are not necessarily the final product of the street template. It is likely that in many cases the total dimensions obtained will contradict the principles or anchors established in the process of formulating the profile - for example, when the desired cross-section width exceeds the right-of-way, or when it contradicts fixed elements in the street (such as existing street trees). In such cases, it is necessary to re-examine the characteristics of the profile, the principles formulated, and the defined anchors, and to return to the specific guideline books to explore additional alternatives. 

It is clear, therefore, that the process of transitioning from profile to template is a iterative process that will continue until the right and optimal balance for the specific street is found. The street template is an optimal balance between the dimensions required for each component, according to the priorities of the street and its spatial limitations.

C. Description of the street intersections  
The design of the intersection will largely reflect how to connect the different strips in the streets meeting at the intersection. By its very nature, the intersection becomes an urban focal point, but also a point of vulnerability - both operationally and safety-wise. Therefore, the intersection will be designed separately according to a system of considerations and rules formulated for urban intersection design. This process also includes the formulation of a profile and template for the intersection, described in a separate book within the system - "Guidelines for Urban Intersection Design."

From this stage, a balancing process takes place in practice - a methodical iterative process of the stages of formulating the template in a manner that is as faithful as possible to the priorities, principles, and anchors established in the street profile.

Balancing the Space  
The optimal situation in which sufficient space can be allocated to each user in the street for their activity is not only impractical but largely undesirable. A clear example of this is the desire to provide a satisfactory solution for motor traffic during peak hours, a situation that creates waste of space throughout the day and even poses safety risks - an excess of traffic lanes that encourages fast driving on one hand, and careless crossing on the other hand.  
The need to save space and optimize its use requires street planners to deal with compromises and informed concessions, which can be made through the following means:  
- Informed choice to allocate in the street a reduction in the number of users that require space allocation for their activities.

The use of it requires street planners to deal with compromises and informed concessions, which can be made through the following means:
- Informed choice to allocate space on the street by reducing the number of users that require space for their activities and avoiding providing space for other users. Examples include completely giving up a parking lane on narrow streets, giving up a lane for stationary objects on one side of the street, and relinquishing motorized traffic to grant exclusivity to pedestrians on narrow streets (pedestrian zones).
- Minimizing the dimensions of the planned lanes to the reasonable minimum, even at the expense of operational efficiency. Examples include narrowing motor vehicle lanes or giving up part of the traffic lanes, which reduces traffic efficiency; relinquishing a travel direction (one-way traffic only); reducing the dimensions of the lane designated for infrastructure that allows for tree planting along the street; allocating a minimal width below the width of the pedestrian lane in a way that hinders their movement, and so on.
- Creating shared spaces for multiple users, even in a way that compromises the service level of the street. Examples include a shared traffic lane for private vehicles and public transportation (a common practice in most urban areas).

In a way that burdens their movement and similar issues. - Creating shared spaces for multiple users, also in a manner that compromises the sharing of spaces at the street service level. Examples - a shared traffic lane for private vehicles and public transportation (a common means in most streets); a shared traffic lane for motor vehicles and cyclists (usually requires a speed limit of 30 km/h); a shared strip for stationary objects and parking, at the cost of impacting the number of parking spaces, the number of trees, signage, and similar elements.

Templates for Existing Narrow Streets  
General Principles  
A large part of the planning tasks for urban streets in the coming years is expected to be within the existing fabric of cities as part of rehabilitation, infrastructure renewal, urban renewal, and similar initiatives. Planning within a rigid space, characterized by modest dimensions that define a large part of our streets, intensifies the competition among different space users for the allocation of space to their needs and requires delicate, meticulous, and rigorous 'tuning' to achieve an appropriate balance.  
Engagement in limited spaces necessitates compromises on minimal dimensions regarding the standards required for street users' activities, and even specific deviations that are unacceptable when planning new streets.  
Therefore, the proposed templates for existing narrow streets have been separated from those proposed for new streets. In general, variables presented for existing streets should not be adopted for new streets, except in extreme cases. For example, a one-way street should not be planned as a solution for a new street.  
Minimal Dimensions

Proposals for Streets  
In general, variables presented for existing streets should not be adopted for new streets described in section 5.3, except in extreme cases. For example, a one-way street should not be planned as a solution for a new street.  
Minimum dimensions for strips in narrow streets:  
- The minimum width for a walking strip is 130 cm. The narrowing of the walking strip beyond this measurement is only permitted in specific cases, such as around temporary obstacles, up to 110 cm.  
- The minimum side strip for the installation of stationary objects adjacent to the side is 30 cm for thin objects like signposts and signage, or 40-50 cm for local protrusions of the built side or vegetation extending from the side line.  
- In cases of allocating a narrow side strip of 30 cm, an alternative solution must be provided for the installation of side objects such as infrastructure cabinets, etc.  
- The minimum width for a helper strip for the installation of thin stationary objects is 50 cm (referring to the distance of the object from the curb edge and from the walking strip).  
- The minimum width of a helper strip for planting trees is approximately 120 cm.

Introduction
In addition to the movements and activities occurring on the street, there are various stationary objects on the street that serve as infrastructure for street users and consumers along the street. This infrastructure is a fundamental component of the street's structure and function, enabling life and activity in the city. Environmental infrastructures, along with the use of environmental planning methods for the street, allow for the reduction of nuisances and environmental hazards and improve urban quality of life. 
However, the presence of stationary objects on the street adds an additional burden to the street space and often creates difficulties for movement and activities taking place there. Proper location and execution of the various infrastructures, along with the use of environmental planning methods, will help reduce conflicts with street users, integrate stationary objects more effectively into the street landscape, and maintain a suitable urban environmental quality and sustainable development. 
Therefore, the policy for the installation of objects in the planned street will be determined as part of shaping the street profile and will be subject to the principles guiding the street planning and the street template, as detailed in chapters 3-5, primarily focusing on establishing a priority order among the various users and needs on the street.

The policy for the installation of objects in the street, planned as part of shaping the street profile, will be subject to the principles guiding the design of the street and the street template (as detailed in chapters 3-5). The main focus is to establish a priority order among the various users and needs in the street (including infrastructure and stationary objects) and to ensure a balanced and controlled distribution of space according to these priorities.

The basic principles for the installation of stationary objects in the street are:
- Only infrastructure components that are required to be present in the street will be installed.
- The street's edge will be positioned as much as possible within the boundary. For example: junction boxes, pillars, etc.
- Above the street level, only infrastructure components that are required to be above ground will be installed. Other infrastructure components will be underground.
- Above-ground components will only be installed in designated strips within the street (e.g., in the auxiliary strip, in the boundary strip, in separators).
- The installation of underground infrastructure will be avoided as much as possible, and it will be allowed across the entire width of the street.
- The installation of underground infrastructure should not interfere with street activity and its characteristics (for example: striving to maintain a strip free of infrastructure for tree planting).

For further details regarding above-ground and underground infrastructure in the street, see Chapter 6 "Objects and Vegetation."

Introduction  
The guidelines document for streets in cities establishes sustainable planning principles, fundamentally shifting the priority given in urban street planning to private motor vehicles, towards additional modes of transport such as pedestrians, cyclists, and public transportation. The definition of these new priorities has significant environmental implications related to reducing energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and other environmental aspects.  
The main objectives of sustainable development in streets are:  
- Reducing energy consumption;  
- Reducing the consumption of natural resources;  
- Minimizing negative environmental impacts;  
- Maintaining a good and healthy urban quality of life;  
- Ensuring sustainable development aspects during the implementation stages.  
This chapter addresses two main areas in street planning:  
A. Planning considerations focused on environmental issues that impact the quality of the urban environment.  
B. Aspects of sustainable planning and development that must be taken into account during the planning and execution stages of the street.

Vegetation is attributed with two positive effects regarding the reduction of air pollution: 
1. The filtering effect - vegetation acts as a dust collector that helps filter it out. 
2. The shielding effect - vegetation redirects wind and dust upwards, thereby reducing concentrations at ground level. 
The filtering capacity of vegetation increases as a function of leaf area per unit of ground area, and therefore the effectiveness of vegetation as a dust collector is primarily achieved through broadleaf and evergreen trees, shrubs, and grass.

Detention and Preservation of Stormwater  
Optimal management of stormwater in the street refers to two aspects:  
A. Detention of stormwater to prevent its arrival in large peaks (in quantity and time) to regional systems.  
B. Infiltration of stormwater into groundwater reservoirs by directing it to permeable areas and/or using permeable materials in the street.  
Detailed guidelines for optimal stormwater management are presented in the "Guide to the Preservation of Surface Stormwater" published by the Ministry of Housing.  
Environmental Compensation  
Environmental compensation is a common principle in environmental planning. This means in urban street planning that if the resulting street design includes problematic environmental quality and a high level of nuisance, it is possible to propose environmental compensation in another area, which will be included in the street design and improve the overall picture. For example, in a planned street where high environmental noise is present, compensation for the nuisance can be provided by allocating space and particularly high-quality design of vegetation to act as a barrier between traffic and noise receptors. In this way, the compensation for noise nuisances in the street will be an improvement in the experience of the user in the street.

In recent years, we have witnessed intensive development of infrastructure in general, and transportation infrastructure in particular. This development, which includes roads, public transportation systems, bicycle and pedestrian systems, encompasses all road networks, including urban roads. The development efforts that create infrastructure work areas, combined with the multitude of entities involved in the matter, necessitate, among other things, clear definitions regarding special and changing traffic arrangements during work, warning measures, signage, marking, and the placement of devices and materials at work sites of various types. 

These traffic arrangements, although temporary in terms of their duration of operation, are of great importance, both in terms of traffic flow and safety. This is due to the special and sometimes forced conditions that arise at work sites during the various stages of execution.

The document presented here, "Guidelines for Temporary Traffic Arrangements at Urban Work Sites," was prepared and written by a team of experts, with the writing process accompanied by a broad steering committee that included representatives from government ministries, enforcement authorities, local authorities, and representatives from private planning offices. The aim was to create a comprehensive and accurate guidelines document as much as possible. This document replaces the "Guidelines for the Protection of Road Users on Urban Roads – 1993" and is part of a series of guidelines for traffic arrangements at work sites (alongside guidelines on this topic for intercity roads and for railway crossings, which, due to their significant differences in characteristics from urban roads, warrant separate consideration). 

All existing guideline documents, which were prepared and written in the format of "example solutions" for various types and situations arising during work execution, and for different stages during the process, attempted to cover all situations through examples. In contrast, and in light of past experience which shows that reality, especially in the urban space, presents diverse and complex situations that cannot be predicted in advance, the new guidelines include principles, rules, criteria, and any other means that will provide the authority and its planner the ability to "build and assemble."

This way, planners and the local traffic authority will be able to determine the optimal arrangement according to the local conditions, rather than necessarily choosing from a catalog of examples.

In addition to the above, these guidelines emphasize the importance of adhering to issues of flow and safety for all road users, while incorporating principles of ergonomics, particularly regarding accessibility for pedestrians and people with disabilities. This is in light of the fact that at work sites there is an increased risk for the latter, who are required to contend with a right of way that, in addition to its regular function, also serves for the movement and operation of equipment, workers, materials, and various unusual and sometimes forced situations, unlike what is typical in areas not currently used for work.

On this occasion, I would like to thank all the parties who participated in writing the document, both from within the office and outside of it, and especially Engineer Irit Shperber, under whose leadership most of the document was written while she served as the Director of the Senior Transportation Planning Division and as the Chair of the Steering Committee for its writing. I sincerely hope that these guidelines will bring clarity to the establishment of temporary traffic arrangements at urban work sites, as well as improve the safety of all road users in these areas, particularly for the most vulnerable road users.

Chapter 1 - Introduction 
1.1 Background 
The State of Israel is facing a new era in which the existing transportation and infrastructure systems are on the verge of exhaustion. In the metropolitan areas of Jerusalem, Tel Aviv, and Haifa, there is a surge in the development of public transportation infrastructure: the light rail in Jerusalem, the metropolitan bus system in Haifa, and the light rail lines in the Gush Dan area. The satellite cities of the metropolitan areas are also growing, and in all cities, there is development of new basic infrastructure such as main sewage lines, drainage conduits, and water and electricity pipelines to meet the demands of natural population growth. 
In addition to these infrastructures, there are urban renewal projects in older neighborhoods and street upgrades, in response to the demand arising from population growth in these cities. Over the years, dedicated infrastructures have been developed for public transportation systems above and below ground, including bus public transport, integrated terminals, ride-sharing arrangements, bike paths, walking strips, and the implementation of accessibility arrangements - with additional dedicated infrastructures expected.

A significant difference between these guidelines and the "Guidelines for Traffic Management at Work Sites on Urban Roads" from the 1990s (referred to as "the guide") is that the previous booklet included a series of "principle traffic management plans" (referred to as "diagrams") that were supposed to be "representative plans" for several types of common works. In reality, it turned out that the number of work types increased and became more diverse, so the "diagrams" no longer suited (to say the least) the actual works on the ground, creating a need for adjustments and improvisations. These guidelines are updated in relation to the traffic sign table, regulations, and guidelines for placing traffic signs, and in relation to traffic and safety devices approved by the inter-ministerial committee. These new guidelines incorporate, as mentioned, a new planning approach that has shifted from a 'guide' format to a 'guidelines for the planner' format, reflecting contemporary planning aspects that align with the urban space in the context of all road users: pedestrians, public transport, cyclists, and private vehicles, who need protection from the nuisances of the works, while maintaining and ensuring safety aspects.

For example, in the aspect of public transportation, the guidelines include, for the first time, extensive references and professional tools to address traffic arrangements that have developed in recent years, such as bus rapid transit (BRT) systems, left-turn bus lanes, traffic signal priority, and light rail construction, including tunneling and earthworks that require the transportation of materials to and from the site. These guidelines also address the planning of temporary traffic arrangements for roundabouts and multi-lane intersections. Chapter 2 – Design Principles  
Guidelines for Planning Temporary Traffic Arrangements at Urban Work Sites  
Chapter 2 - Design Principles  
2.1 Background  
This chapter presents the geometric traffic planning principles for designing temporary traffic arrangements. When carrying out infrastructure work in urban areas, consideration must be given to the nature of the area where the activity is taking place. It is necessary to plan in a way that maintains pedestrian and cycling routes, alongside preserving capacity and service levels on travel lanes.  
Short-term work in residential neighborhoods will usually be carried out during the day, while in business and commercial areas, it will be conducted at night, in order to minimize disruption to normal life.  
Carrying out work at night is subject to the regulations for preventing nuisances – noise prevention – and requires special permits that are granted sparingly by the heads of local authorities.

As a preliminary action for planning, it is necessary to characterize the existing situation:
A. Typical cross-section, on-street parking, accessibility and entrances to buildings along the street, existing nuisances on the street, various road users, traffic volumes and composition, street functionality during peak hours, attraction/creation points, and hours of operation.
B. The type of planned works - required width of work equipment, required depth of excavations, and method of execution (open excavation, excavation and covering, work with shoring, etc.). The width of the working tools in a deployed state, such as large cranes, often dictates the width of the activity area. This planning parameter has a direct impact on the design of the work site and the remaining available width for road users. The planning will maintain the needs of users and minimize the area allocated for the work site.
C. The associated impacts of the works: some works have an associated impact beyond the site, for example - performing works that include significant excavation volumes, piling excess soil may create a slide beyond the activity area, including blocking sidewalks/parking lanes and narrowing travel lanes. The removal of excavation excess will also be done with minimal disruption to the environment and users, and without positioning a truck next to the excavation area.

Create a diversion beyond the area of activity, including blocking sidewalks/parking lanes and narrowing travel lanes. The removal of excavation excess will also be done with minimal disruption to the environment and users, and without positioning a truck next to the excavation area that would necessitate closing an additional travel lane. Another example is the deployment of the foundation legs of a crane, which requires obtaining a lifting plan that shows the location of the crane positioning and the width of the foundation leg deployment. The work plans can provide insights into the site's needs for the various works.

2.1.1 Work Site Planning  
The work site organization plan from a safety perspective is defined in the Safety Regulations for Construction Work, 1988.  
Safety requirements for interfaces between work sites and adjacent roads are found in Chapter 9 of the guidelines (highlights and special cases).  
The contractor's organization area is required in cases of short-term and long-term work, in infrastructure and development work, and in engineering construction work. In some cases, construction materials are stored in parking bays or on sidewalks, partially narrowing them. Sometimes these construction materials remain on site for several days and require fencing and separation from the built environment, along with appropriate traffic arrangements.
