2.2.2 Lane Balancing and Preservation of Walking/Cycling Paths  
In general, at work sites in urban areas, sidewalks and walking paths should be kept open on both sides of the road, especially during prolonged works. For short-term works, it is permissible to block the walking paths of pedestrians*, but it is recommended to place a traffic sign/guide in the blocking areas. The placement of the traffic sign/guide is recommended to ensure the safe passage of pedestrians in a controlled manner near engineering machinery.  
Blocking sidewalks and bike paths is not allowed near public institutions in general and schools in particular at the beginning and end of operating hours.  
Blocking sidewalks and bike paths is sometimes not feasible on urban roads with high traffic volumes and actual travel speeds exceeding 50 km/h. Transferring bicycle or pedestrian traffic from one side of the road to the other creates a risk and a lack of willingness to comply on the part of pedestrians.  
In ongoing works, sidewalks for pedestrians and bike paths should be preserved on both sides of the road. In wide streets and during peak hours, there is low willingness among pedestrians and cyclists to move to opposite sidewalks due to heavy traffic congestion and the difficulty of crossing at unregulated intersections or, alternatively, due to long waiting times at traffic signals.

Roadway.  
In wide streets and during peak hours, there is low willingness among pedestrians and cyclists to move to the opposite sidewalks due to heavy traffic congestion and the difficulty of crossing at unregulated intersections or, alternatively, due to long waiting times at regulated intersections (due to cycle length).  
In cases of sidewalk blockage, the blockage should be planned in a location that allows pedestrians and cyclists to access alternative routes that enable comfortable and uninterrupted passage. Blocking a sidewalk in the middle of a segment is undesirable since pedestrians and cyclists will always prefer the shortest route, even if it requires walking in the travel lane.  
Sometimes, street closures are required during construction work. The planner's awareness of different execution methods will greatly influence traffic arrangements. For example, there are casting methods that allow concrete to be transported over distances that enable the placement of the pump in a location where travel lanes do not need to be blocked.  
When the available roadway allows for a minimum lane width of 2.75 m, traffic can be directed in a "stop and go" format. Otherwise, alternative options should be examined, and only if there is no choice should the street be closed to traffic and redirected to a detour.

Traffic can be redirected in a "stop and go" format for 5 meters. Otherwise, alternative options should be examined, and only if there is no choice should the street be closed to traffic and redirected to a detour.

2.2.4 Maximum Allowed Speed  
The basic design policy of a work site is based on the concept that if there is no need to reduce the maximum allowed speed (MAS), it should not be reduced. The goal is to strive for a balance between design speed, maximum allowed speed, and operational speed (the speed at which drivers are observed traveling under free flow conditions). The systemic view of managing travel speeds at the work site will determine the "Target Speed" (the desired travel speed for a defined type of road). The target speeds for different types of work are determined based on a broad consideration mechanism, primarily focused on maintaining mobility and ensuring the safety of road users.  
The maximum allowed speed in the work area will be determined based on the maximum allowed speed prior to the commencement of work. In these guidelines, the maximum allowed speed refers to the maximum allowed speed that exists before the work begins unless stated otherwise, and the speed due to the work is derived from it.  
From the perspective of road users, this is a speed that is appropriate for traveling on a specific road, which the design of the road and its surroundings are supposed to convey. The aspiration is that despite lane narrowing (when it occurs), most vehicles will travel freely at a speed close to the speed.

The road user, this is a speed that is suitable for traveling on a specific road, which the road design and its surroundings are supposed to convey. The aspiration is that despite lane narrowing (when it is implemented), most vehicles will travel freely at a speed close to the designated speed.

2.2.5 Determining Operating Hours  
The determination of operating hours within the built environment is often influenced by the policy of the local authority and by the [Prevention of Nuisances Law, 1961 and the regulations for preventing nuisances] – [Noise Prevention, 1992].  
Carrying out work during lighting hours (night) requires obtaining approval from the head of the local authority for deviations from the provisions of the law and regulations.  
Nighttime work is met with dissatisfaction from residents due to the disruption of normal life. Conducting work during the day has advantages in residential neighborhoods. Parking is often available on one-way or multi-lane roads.

2.3.2 Minimum Width for Pedestrian Passage  
The planning of pedestrian movement at urban construction sites must be done with the recognition that the urban space is a pedestrian area, and therefore it is necessary to ensure safe and comfortable passage for pedestrians.  
The walking route must be arranged during the execution of the work, even at the cost of creating localized disruptions in the roadway used for motor vehicles.  
The extent of pedestrian activity on the street is a significant parameter in determining the type of solution. There is a basic distinction between providing solutions for pedestrians on local roads where pedestrian presence is often sparse, compared to work being carried out on streets with commercial fronts in the city center.  
The work site should be characterized in relation to the extent of pedestrian activity and in relation to the adjacent land uses such as: schools and hospitals, rehabilitation institutions, and nursing homes.  
The maximum period is examined according to the stage of execution, meaning, for development work lasting 3 years and based on 3 stages of execution each lasting one year, it is required to plan the temporary traffic arrangements and the walking strip while adhering to the requirements of the planning guidelines and standard 1918, for a permanent arrangement.

2.3.5.3      Work on Sidewalks / Paths / Bicycle Lanes  
When carrying out any work, the width of the work site is the same as the width of the sidewalk. For this reason, performing work on the sidewalk requires directing pedestrians to an alternative sidewalk. This direction will be given at the last decision point that allows for a transition to an alternative sidewalk.  
Blocking a path / bicycle lane or sidewalk in the middle of the section is undesirable, as in such situations, pedestrians may bypass the work site through the travel lanes. Pedestrians and cyclists will generally choose the shortest route (naturally). For this reason, an alternative (detour) route must be arranged alongside the site without directing pedestrians to the opposite sidewalk. This solution is essential on two-lane roads, where pedestrians, in most cases, will not cross to the opposite sidewalk due to crossing distances and the need to return and cross the road again later.  
In urban areas, there is continuity of activity along the sides, such as businesses, residences, etc. Directing pedestrians to the opposite sidewalk can create situations where pedestrians and cyclists are forced to turn back to reach their destination.  
For all the reasons mentioned above, a passage for pedestrians must be created alongside the work site. Transitioning to the opposite sidewalk will be, as

The sidewalk across the street can create situations where pedestrians and cyclists are forced to turn back to reach their destination. For all the reasons mentioned above, a pedestrian crossing should be created on the side of the work site. Transferring to the sidewalk across the street will, as stated, be the last option to choose. Similarly, when work is being carried out along bike paths and lanes, they need to be blocked due to their width. In such cases, an appropriate solution must be provided for cyclists to avoid diverting them from their intended destination. A separation between motorized traffic and pedestrian movement must be implemented, depending on the speed of the road and the duration of the work. If the duration of the work is short (up to 12 hours) and the speed of travel is not high (30 km/h), light fencing is sufficient for separation. If the speed of travel is high or the duration of the work is long, it is necessary to install an appropriate safety railing. *See Figure 4.6 in Chapter 4 for these guidelines.

2.3.6 Work at Intersections  
Work at intersections is different in nature from work on a road segment, as it affects multiple directions of travel simultaneously. Blocking intersections is only permissible in cases where there are available detours. Signage and guidance for drivers along the route is required, including notification signs for turning vehicles at intersections along the route.  
In cases where partial closure of the intersection is necessary, lane closures or narrowing should be implemented before the point where turning lanes open, according to the principle of lane closures on a road segment. The area of the intersection is considered from the point where turning lanes open or, in the absence of turning lanes, from a measured distance of 12 meters from the tangent to the radius of the intersection (the point where the radius of the curb stones begins). Nevertheless, work near the intersection can affect traffic arrangements at the intersection and may sometimes require prior attention and signage before the turn.

2.3.6.2 Signalized Intersections  
Signalized intersections characterize urban roads with high traffic volumes, which justified the installation of traffic signals at the intersections originally. At each signalized intersection, there is also a system of traffic signs at the secondary approaches that allows the intersections to function even in the event of a traffic signal failure. This point is important, as most work is carried out during off-peak hours, when the intersection can still function and manage traffic volume even without a traffic signal.

For night work at a signalized intersection - if the work is being carried out on the traffic lanes before the intersection and it has been decided to cancel the outgoing traffic from these lanes, it is necessary to ensure the appropriate covering of the traffic lights so that a green light does not continue to be given for a specific movement that has been prohibited by a sign during the work.

In principle, it is necessary to maintain the existing signage system at intersections (for example, it is not customary to replace sign 301 with sign 302). During the execution of the works, the temporary signage deployed serves as an additional warning to drivers to exercise caution. 

The stop lines and turning locations can only be moved to a point where the green matrix does not change. 

Intermittent guidance works at the intersection can be carried out along the approaches to the intersection, where in such cases a guidance point is required at each approach. For ongoing works, the placement of movable traffic lights can be considered.

2.5 Traffic Diversions  
Definition: Traffic diversion - when there is a shift of a work site, but the travel continues on the same route.  
Bypass - when an alternative travel route is used.

2.5.1 Traffic Diversions in Travel Lanes  
Traffic diversions in a travel lane are a component of traffic planning that has safety aspects. In these sections, the driver is diverted from the familiar continuous travel path and is required to adjust their speed to the actual conditions, even though it is a relatively short section.  
The diversion should be planned according to the street planning guidelines in cities, motor vehicle traffic, Chapter 4, geometric design of elements along urban streets.  
In some cases, the route of the bypass is derived from the options created by long execution phases. As a result, it is not practically possible to determine radii and other design details in accordance with the guidelines. Nevertheless, during traffic diversions for short-term work, actual travel speeds are very low, as traffic is conducted in a significantly moderated manner, and even under very constrained conditions (for example, resurfacing work).

2.6.1.4    Street or Road Closure Sign  
Notification of a street or road closure shall be on one of two signs: one with the message in Hebrew and English, and the other with the message in Hebrew and Arabic, according to the target population.  
The content of the road closure notification sign will include several components:  
A. The street or road where the closure will take place: only the name of the street or road will be used.  
B. The section of the street or road that will be closed: it will be specified between the names of intersections that define the section, with a hyphen between them.  
C. The duration of the closure can be one of the following options:  
- For several days during specific hours: it will be indicated by the start date of the closure and the end date of the closure on one line, and the hours of closure on the second line.  
- For several days throughout the entire day: it will be indicated by the start date of the closure and the end date of the closure only.  
- For a specific day: it will be indicated as "on" followed by the closure date.  
- The date will be specified using day, month, and year, separated by a dot. The hours will be indicated in a 24-hour clock format.  
- Unlike directional signs, the use of a hyphen will be done by maintaining a space of the height of the letter before and after it (and not 0.3 of the letter height).

2.6.1.9 Signage for Detours  
The term detour will be used instead of the term alternative travel route, while when there is a diversion of the work site but travel remains on the same route, the term detour will be replaced with the term diversion.  
When streets are blocked (fully or partially), it is necessary to direct road users to alternative routes. Blocking routes is sometimes required for short-term activities, such as grinding and resurfacing work and public events like competitions or parades. In these works, the blockage is for a short period, usually just a few hours. The main handling of the blockage is carried out through notifications and advance publication, using media and distributing information sheets to residents. The signage deployed in these cases is relatively limited and will be based on basic signage and traffic signs in the blocked area.  
When there is an intention for an alternative route, selective access control for street residents should be allowed in certain cases and at specific times.  
In general, the preference will be to carry out the work at night, times when public transportation is usually less crowded, but each area throughout the city has its own unique characteristics. For example: in industrial areas, blocking traffic routes will be prioritized at night, but in residential neighborhoods, blockages at night are difficult due to demand.

Leisure areas vary in nature, as in these cases, the permissible hours for conducting work are very limited since these areas are usually very active at all hours of the day.

2.9 Fences, Safety Barriers, and Additional Devices  
Introduction  
The need for protection in urban areas arises from the fact that construction sites on urban roads are located near pedestrian, bicycle, and other road users, and sometimes even affect their movement.  
Marking or delineating a work area is intended to signal and separate the area of activity from road users and to protect them from the dangers present in the work area. The marking or delineation can be done between the site and the active travel lanes or between the site and the sidewalk/bicycle path.  
The marking or delineation highlights the location of the work and creates a physical barrier that helps to emphasize the location of the site and to alert about the location of work within or near the road.

Image 2.9.1: Light rail construction site, NTA. Transparent windows for viewing the work site.  
2.9.1 Types of various safety devices  
For short-term work, the type of safety device will be implemented using cones (sign 931) and/or vertical signs (sign 930) and/or a mobile fence (which can be made of plastic or metal – according to the approved specification) that highlights the work and protects passing pedestrians.

Table 2.9.1: Type of safety device required according to the characteristics of the type of work and duration of work  
Notes for Table 2.9.1  
A. Low-risk work includes tasks that do not pose a real risk to road users passing nearby, such as: painting, scrubbing/paving, maintenance of broken sidewalk paving, unloading/loading (not performed above road users), gardening, placing tools for static work, dismantling coverings, paving sidewalks, maintenance of existing systems.  
B. High-risk work includes tasks that pose a real risk to road users if they pass nearby (beyond the area defined by safety devices), such as infrastructure work: laying utility lines, sewage, electricity, drainage, earthworks, castings, lifting work.  
C. Fencing to mark a work site is defined as: light fencing, cones, 930/932.  
D. Fencing to delineate the work site is defined as: guardrails, rigid sealed metal at a height of 2 meters, "heavy" fences at a height of 2 meters.

The site fencing is required to withstand wind loads and ensure that pedestrians nearby are not exposed to hazards such as nails, protruding metal, and the like. When installing the fencing, it is necessary to allow for visibility of existing signs and signage.

2.9.3) Fencing of Work Sites on Sidewalks and Along Traffic Lanes (Ongoing Works)  
Prolonged works require the installation of sturdy and permanent fencing, such as a solid fence / metal fence with a height of 2 meters.  
1. As a general guideline, if it is possible to choose the location of the work site, preference should be given to placing the work site in a parking lane rather than on the sidewalk.  
2. The plan for temporary traffic arrangements will include all necessary measures specified in section 2.3, to ensure the safety of pedestrians.

In the case of work that requires temporary entry and exit that do not require signage, such as the opening and closing of fencing for the purpose of bringing in equipment or the entry and exit of workers, the site fencing will be carried out using two-meter-high steel mesh fences, which will be placed on weighted bases. In cases where a field of vision is required, such as at the entry and exit of the work site, a transparent fence should be used. The location of the entry and exit should also be considered in relation to nearby intersections and bike paths. When the work site borders travel lanes, the justification for placing vehicle safety barriers will be made according to the guidelines for the selection and placement of safety barriers for temporary applications. The arrangement of the fence will be planned at a safety distance of 0.6 meters from the travel lanes. 3.1 Existing Street Lighting  
Traffic arrangements at work sites in cities must include lighting for safety reasons in accordance with the applicable guidelines for placing lighting on roads.  
The existing road lighting sometimes serves as a basis for lighting at the site, even when work is being carried out. To rely on it, it must be integrated and marked in the plans; the road lighting must be functional and comply with all relevant guidelines before the work begins.  
3.2 Lighting at Temporary Work Sites on Urban Roads  
On roads and streets where temporary traffic arrangements exist, road lighting should be planned according to the "Guidelines for Planning Road Lighting" in effect, and the lighting intensity should comply with the guidelines.  
• Road lighting must be arranged at every work site.  
• The guidelines for planning road lighting define the required intensity of road lighting in urban areas.  
• If there is a desire to rely on the existing street lighting, its functionality must be checked before the work begins and marked in the temporary traffic arrangements.  
• The lighting intensity should be examined according to the guidelines in the area of the site before the activity begins and continuously on a weekly basis.

If there is a desire to rely on the existing street lighting, its condition must be checked before the start of the work and marked with temporary signs. 
• The intensity of the lighting should be examined according to the guidelines in the area of the site before the start of the activity and on an ongoing basis every week (visual inspection). 
• In the absence of existing street lighting on an urban road where work is required, street lighting must be installed at all stages of execution, with an intensity that meets the requirements of the guidelines for street lighting design. 
• The location of lighting poles on an urban road will be adjusted to the components of the cross-section as will be described later.

3.3 Differences in Typical Lighting Intensities in Work Areas  
At every site where work is conducted at night, there will be a lighting consultant as part of the work team, whose role is to plan the road lighting on the roads while considering various factors that may affect the work environment, such as:

- Various work sites alongside the road that have their own lighting means for the work, even in proximity to active travel lanes.  
The lighting at the site must comply with the standard lighting level according to the road level and not just the existing lighting level. This is because the traffic arrangements at a work site are forced, and it is necessary to compensate for this through standard lighting.

4.1 Pedestrian Safety in Temporary Traffic Arrangements  
Temporary traffic arrangements must be designed to maintain the movements of pedestrians, cyclists, and public transportation activities in their regular form, without compromising their level of service and physical conditions. This may come at the expense of private vehicle traffic.  
Similarly, safety aspects should be prioritized over capacity and service level for motor vehicles. One of the primary measures for safety in traffic arrangements will include, among other things, a significant and gradual reduction of the speed limit, actual travel speed, reduction in the number of lanes, and the establishment of enforced geometry that requires careful and controlled driving.  
Sidewalks for pedestrian movements should protect them from disruptions caused by forced street conditions and nearby construction work. Accordingly, a walking strip should be reserved for pedestrians, with an appropriate width according to Table 2.3.6, free of objects, obstacles, and facilities in general, and specifically due to the construction work.

In short-term work (lasting from 30 minutes to 12 hours, conducted on a daily basis and with the site being closed at the end of the activity), pedestrian access to the road must be prevented due to sidewalk blockage. In ongoing work, it is possible to direct pedestrians to the road using a temporary ramp or another means, provided there is a separation from the traffic lanes. The walking strip must be maintained even at the expense of private vehicle parking spaces, and physical barriers should be used to prevent vehicle parking on the sidewalk, due to the impact on the walking area. A temporary traffic arrangement that allows shared movement (between pedestrians and cyclists) is not permitted, even in cases where a nearby bike path has been canceled. Such a case will only be allowed if the sidewalk is wide enough to allocate a lane or path for bicycles.

7.1 Establishing Traffic Arrangements at a Work Site through a Permit  
The duties and powers of the local traffic authority are detailed in Regulation 18 of the Traffic Regulations, 1961.  
In this context, the local traffic authority is obligated to establish appropriate traffic arrangements at each site, including the approval and documentation process, while adhering to the provisions and rules set forth in Regulation 18. The duties of the traffic authority cannot be transferred to another entity, thus it must also maintain supervision and control as will be presented in the following chapters.  
The general rule is that a local traffic authority may approve temporary traffic arrangements according to Regulation 18 (a) and/or 18 (e), depending on the nature of the work and the duration it will take place.  
If the local traffic authority has received an extension of powers according to Regulation 18 (b), it may also approve temporary traffic arrangements under this regulation.

In principle, despite the purpose of Regulation 18(e) regarding the establishment of temporary traffic arrangements, a local traffic authority can also approve traffic arrangements at a work site based on Regulation 18(b) of the Traffic Regulations. Chapter 8 - Supervision and Control  
A temporary traffic arrangement, especially at a work site, is exposed to harsh environmental conditions due to traffic congestion on urban routes. Traffic arrangements undergo changes by road users through the shifting and dismantling of traffic arrangements, but also by site workers who make changes to the traffic arrangements without permission and contrary to the plans, which jeopardizes the safety of road users.  
It must be ensured that the traffic arrangement - at any given time - precisely matches the arrangement planned and established by the traffic authority. For this purpose, ongoing monitoring, control, and supervision of the traffic arrangements must be carried out.  
8.1   Supervision and Control  
It is the duty of the local traffic authority to supervise the placement, installation, operation, marking, registration, and maintenance of traffic arrangements within its jurisdiction. This is stipulated in Regulation 18(d) of the Traffic Regulations as mentioned in Chapter 7 above.  
The level of supervision and control is divided into two levels:  
8.1.1  Supervision and Control of Ongoing/Extended Works  
Supervision of ongoing extended traffic arrangements will be carried out during the installation and placement of the arrangement with all its components in the field in preparation for its operation and at any time a change (for any reason) is made to the traffic arrangements.

9.1.1 Entry and Exit to/from the Work Site  
The work site begins at the first sign 901 and includes the area of the early warning zone, the entrances to the activity area, the activity area itself, and the end of the activity area, which concludes with the end of the restrictions.  
The organization area, including the contractor's offices, is not part of the work site.  
The entry and exit of the work site are located at the beginning and end of the geometric changes of the roadway, resulting from the temporary traffic arrangements.  
The need for entry arises from the transition between the normal speed on the road and the reduced speed at the work site, due to the forced conditions, and the role of signs 901+932, placed at the entrance to the work site, is to alert the driver and cause them to reduce their speed and be more vigilant.  
At the entrance to a two-lane or one-way section (a lane with two or more lanes), the signs will be placed on both sides of the road. At the entrance to a one-lane two-way section, they will be placed only on the right side.
On a route with two lanes or more, the traffic signs will be placed on both sides of the road. At the entrance to a single-lane two-way section, they will be placed only on the right side.

9.1.3 Site Fencing  
Temporary fencing at construction sites is essential for safety, especially in urban areas where pedestrians, vehicles, and cyclists share the space. The fencing is intended to protect road users and the work crew from various physical injuries that may arise from activities taking place within the site, such as open pits. Additionally, the fencing provides protection against the activities of vehicles on site.  
The fencing system must enclose the entire work area/site, and it is designed to protect pedestrians and cyclists while separating them from the work site, therefore it should not be lenient.  
Disadvantages of fencing and ways to address them:  
1. Fencing may obstruct the field of vision for road users/drivers or cause the obstruction of traffic lights, signage, pedestrian crossings, and/or the entry and exit of vehicles from the work site. To prevent obstruction of the field of vision, corners of the fence can be cut, and signs can be placed on the fence instead of those that are obscured. Additionally, warning signs/general signage related to the types of work should be installed, along with danger signs for pedestrians/passersby and guidance to safe walking/crossing routes.  
2. Disruption to traffic outside the site - due to entry and exit areas to the site. To prevent disruption...

1. General warning signs/signage related to the types of work, danger signage for pedestrians/passersby, and directing them to safe walking/crossing routes.  
2. Disruption to traffic outside the site - due to entry and exit areas for the site. To prevent disruption, the entrance gates to the site will open inwards. Additionally, it must be ensured that the site fencing is secure for the safety of road users and prevents entry to the site other than through the designated entrance, and that the fence can withstand loads applied to it such as wind, impacts, etc.  
3. Blocking walking and crossing paths - in such cases, road users should be directed to a reasonable alternative in the same location.  
4. Impact on the urban landscape - the site fencing should be for the minimal work area that meets the work requirements, and it is advisable to design the outer side of the fence in a way that does not harm the urban landscape (advertisements, special textures, etc.).

9.2 Loading and Unloading and Parking Time Restrictions  
Work sites often require a lot of equipment and building materials, and at the same time, there is a need to clear away many materials such as waste and dirt, as well as equipment that is no longer in use. As part of traffic arrangements, a designated area for loading and unloading must be established, which will minimize the impact on road users to the greatest extent possible.  
The presence of trucks on the road, especially if the work site is located in a residential neighborhood, takes up additional space on the street, and therefore, the hours for loading and unloading should be restricted so that they do not occur during peak hours or maximum activity times.  
For example:  
  In the vicinity of schools - during student arrival times.  
  In residential neighborhoods - during the evening and night hours.  
  In commercial areas - during peak business hours.  
When there is no alternative and for the purpose of unloading and loading at the work site, the parking strip should be used, and the parking hours in this strip should be restricted according to the needs of the residents in the area. If there is no parking strip or reasonable place for unloading and loading under the existing street conditions, a traffic arrangement plan must be prepared to regulate this activity. Notification of parking hour restrictions should be given in advance as outlined in section 2.6 Signs and Traffic Signals. The signage will be in two languages.

For the existing street, a traffic regulation plan must be prepared to manage this activity. Notification of parking hour restrictions should be given in advance as outlined in section 2.6 on signage and traffic signs. The signage will be in two languages.

9.3 Work Sites Near Attractions for Mass Events  
Mass events (such as street closures for Purim holiday celebrations, parades, Independence Day street stages, sports events, marches, festivals, etc.) require special temporary traffic arrangements similar to roadworks, and dedicated temporary traffic plans must be prepared after examining all traffic-related aspects of the event.  
The temporary traffic plan for mass events should present the following aspects:  
1. Closure of gathering areas for pedestrians, and regulation of entrances and exits to the area.  
2. Traffic arrangements for closing intersections that create gathering areas and signage for redirecting traffic accordingly.  
3. Examination of the implications of the arrangements on public transport routes and the establishment of alternative public transport routes as needed, considering that public transport includes through traffic and transport aimed at bringing the public to the event itself.  
4. Ensuring a continuous accessible traffic flow for people with disabilities, and publicizing it to the public.  
5. Arranging directional signage for pedestrians from public transport to the pedestrian entrances to the site, including signage directing to accessible entrances.  
6. Creating peripheral parking spaces for private vehicles with pathways to public transport.  
7. Creating parking lots near the event for vehicles of people with disabilities.  
8. Public notification.

Chapter 11 - Procedure for Submitting Plans to the Traffic Authorities  
The purpose of this procedure is to establish a uniform basis for submitting plans for temporary traffic arrangements for approval, with the intention of creating consistency in the preparation, presentation, and approval of traffic arrangement plans by the traffic authority.  
11.1 Planner's Approval of Compliance with Planning Guidelines  
Every plan for temporary traffic arrangements at work sites on urban roads submitted for approval must include the planner's signature confirming that the plan complies with legal requirements, regulations, standards, and planning guidelines. In the case of changes to traffic lights, this signature must appear on both the engineering arrangement plan and the timeline plan. Additionally, the following must be highlighted on the plan:  
- The planner's name, their registration number in the civil engineering field, the name of the planning office, and its details.  
- The name of the plan, its number, its edition number, and the date of the update.  
- A general description of the plan and its principles (for example: reference to pedestrians, traffic diversions, and changes to bus stops), planning and placement of temporary lighting, diversion of systems, presentation of the method for arranging temporary and permanent accessibility, and so on.  
- A general description of the phases of execution and the duration of execution of

Reference to pedestrians, traffic diversions, and changes at bus stops, planning and placement of temporary lighting, system deviations, presentation of the method for arranging temporary and permanent accessibility, and so on.  
- General description of the phasing of execution and the duration of each phase in projects with multiple execution stages.  
The wording of the planner's commitment will be:  
"I hereby confirm that the submitted plan for approval was prepared by a licensed engineer and complies with the guidelines of the national traffic supervisor, the valid traffic signs, and legal requirements."  
If necessary, the planner may add an appendix to the plan containing additional details not specified in the plan itself. In such a case, a reference to the appendix will be indicated on the plan accordingly.  
11.2 Temporary traffic arrangement plans at work sites on urban roads.

The plan will be based on a map that reflects the existing traffic arrangements at the time of preparing the plan, particularly the traffic signs placed in the area. The background map can be one of the following alternatives (see also illustrations 11.2, 11.3, and 11.4 below):
- Detailed measurement for planning - intended also for geometric changes.
- Photogrammetric measurement - these plans will only be prepared as environmental diagrams, such as guidance for detours.
- Aerial photograph - can serve as a background only when the resolution is sufficient and there is no coverage that impairs the ability to reproduce the traffic arrangements.

The book "Guidelines for Planning Motor Vehicle Traffic in Cities" is the fourth book in the series of guideline books for street planning in cities. While the previous books in the series focused on the soft users of the street, pedestrians and cyclists, more on motor vehicle drivers of various types, and on the characteristics and "heavy" functional requirements, this book deals with the users of the vehicles themselves.  
This book discusses the geometric design of the street, focusing on components related to motor vehicles, which generally occupy the majority of land allocation in the street. These components include the lanes with their various characteristics and widths, the medians and traffic islands, and the issue of parking, a significant component whose presence greatly influences the street's portrait and the nature of the urban space as a whole.  
The current book addresses the typical segments of the street that actually represent most of its length, the characteristics and events occurring within it, and concurrently, a book discussing urban intersections and their surroundings is being published.  
In this book, the components of geometric planning have been updated, thus reflecting the worldview characteristic of the five guideline books in the series, according to which the geometry of the street dictates and determines the behavior of street users in general, and drivers in particular.

The concept underlying the guidelines  
These guidelines for motor vehicle traffic in cities are part of a series of new guideline books for urban street planning, as will be described in the following sections. As explained in the master book of the series - "Planning the Street Space," these guidelines represent a new and more balanced worldview compared to the planning concepts that were prevalent in the second half of the 20th century, which prioritized the 'street for vehicles' concept - the capacity and level of service for private vehicles, as the main planning goal.  
This concept has significantly influenced the direction of the street's other roles and urban planning, which have become less and less inviting and safe for other road users.  
Since the end of the twentieth century, there has been a global aspiration to halt the decline of urban space. In many places around the world, it has been understood that the desire to provide city residents with immediate access by private vehicle to every destination is questionable in terms of long-term feasibility, but its cost in terms of quality of life and well-being is already unreasonable.  
Therefore, the new guideline books for urban street planning are based on a new and more balanced worldview - largely more traditional (and perhaps even more biblical), grounded in several fundamental principles.  
A. A good street is a street that is good for people who are present.

The new guidelines for urban street planning are based on a new and more balanced worldview - largely more traditional (and perhaps even more biblical), founded on several fundamental principles:
A. A good street is one that is good for the people who are in it.
B. The street space has many and varied roles - systemic, visual, social, and others.
C. The street space should provide an efficient and economical response to all the activities taking place within it.
D. Street planning requires a controlled and balanced allocation of street space among all its users.
E. The quality of the street depends on and influences the quality of the entire fabric related to it.
Within this framework of reallocating street space among all its users, private and commercial vehicles must also find their place in a balanced and fair mix with pedestrians, cyclists, public transport, and other users. The guidelines before you detail the planning principles for the traffic and parking lanes allocated on the urban street for motor vehicles, after previous books dedicated to planning for pedestrians and bicycles.

B. Guidelines for Street Planning in Cities - Pedestrian Traffic (hereinafter "Pedestrian Traffic")
This book is the first of the specialized books, and its main subject is detailing the space required for pedestrians on the street - its dimensions and quality.
The first part of the book deals with the centrality of the pedestrian and presents it in two aspects. The first aspect - the pedestrian as a human essence, as the focus of all urban planning, and as the primary consumer of public space. The second aspect - the pedestrian as a 'movement device' and as part of the overall traffic in the city. The first part explains the supreme importance of encouraging pedestrian movement in the city by changing planning priorities.

Walking Strip - A strip on the sidewalk along the street, designated for the longitudinal movement of pedestrians only.

Bicycle Traffic  
This is the first guideline book on this topic in Israel. The book explains the rules and guidelines for integrating bicycle traffic into the urban street network of various types, so that they can move comfortably and safely alongside other street users. The guidelines are based on the assumption that bicycles are an accepted mode of transportation that should be able to reach anywhere from anywhere, especially in the city but also outside of it. Therefore, the guidelines include measures for fully integrating bicycles within the urban framework and the city's transportation system. Bicycles are a mode of transport, and thus they should move separately as much as possible from pedestrians, with the level of separation from other vehicles determined by safety considerations. The guidelines define three levels of separation for bicycle traffic:  
- Level A (no separation) - integration of bicycle traffic with motor vehicles,  
- Level B (minimal separation) - in a separate lane alongside motor traffic lanes,  
- Level C (maximum separation) - in a separate path.  
Accordingly, the guideline book includes tools for selecting and planning the most suitable arrangement for bicycles on road segments and at intersections. The book also presents the necessary traffic signs for each arrangement.

This is with the aspiration to be as clear and transparent as possible to the broad target audience, without losing the professional accuracy required in each field. By necessity, there will be chapters in the guidelines written in a language more understandable to a 'non-professional audience,' and other chapters with a more professional tone, addressing urban planning, transportation planning, landscape planning, physical infrastructure, and additional topics from various professional fields. The scope of flexibility in implementing the guidelines for street planning
The guidelines present the planner with the options available to them. However, the guidelines are not intended to restrict the planner's solutions, but rather to define a framework on one hand, and to broaden their horizons on the other hand, in order to assist them in dealing with non-standard problems. The proposed set of guidelines includes basic definitions of key policies and planning principles on various issues, as well as a wide range of specific guidelines, design details, computational methods, recommended and minimum dimensions, and so forth. The aim of these is primarily to provide planning and thinking tools, as well as to...

Fundamentals of key policies and planning principles on various topics, as well as a wide range of specific guidelines, design details, computational methods, recommended and minimum dimensions, and so forth. The primary purpose of these is to provide planning and thinking tools, as well as to inspire and encourage the planner in searching for the most suitable solutions for the specific case at hand. There is no doubt that the proposed set of guidelines does not provide answers to all future planning challenges, but rather a partial response to the more common and familiar cases. Most planning tasks generate local and unique problems, the solutions of which will require significant effort, creativity, judgment, and decisions from the planning team. In any planning challenge, it is highly recommended to rely on the worldview, policies, and planning principles presented in the guidelines, such as a comprehensive view of public space, a thorough examination of the needs of users, a controlled balance of space allocation, planning for maximum safety (and less for maximum capacity), and so forth.

The general concept of speed planning and management  
Speed is one of the basic characteristics of traffic flow, defining the flow state at both the macro and micro levels. High speed on the road indicates good flow conditions, both as a result of road data and traffic data. On the other hand, from a safety perspective, most studies indicate a correlation between speed and the occurrence and severity of traffic accidents, with the variance in speeds among different vehicles also contributing to road insecurity.  
How to adapt: Therefore, the central issue when dealing with speed on the street is to match the appropriate speed to the street that meets operational, safety, economic, social, and other needs, as there is an inherent contradiction among them.  
The solution lies in establishing a priority order of needs for each street. Subject to this, appropriate travel speeds will be determined for each street, and as a result, the geometric characteristics required by this speed.  
The speed of vehicle movement on the street has a direct impact and connection to other users, the rate of crosswalks, the existence of medians and the type of medians, the presence or absence of: for example, parking lanes.

The speed of vehicle movement on the street has a direct impact and connection to other users, the rate of crosswalks, the existence of medians and the type of medians, the presence or absence of, for example, regulated parking lanes - all of these are influenced by motor traffic speed and affect all other users on the street. They are intended to facilitate traffic flow from area to area in the metropolitan urban arterial road network. There should be an aspiration to plan them to a high traffic standard, so that these roads will carry the majority of the traffic and provide high capacity at a reasonable level of service. The design should reflect the fact that the permitted speeds on these roads should be relatively high compared to the rest of the urban network. The level of safety on these roads will not be compromised, as long as they are designed for a high safety level, taking into account that there are very vulnerable road users (pedestrians, cyclists, light motorcycle riders), whose bodies cannot withstand the consequences of an accident occurring at 70 km/h. One of the main means of maintaining a high level of safety at this speed is to create maximum separation on the roads between vulnerable users and the rest of the motor traffic. In the urban system, mainly collector and local streets are intended for capacity.

In the urban system, the collector and local streets are primarily designated for accessibility purposes. These streets must reflect their lower traffic status in the network, both in geometric standards and in permitted speeds. Their lower traffic status for through traffic, and their primary function for accessibility, will redirect through traffic to higher-level streets that are designed for that purpose. Therefore, safety will increase not only on urban roads but throughout the entire urban network.

The management of travel speeds in the street network should be based on a single systemic rationale. As a first step in this process, a clear definition of the roles of the streets in the network is required - a hierarchy of streets. The hierarchy of streets is determined considering the topographical structure, population concentrations, transportation needs, statutory considerations, and especially considering mobility considerations, traffic transfer and flow, traffic distribution, or access to residential areas. For each type of street, a physical space for establishment (right of way) and design principles are defined. The systemic view of managing travel speeds in the street network requires that for each type of street, a "design speed" is defined, which will determine the desired travel speed for that street. The designation for different types of streets is determined according to a variety of considerations including mobility, safety, environmental quality, quality of life in population concentrations, and more, which are examined at the systemic level (of the entire road network). Restrictions on pedestrian activity along the road turn it into a 'repellent space' along its length. Local streets with minimal vehicle traffic often have low urban significance (small residential streets, etc.), but it is also important to pay attention to the opposite phenomena - local streets that are marginal in terms of traffic but have special urban importance (Shenkin Street in Tel Aviv).

Separator  
Separators - Their Roles and Types  
The separator is a strip within the street that separates different vehicle movements and opposing directions of traffic. The separator has many diverse roles in street planning, as detailed below.  
Roles related to motor vehicle traffic in the street:  
A. To serve as a safety barrier between different vehicle movements, in the same direction or in opposing directions (including bus lanes, bicycles, etc.).  
B. To guide and direct drivers within intersections and to provide an optional area for creating special lanes for left turns.  
C. To moderate the nature of traffic in the street.  
D. An engineering tool for traffic management (preventing left turns, U-turns, etc.).  
Roles related to infrastructure and stationary objects:

Cul-de-sac
Introduction
A "cul-de-sac" is a regular urban street that resembles all its components to those of urban streets, but is distinguished by the fact that the entry into it by motor vehicles from the surrounding area is also the only exit from it back to that area.
The natural and preferred tendency in urban and transportation planning is to create a street that has at least two connection points to the surrounding area for motor vehicles. However, sometimes, due to various urban and engineering reasons, there is no choice but to create a "cul-de-sac."
It should be emphasized that the lack of an exit for vehicles does not necessitate the absence of an exit for pedestrians and bicycles. On the contrary, the more continuity and connectivity of the pedestrian network is ensured, the better its quality will be, and it will guarantee greater usage. Therefore, if necessary, it is advisable to allow multi-directional movement for pedestrians and bicycles even on streets that are dead ends for motor vehicles.
In such cases, it is common to designate "cul-de-sacs" primarily in residential areas, which rely on private vehicle traffic spread throughout the day, and to avoid, as much as possible, designating them next to uses that attract large traffic volumes.

In such cases, it is common to designate "dead-end streets" primarily in residential areas, based on private vehicle traffic spread throughout the day, and to avoid, as much as possible, designating them next to uses that attract large traffic volumes during short periods, such as schools, clusters of kindergartens, cinemas, theaters, etc. In such cases, vehicles block the street and disrupt both the external traffic continuing to the street and the local traffic wishing to exit during these times. It is also recommended to avoid designating "dead-end streets" next to industrial uses and uses that attract trucks and buses, as these vehicles will require significant expansion of several street components, especially the turning area.

Basic Planning Rules
A. It should be ensured that a "dead-end street" has additional connections to the nearby environment for pedestrians and cyclists.
B. The design vehicle according to which the components of the "dead-end street" will be planned is an urban truck in forced movement (mainly for garbage collection and deliveries).
C. All guidelines regarding the characteristics of a regular street, as stated in the five volumes of guidelines for streets in cities and in other applicable planning guidelines, also apply to "dead-end streets."

D. There is no restriction regarding the length of the street, except in a combined street (see guidelines for combined streets), where the maximum length specified is 250 meters.
E. As in other urban streets, it is recommended to moderate traffic along "dead-end streets" and not allow vehicles to develop high speeds along them. When the length of a "dead-end street" exceeds 75-80 meters, it is mandatory to install a turnaround area at the end of the street. The stopping sight distance is the sum of two components - the perception-reaction distance and the braking distance. The perception-reaction distance is the distance the vehicle travels during the time from the moment of detecting an obstacle until the brakes are activated; the perception time is the time that passes from the moment of detecting the obstacle until the decision to apply the brakes, and the reaction time is the time that passes from the moment of the decision to apply the brakes until the actual braking begins. The braking distance is the distance the vehicle travels from the moment the brakes are applied until it comes to a complete stop. Over the years, the braking systems of modern vehicles have significantly improved, increasing the deceleration capability and improving braking distances. At high speeds on wet surfaces, most vehicles can decelerate at 2 m/s². On dry surfaces, most drivers can decelerate at 3.4 m/s² before an object that appears unexpectedly. The deceleration parameter has become the dominant parameter for determining the braking distance, due to the ABS (Anti-lock Braking System) systems installed in most vehicles, which ensure deceleration without the risk of wheel skidding due to locking.

Side Elevation in Horizontal Curves
Needs and Limitations
Changes in direction in the horizontal alignment are made by designing circular arcs between the straight segments. In the circular arcs, a centrifugal force acts on the vehicle, pushing it outward from the curve. This force is balanced by a lateral friction factor that develops between the wheels and the pavement, as well as by a side elevation of the pavement, with a uniform slope greater than that of the normal crown. 
From a traffic perspective, it is preferable to provide side elevations in horizontal curves, thereby reducing dependence on lateral friction; however, in urban areas, there are several constraints that make it practically very difficult or undesirable to change the normal crown of the pavement. Among the various factors limiting the provision of elevation, the following factors exist:
Generally, the drainage of urban streets is through underground drainage, A. Drainage of the pavement, with the inlets located near the curb stones. Therefore, if the drainage line runs along the right curb stone, a side elevation in the opposite direction will transfer the water across the pavement to the median or to the opposite curb stone. Although this issue can be solved engineering-wise.

The collectors are located near the curb stones. Therefore, if the drainage line runs along the right curb stone, a lateral elevation in the opposite direction will direct the water across the roadway to the median or to the opposite curb stone. Although this issue can be solved through engineering, the planner must carefully consider the drainage problems in the elevated section. 

Urban streets are characterized by the presence of many intersections. The processing of heights at intersections along the streets, as well as entrances for side uses, is significant. Therefore, when there is a horizontal curve, or immediately adjacent to it, if there is an intersection, providing lateral elevation may complicate the proper arrangement of slopes and heights at the intersection.

Urban streets provide high accessibility to adjacent land uses. Providing a large lateral elevation may create height differences between the street and land uses. In particular, the elevation may hinder access to buildings.

Raising the roadway may complicate the comfort of boarding and alighting passengers from buses. 

Excessive elevation of the roadway may constitute a visual nuisance in the urban street. Adjusting the heights and slopes of the sidewalks to the heights and slopes of the road may create a visually preferable layout, but it may complicate pedestrian movement due to crossings.

The elevation of the sidewalk may pose a visual hazard in the urban street. Adjusting the visual aspect of the heights and slopes of the sidewalks to the heights and slopes of the road may create a visually preferable layout, but it may complicate pedestrian movement due to the transitions in the slopes on the sidewalks. Purpose of the Widening
Widening the roadway at horizontal curves is necessary to allow vehicles to travel through the curve under conditions similar to traveling on a straight section of road. The required width for the roadway is composed of the following factors:

In 1987, the Strategic Highway Research Program began the largest and most 
comprehensive pavement performance test in history—the Long-Term Pavement
Performance (LTPP) program.  During the program’s 20-year life, highway agencies
in the United States and 15 other countries will have collected data on pavement
condition, climate, and traffic volumes and loads from more than 1,000 pavement
test sections.  That information will allow pavement engineers to design better,
longer-lasting roads.
This manual was developed to provide a consistent, uniform basis for collecting
distress data for the LTPP program.

This manual provides a common language for describing cracks, potholes, rutting,
spalling, and other pavement distresses being monitored by the LTPP program. 
The manual is divided into three sections, each focusing on a particular type of
pavement: (1) asphalt concrete-surfaced, (2) jointed portland cement concrete, and
(3) continuously reinforced portland cement concrete.  Each distress is clearly
labeled, described, and illustrated.

GUIDANCE TO OTHER USERS
As a pavement distress dictionary, the manual will improve communications within
the pavement community by fostering more uniform and consistent definitions of
pavement distress. H

ANCE TO OTHER USERS
As a pavement distress dictionary, the manual will improve communications within
the pavement community by fostering more uniform and consistent definitions of
pavement distress. Highway agencies, airports, parking facilities, and others with
significant investment in pavements will benefit from adopting a standard distress
language.
Colleges and universities will use the manual in highway engineering courses. It
also serves as a valuable training tool for highway agencies. Now when a distress is
labeled “high severity fatigue cracking,” for example, it is clear exactly what is
meant.  Repairs can be planned and executed more efficiently, saving the highway
agency crew time and money.
Although not specifically designed as a pavement management tool, the Distress
Identification Manual can play an important role in a State’s pavement management
program by ridding reports of inconsistencies and variations caused by a lack of
standardized terminology. Most pavement mana

ication Manual can play an important role in a State’s pavement management
program by ridding reports of inconsistencies and variations caused by a lack of
standardized terminology. Most pavement management programs do not need to
collect data at the level of detail and precision required for the LTPP program, nor
are the severity levels used in the manual necessarily appropriate for all pavement
management situations. Thus, you may choose to modify the procedures (but not
the definitions) contained in the manual to meet your specific needs, taking into
account the desired level of detail, accuracy and timeliness of information, available

FATIGUE CRACKING
Description
Occurs in areas subjected to repeated traffic loadings (wheel paths).  Can be a
series of interconnected cracks in early stages of development. Develops into
many-sided, sharp-angled pieces, usually less than 0.3 meters (m) on the longest
side, characteristically with a chicken wire/alligator pattern, in later stages.
Must have a quantifiable area.
Severity Levels
LOW
An area of crac

ces, usually less than 0.3 meters (m) on the longest
side, characteristically with a chicken wire/alligator pattern, in later stages.
Must have a quantifiable area.
Severity Levels
LOW
An area of cracks with no or only a few connecting cracks; cracks are not
spalled or sealed; pumping is not evident.
MODERATE
An area of interconnected cracks forming a complete pattern; cracks may be
slightly spalled; cracks may be sealed; pumping is not evident.
HIGH
An area of moderately or severely spalled interconnected cracks forming a
complete pattern; pieces may move when subjected to traffic; cracks may be
sealed; pumping may be evident.
How to Measure
Record square meters of affected area at each severity level.  If different
severity levels existing within an area cannot be distinguished, rate the entire
area at the highest severity present.

performance problems.  Extent is sufficient to monitor any progression.

INTRODUCTION
This appendix provides instructions, data sheets, and distress maps for use 
in visual surveys for the collection of distress information for ACP, JCP, and
CRCP surfaces. Visual distress survey procedures have been used in the LTPP
program as the primary distress data collection method since 1995. The Distress
Identification Manual for the Long-Term Pavemen

program as the primary distress data collection method since 1995. The Distress
Identification Manual for the Long-Term Pavement Performance Program is the
basis for all distress surveys performed for the LTPP.
During the visual distress survey, safety is the first consideration, as with all
field data collection activities. All raters must adhere to the practices and
authority of the State or Canadian Province.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR COMPLETING DISTRESS MAPS
The distress maps show the exact location of each distress type existing on the
test section. The distress types and severity levels should be identified by using
the Distress Identification Manual. A total of five sheets are used to map; each
sheet contains two 15.25-m maps which represent 30.5 m of the test section
(with the exception of SPS-6 sections 2 and 5, which are 305 m).
Each test section must be laid out consistently each time a survey is conducted.

Sections begin and end at the stations marked on the pavement. Lateral extent
of the section, for survey purposes, will vary depending on the existence of
longitudinal joints and cracks and the relative position of the lane markings.
Figures A1 and A2 illustrate the rules to follow when determining the lateral
extent of the section for a distress survey. The lateral extent of the test sections
should be consistent with prior distress surveys. On widened PCC sections, the
lateral extent of the test section includes the full width (4.3 m) of the slab
measured from the centerline longitudinal joint to the shoulder joint. The
lateral extent of AC test sections with double yellow lines on the centerline are

INTRODUCTION
Measurement of Faulting in the LTPP Program
This manual is intended for use by the FHWA-LTPP Regional Coordination
Office personnel and others responsible for using the faultmeter to measure
JCP faulting, and for measuring lane-to-shoulder dropoff on LTPP pavement
test sites.
The change in joint faulting and lane-to-shoulder dropoff with time are important
indicators of pavement performance. The digital faultmeters will be used to
collect this data. It is the responsibility of each regional coordination office
contractor to store, maintain, and operate their faultmeter for fault

formance. The digital faultmeters will be used to

lane-to-shoulder dropoff data collection.
The Georgia Digital Faultmeter
The electronic digital faultmeter was designed to simplify measuring concrete
joint faulting. This meter was designed, developed and built by the Georgia
Department of Transportation Office of Materials and Research personnel 1. The
faultmeter is very light and easy to use. The unit, shown in figure 1, weighs
approximately 3.2 kg and supplies a digital readout with the push of a button
located on the carrying handle. It reads out directly in millimeters (e.g., a
digital readout of “6” indicates 6 mm of faulting) and shows whether the reading
is positive or negative. The unit reads out in 1 second and freezes the r eading
in display so that it can be removed from the road before reading for safer
operation. The

is positive or negative. The unit reads out in 1 second and freezes the r eading
in display so that it can be removed from the road before reading for safer
operation. The legs of the faultmeter’s base are set on the slab in the direction
of traffic on the “leave side” of the joint. The measuring probe contacts the slab
on the approach. Movement of this probe is transmitted to a Linear Variance
Displacement Transducer to measure joint faulting. The joint must be centered
between the guidelines shown on the side of the meter.
Any slab that is lower on the leave side of the joint will register as a positive
faulting number. If the slab leaving the joint is higher, the meter gives a
negative reading.
The amount of time it takes to complete the faulting survey of a LTPP test sec-
tion depends on the number of joints and cracks encountered, and on the
amount of time needed to measure and record the location of each joint and
crack. Generally, it should take less

amount of time needed to measure and record the location of each joint and
crack. Generally, it should take less than 30 minutes to measure and record
faulting and lane-to-shoulder dropoff on a 150-m test section using this device.
The Mechanical Faultmeter
The mechanical faultmeter was designed as a backup to the Georgia Faultmeter. It
is not intended for use as a primary measuring device for faulting. The mechanical
faultmeter has the same “footprint” as the Georgia Faultmeter and should be used
in a similar manner. It has a dial indicator instead of the Georgia Faultmeter’s
electronic digital readout. The mechanical faultmeter also does not take
negative faulting readings, and must be reversed to read negative faulting.

end of the faultmeter with the measuring probe on the 9-mm calibration block.

should with the measuring probe off the 9-mm calibration block. In this
position, reading of 0 mm should be obtained.

C.1 INTRODUCTION
The Face Company Dipstick is a manually operated device that collects
precision profile measurements at rates greater than traditional rod and level
survey procedures. However, the profile obtained from Dipstick measurements
may have a shift from the true profile because of systematic cumulative errors
in the Dipstick readings. The body of the Dipstick houses an inclinometer
(pendulum), liquid crystal display panels, and a battery for power supply. The
Dipstick sensor is mounted in such a way that its axis and line passing through
footpad contact points are coplanar. The sensor becomes unbalanced as the
Dipstick is pivoted from one leg to the other as it is moved down the pavement,
causing the disp

axis and line passing through
footpad contact points are coplanar. The sensor becomes unbalanced as the
Dipstick is pivoted from one leg to the other as it is moved down the pavement,
causing the display to become blank. After the sensor achieves equilibrium, the
difference in elevation between the two points is displayed. Swivel footpads
with a diameter of 32 mm should be used for all measurements. 
Each LTPP Regional Support Contractor (RSC) has two Dipsticks; a manual
Dipstick (Model 1500) and an automated Dipstick (Model 2000). Both these
Dipsticks display data in millimeters. The spacing between the two feet of the
Dipstick is 305 mm for both models. When the automated Dipstick is used for
data collection, it should be used in manual mode, with data recorded
manually.
Profile measurements on General Pavement Studies (GPS) and SPS sites that
cannot be obtained using the LTPP profiler should be completed using the
Dipstick. Decisions with respect to the need for Dipstick measurement

ents on General Pavement Studies (GPS) and SPS sites that
cannot be obtained using the LTPP profiler should be completed using the
Dipstick. Decisions with respect to the need for Dipstick measurements at
these test sections should be made on a case-by-case basis by responsible
RSC personnel.

single person can collect the data if that person uses a voice activated tape
recorder to record the readings.

C.3.5.5 Closure Error Computation
The total accumulated error in a transverse profile is established by a closed-
loop survey. The forward and return runs along a transverse line are used to
compute this error. At each station, add the readings for the forward and return
runs separately, and record the values in the “Sum” column of form DS-8. Then
at each station, add the values in “Sum” column for the forward and return run,
and record the result in the “Closure” column. At each station, for each
Dipstick reading, add the reading for the forward and return runs, and record
the value in the field “Difference.” 
To compute the allowable closure error for a transverse profile run, multiply
the total number of Dipstick readings (sum of the number of readings for
forward and return runs) by 0.076 (0.076 mm is the allowabl

forward and return runs) by 0.076 (0.076 mm is the allowable average error per
one Dipstick reading). The allowable closure error for typical lane widths that
are encountered are given in table C1. 
If the closure error for a transverse profile is outside the allowable range,

Chapter A  
The Municipal Center  
In the Local Authority – Purpose and Objectives  

The municipal center serves as the important and significant link between three factors that influence the service provided to the residents of the authority and the quality of the relationship between the resident, the officials in the local authority, and the management of the authority.  
Despite the significant differences between the authorities in the State of Israel (the size of the authorities, their characteristics, and the management and operational patterns in the authorities), it can be seen that all municipal centers share a similar understanding of purpose and a list of objectives. However, different authorities have several different operational models for municipal centers.  
This chapter will present the understanding of the purpose and objectives of the municipal centers and will outline the existing operational models in local authorities, addressing the advantages and disadvantages inherent in each operational method.  

1. Purpose of the Municipal Center  
The center is an urban control and monitoring unit responsible for responding to residents' inquiries regarding the receipt and delivery of information about actions and services provided by the local authority, as well as reporting...

Municipal Call Center

1. The municipal call center is an urban control and monitoring unit responsible for responding to residents' inquiries regarding the receipt and delivery of information about actions and services provided by the local authority, as well as reporting on hazards and nuisances within the municipal area of the authority. The center serves as a channel for accumulating valuable municipal and organizational knowledge for decision-making processes and optimal management. The main operations of the center occur during routine and calm hours, but its strength is reflected in its ability to respond quickly and effectively during emergencies, both in peacetime and wartime.

2. Objectives of the Municipal Call Center:
   1. To serve as a professional address providing residents with an available, appropriate, reliable, and transparent response (in a One Stop Shop situation) twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, during both calm and emergency situations.
   2. To direct residents' inquiries to the designated officials in the authority and to monitor their handling.
   3. To identify delays in real-time handling and act to expedite the process.
   4. To enable the authority's management to receive an up-to-date status report on the quality of responses provided to residents through its units, as well as to obtain information on residents' satisfaction levels regarding various areas of service, as they are brought to their attention.
   5. To provide the authority's management with...

The authority can receive an up-to-date status report at any given moment on the quality of the response provided to residents through its units, as well as obtain information on the level of satisfaction of residents with various areas of service, as they are brought to their attention. 

5. To provide the authority's management with data, information, and knowledge for data-driven decision-making regarding the improvement of processes and services.

3. Models for operating the municipal call center
Three main models can be identified for operating municipal call centers:
1. A municipal call center under the full operational responsibility of the authority.
2. A private call center operated partially by the municipality and supported by a private company.
3. A municipal call center managed by the municipality and fully operated by an external contractor.

A well-defined role perception and correct work perception of the municipal center manager are key to achieving the center's purpose and realizing its goals. To enable this, the municipal center manager must recognize and understand the core activities within their area of responsibility as well as the areas of responsibility and authority at their disposal.  
In this chapter, we will address the definition of the main work channels of the center manager, in routine situations and in emergencies, the definition of their main areas of responsibility, as well as a description of the characteristics of their main work interfaces.

In this section, we will address the definition of the main work channels of the call center manager, in both routine and emergency situations, the definition of their main areas of responsibility, as well as a description of the characteristics of their main work interfaces.

1. The core role of the municipal call center manager focuses on two channels and refers to three operational states:
   1. Managing the information cycle between the public residents and the local authority's management and interface entities working for the authority.

The service representatives are responsible for receiving residents' inquiries and forwarding them for processing by the execution entities within the authority. Introduction  
An emergency situation is an external condition that poses a threat to human life or the lives of their relatives and disrupts the functional, cognitive, and emotional continuity of the individual, family, group, and community.  
A municipal center, by its nature, deals with a reality of "emergency routine" – a work routine in which behind every call there may be an emergency situation. Therefore, it must be prepared to deal, at any time, with two types of emergency situations:  
1. Emergency situations/exceptional events during routine – such as a major water main break that disrupts water supply to many streets for long hours; a fire in a business that contains hazardous materials.

Prepared to deal, at any time, with two types of emergency situations:
1. Emergency situations/exceptional events during routine – such as a major water main break that disrupts water supply to many streets for long hours; a fire in a business that contains hazardous materials; a traffic accident that blocks a major traffic route, etc.
2. Emergency situations during a crisis – natural disaster, state of war, earthquake, and mass casualty events.
The main difference between the two types of emergencies:
In a routine emergency, a specific emergency situation is identified for a resident or a group of residents. The municipal center continues to operate normally and increases, if necessary, the number of service representatives working there.
In emergencies during a crisis, the head of the authority becomes the chairperson of the emergency committee, and the authority operates according to national emergency regulations – it opens an operations center and acts through emergency units responsible for providing information, addressing special populations, supplying water, nursing and social services, education, sanitation, infrastructure, ensuring the opening of grocery stores for food supply to residents, and works in cooperation with national emergency agencies (Home Front Command, police, MDA, fire department).

At the end of the COVID-19 crisis and out of necessity, this chapter was added to the Call Center Management Guide in September 2020, based on insights and knowledge sharing from call center managers during two digital meetings and a questionnaire.  
During a crisis, the service provided to residents, in order to meet their needs, must be the central challenge for the authority. Those who face the challenge of receiving instructions, coordinating services, responding to questions, inquiries, and clarifications regarding the situation in general and the authority's services in particular are the urban call center, which must demonstrate expertise, dedication, and great responsibility - to monitor changes, consolidate information, and update them, sometimes proactively and sometimes in response. However, it should be remembered that the call center is a central entity that identifies and conveys information and not an operational and treatment entity.  
In an emergency, the immediate challenge is to stabilize the work in the call center according to scenarios that have been clearly defined in advance.  
The call center manager must prepare for various types of emergency scenarios and the challenges they will bring. This planning will be implemented in CRM systems, notification distribution systems, etc.
