D.5.3.21. A visual inspection of each lighting column and illuminated traffic sign post

D.5.3.24. A strategy for the management of the structural safety of lighting columns and 
illuminated traffic sign posts should be developed and implemented. This 
strategy should include risk management procedures for prioritising the 
inspection and testing of lighting columns and illuminated traffic sign posts and 
the development of non-destructive testing programmes to determine the 
structural integrity of these items. 
Structural Testing 
D.5.3.25. An assessment of the structural condition of lighting columns and illuminated 
traffic sign posts can be made by a number of methods. These methods vary 
from “indicative tests”, such as ultrasonic testing at critical points on the unit, to 
“strength tests”, such as a full dynamic test, where a unit is subjected to a load 
equivalent of the maximum design load and its deflection at ground level 
recorded. Indicative tests do not give a direct measure of the structural strength 
of the unit tested; the data has to be

residual structural strength of the lighting column at the time of testing. 
D.5.3.26. Most of the tests and in particular the strength tests need to be carried out by 
specialist contractors with the correct equipment and procedures. 
D.5.3.27. Structural testing should be carried out using a risk based approach.  The risk 
based approach to structural testing should include the following factors for the 
testing of lighting columns and traffic sign posts: 
 locations where the poor condition of the lighting columns has been 
established as a result of routine visual inspections or other reports;

 lighting columns mounted on over-bridges; and 
 volume of traffic. 
D.5.3.28. The above criteria should provide sufficient detail on which the testing of steel 
lighting columns and illuminated traffic sign posts can be prioritised.  However, 
each authority should establish its own priorities based on the types, ages and 
condition of their stock. The results obtained from the testing programme should

D.6.8.3. A burn to extinction lamp replacement strategy will run all lamps until they 
eventually fail.  The performance of discharge lamps depreciates over time and 
more significantly towards the point of ultimate failure, so just before failure the 
lamps will be emitting significantly lower levels of light than required by design.  
Best value will not be obtained from the electrical energy consumed, as at end of 
life lamps are performing well below optimal performance.

D.6.8.4. With a burn to extinction policy each individual lamp will fail at a different time to 
its neighbours, this may lead to a peak of replacements being required in the 
winter months when lamps are burning longer and the risk of failure is higher, 
this places peaks and troughs in the workload.  Eventually each street will 
contain a mixture of new and old lamps, some giving more light than others and 
leading to patchy lighting levels.  While this may not be acutely obvious, frequent 
changes in light levels will fatigue the driver’s eye, resulting in a road safety 
hazard. 
D.6.8.5. If a burn to extinction policy is adopted, then consideration should be given to 
introducing ‘find and fix’ night scouting.  The alternative is that the authority will 
incur the financial and environmental cost of attending to widely dispersed and 
sporadic faults, which can be significant, both in urban and rural areas.

CoP for the Classification of Highway Safety Defects & Hazards: v 3.0, r 0 4

Hazards & defects affecting the safety and/or the serviceability of the highway 
network can be identified through various routine highway maintenance operations 
such as scheduled safety inspections, ad-hoc inspections carried out in response to 
public enquiries and during cyclical maintenance activities e.g. gully emptying.  In 
addition, emergency events such as road traffic collisions or fallen trees can also 
compromise the safety of the highway user.

This version of the CoP also continues to develop our risk assessment process for 
determining an appropriate response to each hazard or defect consistent with the 
recommendations set out in the Road Liaison Groups highway code of practice, 
Well-Managed Highway Infrastructure [WMHI], and was published on 28th October 
2016.It replaces Well-Maintained Highways and Well-Lit Highways, with a single 
code focussing on the need to promote an integrated approach to asset 
management that is based on local needs, priorities and with the key factor of 
affordability. The underlying principle of the new code is that authorities should 
adopt a risk-based approach and a risk management regime, such as that set out 
within ISO31000, for all aspects of highway maintenance policy.

1.2    Document Structure 
Part 2 of this document provides an explanation of the risk assessment process and 
its application to defect / hazard categorisation. 
Part 3 contains worked examples of this risk assessment process. 
Part 4 details important additional operational information relating to the 
identification, recording and notification of hazards and defects. 
Part 5 contains detailed information for each specific hazard or defect.

Having identified a defect or hazard, assessed its likely impact and quantified the 
risk probability (by determining the location of the defect / hazard within DC’s 
network hierarchy), a specific risk matrix can then be used to provide a response 
category which prescribes the timescale within which the defect / hazard should be 
made safe or repaired.

Category 1E:  Those Category 1 defects or hazards which are considered to pose 
a particularly high risk and require emergency response.  Extremely hazardous 
defects or situations, e.g. missing inspection chamber covers, must not be left in an 
unsafe condition by the attending officer. They should notify the appropriate 
repairing team and wait until emergency assistance arrives.  If appropriate and / or 
practicable use a vehicle to cover / remove access to the defect ensuring that 
hazard lights & amber beacons are activated. If a temporary action is undertaken, 
there must also be a follow up permanent action carried out within a maximum of 28 
days from the time that the defect / hazard was first identified.

Category 1:  Defects & hazards that require prompt attention because they 
represent an immediate or imminent hazard, or because there is a risk of rapid 
structural deterioration.  Category 1 defects / hazards should be made safe at the 
time of the inspection, if reasonably practicable.  In this context, making safe may 
constitute displaying warning notices or coning off to protect the public from the 
defect.  If it is not possible to make safe the defect / hazard at the time of inspection 
then a repair, either temporary or permanent, should be carried out within a period 
of 32 hours. If a temporary action is undertaken, there must also be a follow up 
permanent action carried out within a maximum of 28 days from the time that the 
defect / hazard was first identified.
CoP for the Classification of Highway Safety Defects & Hazards: v 3.0, r 0 10

Category 2a:  Category 2 defects & hazards are those which, following a risk 
assessment, are deemed not to represent an immediate or imminent hazard, or risk 
of short-term structural deterioration. Such hazards & defects may have safety 
implications, although of a lesser significance than Category 1 defects & hazards 
but are more likely to have serviceability or sustainability implications.  Category 2 
defects & hazards are categorised according to the risk probability and its likely 
impact, and the response time for a Category 2a defect or hazard is a maximum of 
10 days. If a temporary action is undertaken, there must also be a follow up 
permanent action carried out within a maximum of 28 days from the time that the 
defect / hazard was first identified.

Category 2b:  This category is used for defects & hazards in less urgent need of 
repair but nevertheless, where essential maintenance work is required. The 
maximum period of time for repair to be allocated to this category of defect or 
hazard is 28 days, and it is foreseeable that efficiencies may be gained from 
effective co-ordination of defects & hazards requiring a similar treatment, e.g. 
velocity or infra-red patching.

Category 2c:  Non- safety defects that could be carried out as part of a proactive 
maintenance program or improvement works. These will be addressed according to 
available resources and budgets.

4.4 Pothole type defects raised from Public enquires  
To help us to provide a cost effective and robust service to the public we do not 
separately inspect all types of defect that are reported to us through our public 
interfaces. To remove unnecessary hand offs, defects are automatically raised from 
the information given by the public. It is our intention to inspect and repair these 
defects at one visit however we have increased the minimum repair time from 32 
hours to 10 days.  
This will still give us an equlivilant response time than the original system, when an 
officer had the agreed ten days to investigate the public enquiry as

This does not affect defects that are categorised as requiring an immediate

4.6 Signs 
Due to the complexity and location of some signs it would be impracticable and 
unnecessary to replace signs in the time scales given. These should be adhered to 
in relation to the time allowed to react to any immediate safety hazard, e.g. a sign 
leaning into the road or one that could fall in tointo the footway but are only given as 
a guide in relation to replacement. 
We will replace the sign, if required as soon as reasonably practical. There will be 
times that the sign will not need replacement under the new traffic signs and general 
directions regulations, and this should be checked before completing the work.

Some highways have been dedicated and adopted with historic features that would

slopes, and drainage arrangements that present potential hazard situations worse 
than the investigatory levels suggested in this document. These should not be 
recorded as defects, as the highway has been adopted with these encumbrances 
and the public must take appropriate care. 
This would also include features such as stone sets or stone paving that is by its 
nature irregular in construction and should be treated consistently with the character 
of the area. Any defects untypical of the construction and design meeting 
investigatory level in such a location will be raised.

Defects caused by tree and vegetation roots are difficult to deal with in a permanent 
lasting manner. The environment, requirements of the trees and surface regularity 
need to be balanced. 
The following statement is made in the national guidance (roads liaisons group, well 
managed highway infrastructure). 
“Extensive root growth from larger trees can cause significant damage to the 
surface of footways, particularly in urban areas. A risk assessment should therefore 
be undertaken with specialist arboriculture advice on the most appropriate course of 
action, if possible, to avoid harm to the tree. In these circumstances, it may be 
difficult for authorities to reconcile their responsibilities for surface regularity, with 
wider environmental considerations and a reduced level of regularity may be 
acceptable.” 
Taking this into consideration defect caused by roots should be risk assessed and

Taking this into consideration defect caused by roots should be risk assessed and 
local conditions taken into consideration. This should include likely speeds of 
vehicles in the area and the type of user likely to be affected. Investigatory level 
defects that are likely to affect pedestrians or cyclists will need careful examination 
and, in most cases, should be repaired. 
Before repairing areas damaged by roots, advice from the arboriculture team should 
be obtained as to what can be done with the roots causing the problem so wherever 
possible a lasting repair can be carried out. 
If any investigatory level defects caused by tree roots are not to be repaired, then 
notes must be made in the confirm system detailing the reason and mitigation 
that has been put in place.

of	Practice	deals	with	the	“Routine”,	“Preventive”	and	“Periodic”	maintenance	of	bituminous	
surfaces.

SECTION 3
IMPORTANCE OF MAINTENANCE
3.1	 The 	timely	upkeep	and	maintenance	of	bituminous	surfacing	offers	numerous	benefits	
for preservation of road asset. The importance of overall maintenance is described below:
i) Reduction in rate of deterioration and improvement in life of road 
ii)	 Reduction 	in	Vehicle	Operation	Costs	(VOC)
iii) Reduction in rate of accidents 
iv)	 Keeping 	roads	traffic	worthy	in	all	weathers
v) Reduction in pollution due to reduced fuel consumption on well maintained pavem

Vehicle	Operation	Costs	(VOC)
iii) Reduction in rate of accidents 
iv)	 Keeping 	roads	traffic	worthy	in	all	weathers
v) Reduction in pollution due to reduced fuel consumption on well maintained pavement 
surface
vi)	 Savings 	in	budgetary	expenditure	of	restoration/	reconstruction	
3.2	 Timely 	 and	 regular	 maintenance	 of	 roads	 have	 been	 known	 to	 provide	 economic	
rate	of	return	as	high	as	15	to	20	percent	depending	upon	the	category	of	road	and	traffic	
volume. Moreover, it helps in deferring the demand for rehabilitation which otherwise is far 
more costlier than preventive maintenance. Therefore, timely and appropriate maintenance 
of	 bituminous	 surface	 using	 sustainable/suitable	 materials	 and	 methods	 is	 significant	 for	
preservation of road asset and to serve the intended purpose.

TYPES OF MAINTENANCE
4.1	 Maintenance 	 operations	 covered	 in	 this	 Code	 of	 Practice	 are	 classified	 into	 three	
broad categories
a) Routine Maintenance: This	 covers	 items	 such	 as	 filling	 of	 potholes,	 repairing	 of	
cracks	 and	 patch	 work,	 which	 are	 undertaken	 by	 the	 maintenance	 staff	 almost	
round	the	year.	Routine	maintenance	is	also	required	for	pavement	markings	on	the	
bituminous surfaces to guide the road users and improve road safety.

iii) Deformation: These include rutting, corrugations, shoving including those caused

7.2.1.1 Symptoms
A	surface	having	a	thin	film	of	excess	or	free	bituminous	binder	on	it,	which	creates	a	shiny,	
glass	like	reflecting	surface	tending	to	become	soft	in	hot	weather	and	slippery	in	cold	and	
wet	 weather

surface	having	a	thin	film	of	excess	or	free	bituminous	binder	on	it,	which	creates	a	shiny,	
glass	like	reflecting	surface	tending	to	become	soft	in	hot	weather	and	slippery	in	cold	and	
wet	 weather,	 eventually	 developing	 low	 skid	 resistance	 is	 referred	 to	 as	 bleeding	 or	 fatty	
bituminous surface. 
7.2.1.2 Location
Generally such defects develop along the wheel path but sometimes these are restricted 
to	isolated	locations	and	specific	lanes.	Many	a	time,	these	defects	are	seen	on	the	entire	
carriageway.
7.2.1.3 Causes 
Bleeding	occurs	in	hot	weather,	when	the	bituminous	binder	after	filling	the	available	voids	in	
compacted	bituminous	layer	moves	upward	under	traffic	movement	and	collects	as	a	thick	
film	on	the	surface.	The	process	is	not	reversible	during	cold	weather,	leading	to	permanent	
accumulation	of	binder	on	the	surface	with	passage	of	time	making	the	surface	fatty,	slippery	
and	skid	prone.	This	can	be	caused	by	one	or	combination	of	the	following	factors:

i)	
Excessive	binder	in	hot	mix	due	to	faulty	mix	design	or	lapses	in	quality	control	
ii)	 Lower 	voids	in	hot	mix
iii) Use of softer grade binder

v) Loss of cover aggregates in surface dressing
vi)	 Excessive 	application	of	binder	or	non-uniform	spreading	of	cover	aggregate	or	flaky/
elongated cover aggregate in surface dressing

A	 smooth	 surface	 has	 a	 low	 skid	 resistance	 and	 becomes	 very	 slippery	 when	 it	 is	 wet.	 
Such	a	condition	invites	safety	hazards,	especially	on	gradients,	bends,	and	intersections,

Smooth surface may be restricted to a lane/carriageway.

A	primary	cause	for	a	smooth	surface	is	the	polishing	of	aggregates	under	traffic.	Excessive

The	 severity	 level	 of	 smooth	 surface	 may	 be	 defined	 by	 skid	 number.	A	 surface	 with	 skid

The	rectification	consists	of	resurfacing	with	a	surface	dressing	course	or	a	premix	carpet	or	
microsurfacing	depending	upon	the	type	of	existing	surface.	Care	should	be	taken	to	select	
aggregates which have proven non-polishing characteristics. The carpet can be an open 
graded	mix.	A	slurry	seal	can	also	be	used	to	impart	anti	skid	texture	on	a	smooth	surface.

7.2.3.1 Symptoms
Streaking	is	characterized	by	the	appearance	of	alternate	lean	and	heavy	lines	of	bitumen

7.2.3.2 Location 
Streaking	may	occur	in	a	lane	or	a	carriageway.	
7.2.3.3 Causes
Longitudinal	streaking	results	when	alternate	longitudinal	strips	of	surface	contain	different	
quantities of bitumen due to non-uniform application of bitumen across the surface. Some of 
the	more	common	causes	of	streaking	are	mechanical	faults,	improper	or	poor	adjustment	
and	 operation	 of	 bitumen	 distributors.	 These	 streaks	 can	 also	 be	 formed	 as	 a	 result	 of	
applying the bituminous binder at too low temperature; a temperature at which bitumen is 
not	fluid	enough	to	be	delivered	in	a	uniform	and	smooth	flow	from	the	nozzles	on	the	spray	
bars.	All	these	causes	can	result	in	transverse	streaking	also.	Transverse	streaking	may	also	
be caused by spurts in the bitumen spray from the distribution spray bar. These could be as 
a	result	of	mechanical	faults	in	the	bitumen	distributor.	Transverse	streaking	may	result	in	
corrugation in the pavement s

a	result	of	mechanical	faults	in	the	bitumen	distributor.	Transverse	streaking	may	result	in	
corrugation in the pavement surface.

Not applicable
7.2.3.5 Treatment 
The	satisfactory	repair	for	longitudinal	and	transverse	streaking	is	to	remove	the	streaked

streaking	than	to	correct	it.	Whenever	mechanical	equipment	is	used	for	spraying	of	bitumen,	
distributor should be carefully operated.

50 mm deep and 500 mm wide. The large potholes are those greater than 50 mm deep and 
500 mm width.

8.1  Introduction 
8.1.1 Delays in maintenance increase the severity of distress in pavement leading to higher 
maintenance	expenditure.	Preventive	maintenance	is	a	planned	maintenance	activity,	which	
decreases	rate	of	surface	deterioration	and	extend	service	life	of	bituminous	pavement.	It	is	
a	maintenance	activity	as	a	planned	strategy	of	cost	effective	treatment	of	existing	roads	and	
its appurtenances that preserves the system, prevents future deterioration and improves the 
fu

.	It	is	
a	maintenance	activity	as	a	planned	strategy	of	cost	effective	treatment	of	existing	roads	and	
its appurtenances that preserves the system, prevents future deterioration and improves the 
functional condition of the system without contribution to load carrying capacity of pavement. 
Such treatments are cost effective, if provided on a pavement in fair to good condition. The 
placement of right preventive maintenance treatment at the right time saves pavement from 
leading to poor condition (Tables 5.1 to 5.3), where rehabilitation and reconstruction would 
be inevitable.

mitigated before their occurrence. This provides following long term solutions:
 Improved level of service resulting from improved pavement performance 
  Delayed need for rehabilitation and reconstruction 
 Life cycle cost saving

9.1 Need and Importance of Periodic Renewals 
Periodic renewals consist of the provision of a surfacing layer at regular intervals of time or 
at	a	specified	condition,	so	as	to	preserve	the	required	serviceability	level	of	the	pavement	
surface	 and	 offset	 the	 wear	 and	 tear	 caused	 by	 traffic	 and	 weathering.	 Periodic	 renewals

10.2.3 Bitumen Emulsion
Bitumen emulsion is a two-phase system consisting of bitumen, water and one or more 
additives	to	assist	in	formation	and	stabilization	and	to	modify	the	properties	of	the	emulsion.	
The bitumen is dispersed throughout the water phase in the form of discrete globules, typically

by	an	emulsifier.	Bitumen	emulsions	conforming	to	IS:	8887	are	recommended	for	various

maintenance	applications	including	preparation	of	cold	mixes	and	patching	mixes.
10.2.4 Foam Bitumen
Foaming of bitumen is a means of reducing the binder viscosity and increasing the binder 
volume.	Foam	bitumen	is	produced	in	an	expansion	chamber	in	which	cold	water,	between	
1	and	5%	by	weight	of	bitumen,	is	injected	under	pressure	into	hot	bitumen	to	produce	foam.	
Expansion	ratio	and	half	life	are	two	important	properties	of	foam	bitumen.	The	expansion	
ratio	is	defined	as	the	ratio	of	the	volume	of	foam	produced	to	the	volume	of	liquid	bitumen	
injected.	The	life	time	of	foam	is	expressed	as	the	‘half-life,	defined	as	the	time	after	which	
the	maximum	volume	of	foam	is	reduced	by	a	factor	of	two.	It	is	measured	in	seconds.	The	
foam	bitumen	is	used	for	stabilization	of	recycled	asphalt	pavement.

11.2 Pothole Filling/Patching
There	 are	 two	 main	 elements	 of	 durable	 pothole	 filling/patching;	 the	 material	 and	 the	 
repairs process. For every combination of these two factors, the cost effectiveness of the 
overall	 pothole	 filling/patching	 work	 will	 depend	 on	 material,	 labour	 and	 equipment	 costs	 
and	the	quantity	of	the	work.	The	most	economical	 	combination	of	materials	and	process	
to	 the	 extent	 possible	 should	 be	 adopted	 to	 produce	 long	 lasting	 and	 cost	 effective	 patch	
repairs.
11.3 Tools and Equipment for Pothole/Patch Repairs

The Long-Term Pavement Performance (LTPP) program has provided a wide variety of  
benefits related to field data collection equipment and procedures. It is estimated that  
90 percent of  State highway agencies use LTPP data collection equipment or test methods. 
Numerous LTPP data collection procedures have been adopted by the American Association 
of  State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) and industry, with the most 
widely implemented being this Distress Identification Manual for the Long-Term Pavement 
Performance Program (DIM) with thousands of  requests for copies of  the DIM being fulfilled. 
First issued in 1987, the DIM was developed to provide a consistent, uniform basis for 
collecting pavement distress data for the LTPP program. It has now been updated to this  
5th edition. 
The DIM provides a common language for describing cracks, potholes, rutting, spalling, 
and other pavement distresses being monitored by the LTPP program. Highway agencies 
at all levels

16. Abstract
Accurate, consistent, and repeatable distress evaluation surveys can be performed by using the Distress Identification Manual 
for the Long-Term Pavement Performance Program. Color photographs and drawings illustrate the distresses found in three basic 
pavement types: asphalt concrete-surfaced, jointed (plain and reinforced) portland cement concrete, and continuously reinforced 
concrete. Drawings of the distress types provide a reference to assess their severity. Methods for measuring the size of distresses 
and for assigning severity levels are given. The manual also describes how to conduct the distress survey and measu

a reference to assess their severity. Methods for measuring the size of distresses 
and for assigning severity levels are given. The manual also describes how to conduct the distress survey and measure cracks in 
the pavement. Sample forms for recording and reporting the data are included. The manual also tells how to calibrate and operate 
fault measurement devices.

distress. Highway agencies, airports, parking facilities, and others with significant investment  
in pavements will benefit from adopting a standard distress language.

fatigue cracking,” for example, it is

reports of  inconsistencies and variations caused by a lack of  standardized terminology.

FATIGUE CRACKING
Description
Occurs in areas subjected to repeated traffic loadings (wheel paths). Can be a series of  
interconnected cracks in early stages of  development. Develops into many-sided, sharp-
angled pieces, usually less than 0.3 m on the longest side, characteristically with a chicken 
wire/alligator pattern in later stages.
Must have a quantifiable area.
Severity Levels
LOW
An area of  cracks with no or only a few connecting cracks; cracks are not spalled or 
sealed; and pumping is not evident.
MODERATE
An area of  interconnected cracks forming a complete pattern; cracks may be slightly 
spalled; cracks may be sealed; and pumping is not evident.
HIGH
An area of  moderately or severely spalled interconnected cracks forming a complete 
pattern; pieces may move when subjected to traffic; cracks may be sealed; and pumping 
may be evident.
How to Measure
Record affected area at each severity level in square meters. If  different severity le

Visual distress survey procedures have been used in the LTPP program as the primary 
distress data collection method since 1995. The Distress Identification Manual for the Long-
Term Pavement Performance Program (DIM) is the basis for all distress surveys performed for 
the LTPP program.
During the visual distress survey, safety is the first consideration, as with all field data 
collection activities. All raters must adhere to the practices and authority of  the State or 
Canadian Province and follow the guidelines in LTPP directive D-42 or its latest version.

high, except as indicated on the form. Enter “0” for any distress types and/or severity 
levels not found. The distress types and severity levels should be identified by using

Description of  Data Sheet 9
This sheet is a continuation of  the distress survey data recorded on sheet 8 and is 
completed as described under data sheet 8. In addition, space is provided to list  
“Other” distress types found on the test section but not listed on data sheets 8 or 9.
Description of  Data Sheet 10
This data sheet provides space to record lane-to-shoulder dropoff  and lane-to-shoulder 
separation. Measurements are taken at the beginning of  the test section and at 15.25-m 
intervals (a total of  11 measurements for each distress) at the lane/shoulder interface  
or joint.
Lane-to-shoulder dropoff  i

rements are taken at the beginning of  the test section and at 15.25-m 
intervals (a total of  11 measurements for each distress) at the lane/shoulder interface  
or joint.
Lane-to-shoulder dropoff  is measured as the difference in elevation (to the nearest  
1 mm) between the pavement surface and the adjacent shoulder surface. Lane-to-
shoulder dropoff  typically occurs when the outside shoulder settles. However, heave of  
the shoulder may occur due to frost action or swelling soil. If  heave of  the shoulder is 
present, it should be recorded as a negative value.
Lane-to-shoulder separation is measured as the width of  the joint (to the nearest 1 mm) 
between the outside lane and the adjacent shoulder surface.
When the surveyor is unable to take a measurement due to an anomaly such as a sealant 
or patch material, a null value  is recorded and entered into the database.
At each point where there is no lane-to-shoulder dropoff  or lane-to-shoulder separation, 
enter “0.”

personnel and others responsible for using the faultmeter to measure JCP faulting and

al is intended for use by the FHWA-LTPP Regional Support Contractor (RSC) 
personnel and others responsible for using the faultmeter to measure JCP faulting and 
lane-to-shoulder dropoff  on LTPP pavement test sites. The change in joint faulting and

A. Response to Emergency Calls  
According to the procedure of the center regarding "Emergency Calls" -  
"Any call regarding all types of violence, abuse, neglect of the helpless, threats of murder,

- Immediate report to the police

It was found that some inquiries on emergency issues (violence) were directed by representatives of the center for further conversation with a social worker, while others were not, contrary to the procedure. For example:  
In two calls (see appendix calls number 6, 29), a third party reported violence between partners,  
where in one call (6) the representative told the caller to direct the abused woman to call center 106,  
where she could speak with a social worker, while in the second call (29) the representative told the caller to direct the woman back to them at center 118,  
where she could speak with a social worker. It should be noted that failing to transfer an emergency call  
to a social worker may prevent optimal handling of the caller and contradicts the essence of the assistance that the center is supposed to provide.

It should be noted that failing to transfer an emergency call to a social worker may prevent optimal treatment for the caller and contradicts the essence of the assistance that the center is supposed to provide.

Supplier's Response  
According to the procedure, the social worker at the center is not supposed to provide a long-term solution. When a caller is capable of reaching out independently to an authorized entity – police, social worker at the council, and if they are willing to do so, we direct them to the relevant parties directly and there is no need to refer them to the social worker at the center.  
The role of the social worker is to respond to the emotional state of the caller at that moment. If the caller is incapable – crying, agitated, emotional – they are referred to the social worker at the center whose sole role is to improve the caller's capability and persuade them to reach out to an entity that will provide a long-term solution.  
Therefore, if a third party is calling – there will never be a referral to the social worker at the center, but rather a referral to an external authorized service.  
Since in calls 6 and 29 the caller is a third party, the representative's actions were completely appropriate when they directed the caller to the third party and not to the social worker at the center.

The State of Israel is investing significant efforts and resources in the development, upgrading, and maintenance of transportation infrastructure in the urban area. As a result, there is a growing need to carry out numerous works, which require the regulation of traffic to ensure the safety of both workers and road users. 

The guide to traffic arrangements at work sites on urban roads below details the various options for the placement of temporary traffic arrangements required for carrying out works on the road, with the aim of reducing risks, maintaining a high level of safety, and providing maximum service to all road users. 

In light of the above, by virtue of my authority as the national traffic supervisor (according to Regulation 16 of the Traffic Regulations, 1961), I hereby approve the traffic arrangements appearing in the diagrams (without change) for placement on the road in accordance with and subject to the instructions of the competent authorities as determined in the permit. 

I hereby instruct all local traffic authorities to allow the establishment of temporary traffic arrangements for carrying out works on the road using diagrams from this guide. 

This guide cancels all 'diagrams' in the urban area that were used prior to the publication of this guide, in order to achieve standardization of temporary traffic arrangements at work sites on the road in the State of Israel.

This is aimed at standardizing temporary traffic arrangements at work sites on the roads in the State of Israel. In any case where a diagram from this guide does not fully match the actual conditions on the ground (according to the professional standards detailed in the guide), diagrams from the guide should not be used, and the local authority must prepare a detailed traffic arrangement plan and approve it legally in accordance with the provisions of the law and regulations. This plan will be limited and valid only for the planning location. For clarification, a local traffic authority does not have the authority to approve generic traffic arrangements (diagrams). If a local traffic authority believes that a traffic arrangement (diagram) is needed that is not included in the guide, the authority must contact the national traffic supervisor along with its proposal to update the guide, which will be examined within a permanent steering committee that will operate to update and improve this guide from time to time.

Pavement Maintenance  
A paved road is subject to physical pressures from traffic loads and the effects of weather. The upper part of the road, which bears the pressures and loads, is called the pavement. It consists of various processed layers of subgrade, infrastructure, and asphalt, laid on the subgrade. From engineering and economic perspectives, different pavements may exist, each with different costs and life expectancies. The structure of the pavement, its cost, and its life expectancy depend on the thickness of the processed layers and their quality; the desired level of service (quality and comfort of travel under safety conditions); maintenance measures during the service period; traffic load forecasts during this period; and environmental conditions, including the type of soil on which the pavement is built. Below are details of the metrics used to determine the quality of the pavement.  
1. Pavement Condition Index: The Pavement Condition Index (PCI) is calculated based on a visual survey of the pavement surface and determines the types of damage caused to it and the severity of that damage. These damages can result from asphalt aging, cracking, structural material issues, lack of friction, lack of drainage, depressions in the road, and wear. The index establishes the level of damage to the pavement on a scale ranging from 0 (very distressed road) to 100 (new and intact road).

These can be caused by asphalt aging, cracks, structural material, lack of friction, lack of drainage, depressions in the road, and wear. The index determines the level of damage to the pavement on a scale ranging from 0 (very rough road) to 100 (completely new and intact road).

2. Surface Roughness Index: The Surface Roughness Index, Present Serviceability Rating (hereinafter - PSR), reflects the level of unevenness in the road surface height and the issues in the upper asphalt layer of the pavement. This index objectively determines the level of vehicle vibration during travel. The source of the vibration is the roughness of the pavement, which determines the quality and safety of the ride. The level of quality

Safety actually reflects the level of service of the road. The level of service is ranked on a scale ranging from 0 (unacceptable service level due to a very bumpy road) to 5 (very high service level due to a smooth and comfortable road). Among other things, the maintenance of the pavement is intended to reduce the roughness of the pavement surface, thereby improving the quality of the ride and its safety. The damage caused to road users due to the deterioration of the pavement and the postponement of the necessary maintenance is reflected not only in an increasing risk to travel safety and the occurrence of accidents but also in rising operational costs. 

3. Structural Deficiency Index: The structural deficiency index expresses the difference between the existing tolerance of the road in its current state and the calculated tolerance required for the planning horizon over the next 10-20 years. The index is measured in centimeters or inches. Structural deficiency can generally range from 0 to 20 cm: a deficiency between 0 to 5 cm is negligible and usually does not require maintenance; a higher deficiency requires renewing the existing asphalt layer and adding an additional asphalt layer.

Maintenance of Lighting  
Driving at night, when visibility is naturally limited compared to daytime driving, affects the driver's perception and reaction time, orientation ability, and overall performance. Two infrastructure factors will assist the driver under these conditions: the quality of the lighting and the quality of the road surface on those roads. For nighttime driving to be safe, the infrastructure must allow the driver to see further than what the vehicle's lights provide. According to a publication by the Ministry of Transport, the average impact of good lighting will lead to a reduction of about 30% in road accidents at night on those roads.  
According to the Ministry of Transport's guidelines from 1996, there is an obligation to install lighting at the following sites: every intersection, even near sections of road that are not illuminated along their length; continuous road sections between intersections where the distance between them does not exceed one kilometer; transition lighting at the approaches to the intersection; and in any place of security or safety importance.  
As of the end of the audit, March 2017, no updated data was found in the company's offices regarding roads that do not comply with the Ministry of Transport's guidelines. Road Marking  
Road signs along the way are included in the traffic management system of the road network and are part of the valid signage board. Road signs are intended to convey various messages to road users, and they are important to ensure safe traffic flow on the road. The meaning of the markings pertains to all road users, including drivers and pedestrians. The functional and safety importance of markings on the road is particularly evident at night and in adverse weather conditions. An insufficient level of visibility of markings with immediate safety significance can lead road users to make incorrect decisions while driving, which increases the risk of accidents. For example, inadequate marking of crosswalks. Additionally, in certain cases, markings have even greater safety significance. In these cases, the markings do not have additional "backup" that reinforces the message they convey. For instance, the safety importance of marking a boundary is less critical when there are guide posts at the roadside. If the marking is the only means of conveying the message to drivers, its absence can severely impact the safety level of the road. Maintenance of Safety Barriers  
A safety barrier is intended to serve two purposes: on one hand, it must stop the vehicle to prevent it from leaving the roadway, and on the other hand, it must minimize the injury to the vehicle's occupants in the event of a collision with it. The stronger the barrier, the better it will perform in meeting the first requirement; the more flexible the barrier, the better it will perform in meeting the second requirement. The inter-ministerial committee for examining traffic and safety devices, headed by the Ministry of Transport, is responsible for examining the various means and approving them.  
In August 2005, the inter-ministerial committee decided that the State of Israel would adopt both the methodology for examining and approving safety barriers used in Europe and that used in the United States. Accordingly, any barrier submitted for approval by the inter-ministerial committee for examining traffic and safety devices must meet the requirements specified in one of these two standards. As early as January 2009, the then Deputy Director of Operations and Maintenance at the company instructed that every new safety barrier installed on the company's roads as part of maintenance or development activities would be a safety barrier approved by the inter-ministerial committee and the authorized bodies within the company. People  
The intersection - the meeting place of the city's streets - is a gathering place for people. At the urban intersection, many people see even more people, and as a result, these intersections are the catalysts of city life. Urban intersections are developed (or planned) to be centers of urban activity, typically housing commercial uses, public buildings, and significant cultural institutions, among others.  
Movements  
The intersection is the meeting place of movements on the street. At the intersection, pedestrians, cyclists, and motor vehicle passengers meet each other. Different movements, in their nature, speed, and scope, transition from a state of direct and simple movement on the street to a state of consideration, integration, and intertwining with other movements.  
The movements that occur simultaneously 'next to each other' along the street change at the intersection to 'one after the other.' The transition from 'street movement' to 'intersection movement' requires a completely different awareness of movement for all street users. The transition necessitates corresponding planning awareness from street planners.

Spaces
The special needs of the intersection as an urban focal point with increased activity, and the fact that at the intersection the nature of movements changes from continuous traffic to crossing traffic, necessitate the creation of unique spaces at the intersection. In addition to the exclusive traffic lanes for all street users, the intersection includes spaces for special activities, stopping, waiting, directing, and monitoring, among others. The most problematic and challenging space is the "crossing area" - a space shared by different movements, where movements occur in different directions, at different speeds, with varying intensities and a greater scope of conflicts. This is a space that requires special safety preparations from all those involved in street planning and operation.
This book deals with the people at the intersection, movements at the intersection, and spaces at the intersection.

B. Guidelines for street planning in cities - pedestrian movement  
This book is the first of the specialized books, and its main subject is the detailed space required for pedestrians in the street - its dimensions and quality. The first part of the book deals with the centrality of the pedestrian and presents it in two aspects: the first aspect - the pedestrian as a human essence, as the focal point of all urban planning, and as the primary consumer of public space. In the center of the guidelines, the areas to be allocated for pedestrians are defined according to the expected activity characteristics in the street, and the dimensions of these spaces according to the scope and nature of the activity.  
Walking strip - a strip on the sidewalk along the street, designated for longitudinal movement of pedestrians only.  
Auxiliary strip - the strip on the sidewalk or along the roadway/parking, designated for the installation of stationary objects and overhead infrastructure, with the aim of clearing the pedestrian strip from obstacles and nuisances.

Introduction  
The initial characteristics of the intersection are usually formulated during the descriptive planning phase, where the city streets are determined as part of an overall urban fabric. The planning principles of the intersection in the space constitute the "iron rules" that must guide the planning team, and deviation from them constitutes a significant and substantial harm to the design of the intersection.  
Maximum Visibility of the Intersection  
The intersection must be visible and exposed to its users before they reach it, allowing for quick and easy identification. The topographical structure of the planned intersection area, the vertical and horizontal curves of the road along the proposed intersection, the scenic environment of the intersection area - all these and others are the characteristics that influence the determination of its location, already in the initial planning stage.  
Below are some examples to avoid during the initial planning of the intersection:  
- Establishing an intersection near or at the peak of a vertical curve with a small radius;  
- Establishing an intersection near or within the limits of a horizontal curve with a small radius;

Maintaining the correct distance between intersections  
The distance between two intersections should, on one hand, be large enough to allow proper functioning of the traffic between them, and short enough, on the other hand, to allow accessibility and space for choice in traffic from one place to another.  
Thus, the determination of the distance between intersections will be influenced by the types of streets along which they are located.  
In urban streets, the distance will be smaller to allow good accessibility for vehicles and pedestrians and to distribute the load for turns among more intersections, while along urban roads, the distance will be larger to allow a better level of service for motor vehicle traffic.

B. Intersection with Traffic Sign Control
An intersection with traffic sign control characterizes a significant portion of urban intersections, where traffic volumes do not justify traffic lights, and traffic is directed and guided by signs and various geometric means (medians, traffic islands, sight triangles, etc.). Compared to other intersections, a regular intersection with only traffic sign control is mainly characterized by its small area requirement and the fact that it lacks the features present in a signalized intersection and a roundabout. There is no clear time allocation for different road users to cross the intersection. As a result, it is less unambiguous regarding pedestrian traffic than the signalized intersection and the roundabout. Larger sight distances are required for its existence compared to a roundabout.

C. Roundabout
In a roundabout (or circular intersection), the arms of the intersection connect to a one-way circular path that links them. The roundabout intersection stands out with several distinct characteristics. It is convenient for vehicle movement, as traffic flows in only one direction, and the types of conflicts are less severe than those at other types of intersections. It is less convenient for pedestrian movement due to the traffic structure for vehicles, but it is safer for all road users. A. Introduction  
It is reasonable to assume that the initial formulation of the intersection template will involve the combination of planning variables according to the thematic guidelines of the guideline books. From this stage, a balancing process takes place in practice - a cyclical methodological process of stages in the formulation of the template as faithfully as possible to the priorities, principles, and anchors established in the portrait.  
The product of this planning stage will be a variety of alternatives for the intersection template, from which the one that serves the principles of the portrait as faithfully and balanced as possible will be selected.  
B. Balancing the Space  
The optimal situation in which sufficient space can be allocated to each user at the intersection for their activity is not only impractical but largely undesirable. A clear example of this is the desire to provide a satisfactory solution for motor traffic during peak hours, a situation that creates waste of space throughout the day and even poses safety risks - an excess of traffic lanes at the intersection without encouraging fast travel on one hand, and careless crossing on the other hand.

The need to save space and optimize its use requires planners to deal with compromises and informed concessions, which can be made through the following means:

- A thoughtful choice to allocate space at intersections to reduce the number of allocations for certain users, while avoiding providing space for other users. Examples include completely giving up parking lanes on narrow streets and relinquishing a lane for stationary objects on one side of the street.

- Minimizing the dimensions of the planned lanes at intersections to the smallest reasonable size, even at the expense of their operational efficiency. Examples include narrowing motor traffic lanes or giving up part of the traffic lanes in a way that reduces traffic efficiency.

- Creating shared spaces for multiple users, even if this sharing diminishes the level of service at the intersection. A detailed outline plan defining the dimensions of the intersections and network components cannot be completed. This stage is relevant and necessary in the rehabilitation of existing fabrics, as a system without the execution of this stage may redefine the way the area of the intersection - statutorily anchored - is allocated among the various intersection users in order to create a new balance among them.

4.3.3 Raw Materials for Intersection Planning  
In addition to the measurements required for any intersection planning at any level (conceptual, outline, detailed design), additional raw materials are needed for the planning of the intersection.  
A. Statutory City Building Plan and Development Plan  
The planning team must be familiar with the valid statutory plan that includes the intersection and its surroundings. In this context, the planning team must obtain information about the planned changes in the area of the intersection regarding construction and development, particularly concerning the boundaries of streets and plots, connections of new streets, and additions of uses and activity centers in the vicinity of the intersection.  
B. Traffic Counts and Traffic Forecasting  
Each intersection must be planned based on quantitative data relating to traffic volume throughout the day and during peak hours, as well as the distribution of traffic at the intersection in its various directions. At intersections of local streets, the count can be sample-based or limited to peak hours only. At intersections of collector roads and major intersections, the count should be complete for at least 14 hours a day. In commercial areas, shopping malls, and uses with different days and times of activity, counts will also be conducted on Fridays, Saturday evenings, and at other times and days suitable for the activity hours of each use.

In the areas of 14 collectors and at road intersections, the counting will be complete for commerce, in malls, and in uses with different days and times of operation. Counts will also be conducted on Fridays, Saturday evenings, and at other times and days suitable for the operating hours of each use. The traffic planner must check if an increase in traffic volume at the intersection is expected beyond the normal anticipated traffic growth in the entire system. In particular, they must examine whether a change in the distribution of movements is expected in the future.

C. Profiles of the streets meeting at the intersection  
There is great importance in having profiles of the arms of the intersection, which are prepared according to the procedures in the guidelines for street space planning.

D. Data collection and photographing the intersection area  
Planning changes at an existing intersection will only be carried out after the planning team has surveyed the intersection and studied its characteristics and components directly and without intermediaries, and has recorded and marked the main components and characteristics of the intersection. It is advisable to accompany the survey of the intersection with photographs of its areas and characteristics, to allow for a visual memory of the intersection even weeks and months after the survey takes place.

E. Traffic accident data at the intersection  
In the case of planning improvements at an existing intersection, data must be collected regarding the number of traffic accidents and their types over the past three years. An analysis of the causes of the accidents should be conducted.

The choice between the capacity of the intersection and its friendliness and safety is primarily expressed in the intersection design. In a crossroads, we aim to provide mainly capacity: during the establishment of its basic characteristics for the fast and efficient passage of vehicles through it, as opposed to a street intersection where we will ensure to design the intersection as an integral part of the urban fabric, with greater attention to soft movements and a balance between the different movements within it.
The basic characteristics of the intersection and the profiles of the streets meeting within it are the main raw material required for its design, and it will often become apparent that there is a mismatch between the characteristics of the lanes in the street segments (or roads) and the characteristics of the lanes crossing the intersection.
In the street segment, each lane carries traffic in only one direction, whereas in the intersection, the traffic splits into different directions; 
In the street segment, there are few 'partners' for the passage time along it, whereas in the intersection, there are many 'partners' for the passage time at many points within it; 
Blocking a lane in a street segment usually causes delays in only one street, whereas blocking a lane at an intersection can affect multiple streets.

From the passage along its length, and conversely at the intersection, there are many 'partners' for the passage time at many points within its area; blocking a lane on a street segment usually causes delays on just one street, whereas blocking a lane at an intersection can affect a much larger area than the intersection itself. Therefore, creating the intersection is a complex process, in which the planning team must find the necessary balance between the different needs of road users and their immediate and distant environment. The purpose of the following sections is to establish preliminary rules to guide the planning team during the determination of the number of lanes at the intersection.

Lanes at an Intersection  
A. Signalized Intersection  
The number of lanes at a signalized intersection (an intersection will generally be signalized) depends on the ability of the traffic signal to operate during peak hours at a reasonable level of service and with minimal delays for motorized road users. At a signalized intersection, there is no fundamental limitation on the number of lanes that can be established on each arm of the intersection, and it will be adjusted, as much as possible, to the determining number of traffic volumes at the intersection.  
However, it is worth noting that it is not always possible to adjust the number of lanes to the traffic volumes at the intersection due to three main reasons:  
1. The number of lanes in the existing situation is limited due to right-of-way data and the need to allocate traffic lanes also for other movements such as public transportation/light rail, bike lanes, sidewalks for pedestrians, etc.  
2. Establishing a large number of lanes on each arm leads to the extension of crosswalks and results in longer green time intervals, which reduces the overall green time in the cycle.  
3. As crosswalks are extended, the exposure of pedestrians to motorized traffic increases, and the level of safety decreases.

A. Justifications for implementing a free right turn lane  
A free right turn lane is a lane that allows vehicles turning right to move from one street to another without crossing the intersection's core area (Diagram 5.6). On one hand, free turns help, especially at high-capacity intersections, to alleviate motor vehicle traffic congestion. On the other hand, they complicate pedestrian movement and lengthen their travel paths, pose a significant safety hazard for cyclists, and hinder visibility during the merging with the lane they intersect. A separate right turn in two lanes must be signalized.  
Here are the justifications for implementing a free right turn or avoiding its implementation:  
Free right turns are allowed in the following cases, and only when there is a triangular traffic island:  
1. At road intersections;  
2. At signalized street intersections, when the two intersecting streets are dual-lane collectors;  
3. When connecting to an urban road or a dual-lane collector street, where only right turns are present at the intersection;  
4. At roundabouts on divided streets and roads ("banana").

A. Introduction  
Right turn lanes are generally special lanes that are added to the continuous lanes approaching the intersection. A situation where a lane is designated for right turn only is possible when the volume of traffic turning right is particularly high, and separating the right-turning traffic from the continuous traffic will greatly facilitate the operation of the intersection. Special right turn lanes are usually found at intersections of two-lane collector streets or at road junctions. A special right turn lane should not be constructed on a single-lane two-way street.  
There are two different cases for implementing right turn lanes:  
The first case - a lane leading to a free right turn as described in section 5.5.2. Such a free turn is not efficient if it opens too close to the intersection to provide sufficient storage length for vehicles that may use it - in such a case, we will encounter its disadvantages for all road users (mainly vulnerable users), without fully realizing its advantages.  
The second case - a lane leading to a signalized intersection where, for various reasons (geometric structure of the intersection...

They may be used - in such a case we will receive the disadvantages of addressing all road users (mainly vulnerable users), without fully utilizing its advantages. The second case - a lane leading to a signalized intersection where, for various reasons (geometric structure of the intersection, pedestrian and bicycle traffic, preference for public transportation), the right turn is separated at the traffic light from the straight movement, and then a separate lane of sufficient length for storage is required for the efficient functioning of the turn. In the case of a busy turn at a signalized intersection, there may even be a signalized right turn from two lanes, and storage will be required accordingly.  
B. Justifications for implementing special lanes for right turns  
Below are the justifications for implementing special lanes for right turns (the justification marked with an asterisk (*) is a prerequisite for the justifications that follow):  
1) The right turn lane is not executed at the expense of the pedestrian traffic lane, and a standard lane remains.  
2) There is an appropriate safety solution for integrating the right turn with the continuous traffic of bicycles.  
3) The volume of traffic to the right justifies the implementation of a separate lane.  
4) The right turn is integrated with a continuous lane for public transportation.

A. Introduction  
Special left turn lanes are required to allow turning vehicles to slow down without disrupting the main traffic, to wait if necessary without interfering with the continuous traffic, and to turn left when there is a gap available in the opposing continuous direction.  
There is a particular need for left turn lanes mainly at signalized intersections, where it is essential to separate the continuous traffic, which has high volumes, from the left turns, which have lower traffic volumes.  
B. Justifications for Implementing Special Left Turn Lanes

At least one lane must always be reserved for left turns at intersections where a left turn is planned, with one lane reserved for left turns on each approach. At signalized intersections on high-traffic roads, it is advisable to reserve two lanes for left turns along the urban road.  
The establishment of left turn lanes shall not, under any circumstances, come at the expense of pedestrian traffic.

The longitudinal slope is an additional component in the longitudinal profile of two roads meeting at an intersection, which must be considered for evaluating the location of the intersection. An excessively steep slope in the intersection area causes four problematic phenomena:

B. Starting uphill at a controlled access (either by a traffic sign or by a traffic light) is difficult when the slope before the intersection is steep;  
C. The slope reduces braking ability when going downhill;  
D. A vehicle making a turn from the downhill direction to the right or left, or turning from the right or left into the downhill direction, receives an opposite lateral slope (Diagram 5.8).

Sight Distance at Intersections  
Introduction  
One of the most influential issues in the design of the intersection and its surroundings, in determining its physical boundaries and its safety aspects, is the sight distance at the intersection (Diagram 5.28). The sight distance at the intersection is the area required at the intersection and its surroundings, so that all road users coming from different directions and in different traffic lanes can see each other and respond appropriately.  
The sight distance is, therefore, the basic area that determines the intersection space, its physical boundaries, and the right-of-way lines at all corners of the intersection, including the determination of permissible building boundaries on the corner lots at the various arms of the intersection. Due to its safety importance, this area cannot be reduced below the necessary threshold; however, it can be expanded for various reasons, including urban, physical, scenic, and other aspects.  
The street where traffic has the right of way at that intersection will be referred to in the following section as "the main street," "the primary direction," or "the principal street," regardless of its classification in the network, and the street where traffic is required to yield the right of way will be referred to as "the secondary street" or "the secondary direction."

Components of the visibility area and their engineering significance 
Within the visibility area at an intersection, there are three zones that require examination (some of which overlap): 
- The area required for a driver coming from the secondary direction to see the visibility triangle of approaching vehicles on the main street, in order to make a decision whether to cross the intersection or wait for the approaching vehicle to pass in order to cross safely. 
- The area that is very close to the intersection, where pedestrian movements occur. This is the corner area of the street where vulnerable users are on their way to cross one of the arms of the intersection. 
Maintaining a clear visibility area in the corner of the street will minimize as much as possible the conflicts between intersection users.

Introduction  
As can be understood from the description of the planning process in the previous chapters, the final design of each intersection is a unique case that meets the profile of the intersection as characterized by its planners above. No two intersections are identical - each design reflects the optimal balance of all planning variables as explained there. The purpose of the guideline book is not to dictate fixed solutions for typical intersections, but to encourage a planning process that emphasizes the unique physical and movement expression of each intersection. At the same time, the book presents systematic principles that will "help road users understand the expected behavior at intersections and improve their movement and safety performance.  
To illustrate the desired outcomes from the design process, this chapter presents several templates of common intersections. The templates showcase typical cases of hierarchical interactions between urban streets - local with local, local with collector, divided collector with collector. These templates incorporate the information and design principles as presented in the various guideline books for street planning, so they display the recommended solutions for pedestrian, bicycle, and motor vehicle movement, and their integration into the components of the intersection.

In the years of the State of Israel, various trends of population dispersion and concentration have led to the current distribution, in which 70% of the population is concentrated in four metropolitan areas that are not as dense as most metropolitan areas in the world. Alongside them, there are urban and rural settlements in the periphery of the country. Despite all this, the State of Israel ranks high among countries where most of the population lives in cities, and thus the street, which is the artery of life, culture, and economy of the city, occupies a central and irreplaceable space in the daily existence of most citizens of the state.  
In light of this, and due to the special importance given to the street among all those engaged in the fields of engineering, behavioral sciences, and the humanities, an innovative system of guidelines for street planning was prepared about a decade ago, which replaced the previous guidelines and connected the best knowledge in Israel with the best global knowledge accumulated in the field of urban construction and architecture, combined with the transportation sector. This was done after the government policy for land conservation and mixed-use, prioritization of public transportation, safety, and quality of life was also integrated into the books.  
The urban structure, in which residential, employment, education, culture, and commercial uses are grouped together, inherently generates significant traffic.

The government's policy is also focused on land conservation and mixed-use, prioritizing public transportation, safety, and quality of life. The urban structure, which combines residential, employment, education, culture, and commercial uses, inherently generates significant movement of diverse populations for various purposes and between different locations. The Ministry of Transportation's policy generally states that walking is the preferred mode of transport that should be encouraged as much as possible as an alternative to motorized travel, followed by prioritizing public transportation and bicycle use.

First and foremost, we are pedestrians before we are drivers, which is why an entire book in the series is dedicated to guidelines for pedestrian movement in Israel, emphasizing safety aspects, as the number of accidents involving pedestrians is still high, necessitating efforts for their prevention. 

Bicycle use, as an alternative to car travel, has gained significant momentum in Israel over the past decade, aligning with sustainability. This policy states that bicycle use as a complementary and alternative means to private vehicles and public transportation is worthy of encouragement, evidenced by the increasing investment in bicycle infrastructure in Israel, alongside the understanding that investment in the safety of cyclists as road users is essential.

Complete and Alternative Transportation Policy of the Ministry of Transportation for private vehicles and public transportation is worthy of encouragement, as evidenced by the increasing investment in bicycle infrastructure in Israel, alongside the understanding that safety for cyclists as vulnerable road users must be prioritized. The update of the guidelines was requested in light of the intensive use of them by planners and authorities, which led to the accumulation of requests, comments, recommendations, and insights for updates and additions to the guideline books. Additionally, there has been significant progress in paving infrastructure for cyclists. In light of all the above, an updated edition of the guidelines for street planning in cities is presented to you. Special thanks to all those involved in this work, to the steering committee, to the team writing the guidelines, and to the Senior Transportation Planning Division that promoted this important update. With great appreciation.

The city centers have become a deterrent and harmful place. Even in new construction areas, it is not possible to guarantee road dimensions that allow everyone to move quickly from any point to any point by private vehicle and to park their car conveniently and close to their destination.  
The perception that addressed traffic in cities, mainly from the aspects of capacity and service level for vehicles, has been replaced in developed countries by a new perception that emphasizes quality of life, safety, and a redistribution of public space. The new urban planning reduces the area allocated to private vehicles in favor of space for public transportation, soft movements (bicycles and pedestrians), and for protective areas and permeable surfaces for stormwater drainage.  
In this new worldview, there is also a notable increase in listening and attention to the public's desires. Experience worldwide shows that public opinion has changed, and people are willing to give up some of the advantages of private vehicles in favor of improving their quality of life. The central issues that have become part of an ongoing dialogue with the public are: more safety, less traffic flow, less noise and air pollution, less space for private vehicle movement, and more space for gardening, play, walking, and cycling.

As part of the new approach, greater attention is directed towards pedestrians; exclusive walking paths for pedestrian traffic are defined, and any other use is prohibited. Urban pedestrian traffic is receiving renewed recognition, and it is not permissible to harm it whenever there is a need to improve the traffic conditions for vehicles. Increasing the number of pedestrians at the expense of private vehicle use saves space in the urban environment, allows for direct contact with the community, and strengthens the sense of security in the urban space. Pedestrians are being recognized anew as a means of transportation and as a central entity in the city, with guaranteed maximum space for their activities, independent of the needs of other road users.  
However, the pedestrian is not merely a 'traffic device' that integrates into the array of transportation means in the city. The pedestrian embodies the human essence of the city, and their spontaneous and human movement is the primary expression of the connection between the environment and the community. Therefore, a new perception is emerging in cities around the world that sees the urban street not only as a route for movement but also as a space for community life.  
The strengthening of pedestrian traffic and its return to the streets occurs alongside two other significant changes in the transportation system of the city: substantial strengthening and improvement of public transportation in all its forms, and the integration of bicycles as a distinct urban transportation tool alongside vehicles, but without compromising pedestrian conditions!

It addresses the various components of the public space in city streets and is consolidated in several guideline books as detailed below:

A. Guidelines for Planning the Street Space
This book serves as the foundation and overarching framework of the guideline system, in which the fundamental guidelines for street planning are consolidated. The book details the foundational concept of the guideline system, placing the individual and their well-being at the center of the public space.

The book emphasizes the essential distinction between 'urban street' and 'urban road,' which serves as a basic benchmark for the planning of public space, as detailed below:

Urban Street - A space in the city that serves all urban activities (traffic, housing, commerce, etc.), where the important movement component is accessibility.

Urban Road - An urban space primarily used for transit between parts of the city, where the important movement component is mobility.

The core of the book is to provide guidance for the planning process of the street in a way that includes a balanced consideration of all planning components - this is the formulation of the street's portrait and its pattern.

Street portrait - the program for street planning. In formulating the street portrait, the planning team is guided to consider all the components that influence the design of the street.  
Types of expected movements on the street - pedestrians, bicycles, public transportation, private vehicles, service and emergency vehicles.  
Components of expected stay on the street - sidewalk activity and street activity of pedestrians, bicycle parking, public transportation stations, private vehicle parking, stopping areas for service vehicles.  
Interactions between different movements - intersections, crosswalks, etc.  
Components of above-ground and underground infrastructure as well as landscape and environmental design elements - trees, vegetation, shading elements, street furniture, etc.  
The planner is required to determine the existence of the various components in the planned street - their quantity and intensity. Definitions and Concepts
Below are the main definitions and concepts used in these guidelines for planning 
traffic arrangements for pedestrians:
Soft movements - a collective term for the movement of soft users - pedestrians,

Public space - everything that is not included in the private or built areas of the city, namely - 
rights of way and open public spaces (parks).
The sidewalk - a part of the right of way in the street designated for pedestrians and street facilities. 
The sidewalk includes the walking strip, the auxiliary strip, the curb strip, and the activity space, 
as explained below.
Walking strip - the walking strip is the part of the sidewalk designated exclusively for pedestrian 
movement along the street (see details in section 4.3).
Auxiliary strip - the auxiliary strip is the part of the sidewalk designated for housing street facilities and 
fixed infrastructure that serve all street users. Additionally, local stationary activities for pedestrians 
may be allowed in it (see details in section 4.4).
Curb strip - the curb strip is the part of the sidewalk located adjacent to the street curb, and is intended 
to expand the pedestrian space according to the needs of the street curb.

Additionally, local stationary activity can be allowed.  
4.4 The curb strip - The curb strip is a part of the sidewalk located adjacent to the street curb, intended for expanding the pedestrian space according to the needs of the street curb, as well as for accommodating facilities and aids for activity and design of the curb (see details in section 4.5).  
Activity space - Activity space is an extension of the pedestrian space (along the entire sidewalk or in parts of it), intended for increased pedestrian activity, or for design considerations of the street space (see details in section 4.6).  
Pedestrian path - A movement strip for pedestrians that is not within the right-of-way, or a movement strip that is within the right-of-way but is disconnected and distanced from the road (mainly in intercity areas).

Who is (and what is) a pedestrian
Traffic devices of various kinds are designed to lead us quickly, efficiently, comfortably, and as safely as possible to our desired destination. We, as pedestrians, also constitute a 'traffic device' - a key partner in the array of traffic devices in the city. We are a sophisticated device, without propulsion systems, without mechanical steel enclosures, without engines and accelerators, and with very few laws and regulations dictating how to behave at any moment.

However, walking is much more than just movement - it is our natural state. Often, it is itself our desired destination. Walking encompasses, in addition to movement efficiency, a response to our feelings, our mood, our desire to see and be seen, to do things together - to meet, participate, and enjoy the open space.

The pedestrian is the most important consumer of public space in the city. It is their human essence. The nature and quality of the city's streets (as opposed to "urban roads" where the pedestrian is mentioned above) are primarily based on the presence of pedestrians. Contrary to the common practice for decades, the allocation of spaces and resources to various users in the street domain should be done "from the edges inward" - allocating space to the pedestrian first.

Firstly, the allocation of spaces and resources to different users in the street should be based on the presence of pedestrians. Contrary to the common practice for decades, it is appropriate that the allocation be done "from the edges inward" - the pedestrian should be allocated what is necessary for them at the sides of the street, and the remaining space should be allocated to other users according to urban priority. 

As pedestrian accessibility increases and its quality improves, it can be expected that a larger population will prefer this mode of transportation in the city. Proper design and good maintenance of pedestrian infrastructure encourage and promote walking in larger volumes. Pedestrians prefer safe, attractive, comfortable, and easy-to-use arrangements. Large volumes of pedestrians help provide a sense of security and contribute to the success of urban activity areas and commercial streets, enhancing community vitality and the urban economy.

Contrary to common sentiments, the sidewalk should not be seen as the leftover space for walking after allocating the road for vehicle traffic and parking, and care should be taken to avoid placing in it the 'remnants of the street.'

Why Pedestrians Do Not Walk  
Many factors can deter potential pedestrians from walking and lead to a preference for using private vehicles, even for short trips. Since pedestrians are the most vulnerable and slowest among street users, traffic volumes, vehicle speeds, air quality, safety, personal security, poor street environment quality (design, space, cleanliness, lighting, maintenance, etc.), and the lack of information and guidance all act as barriers preventing many people from considering walking as an option. Understanding these factors is the first step in identifying the needs of pedestrians.  
- Large traffic volumes of vehicles are among the most significant factors deterring people from walking in the streets. The fear of accidents (e.g., Appleyard 1981) and the difficulty of crossing streets are directly related to traffic volume. Planning Variables for Pedestrians  
Designing the space for pedestrian movement is quite complex compared to spatial planning for other "traffic devices." Here are several reasons:  
A. The dimensions occupied by pedestrians vary greatly - for example, the small space taken up by a child compared to the space occupied by a parent pushing a stroller.  
B. The movement capabilities of pedestrians differ from one another - the walking speed of a teenager versus the movement speed of an elderly person or someone with mobility limitations.  
C. The significant impact of the environment on pedestrian movement - topographical conditions, climate conditions, shade or sunlight, the material of the sidewalk, obstacles, interest and attraction, etc.  
Another difficulty in designing the pedestrian movement space is the need to include in their movement space also the personal and sensory "mental" space, that fluid, changing, and undefined space that is not required for other traffic devices. It is also important to remember that pedestrians have a "group" or community space, which is the space needed for a group of pedestrians to move together. A family walking down the street or a group of children heading to school effectively becomes a single unit that requires a cohesive space.  
Therefore, the "dimensions of the pedestrian" are a mixed component.

In a group or community context, this is the space required for a group of pedestrians to move together.
