Important urban elements are at the service of the pedestrian network.

The streets that form the skeleton of the public space in the city are the pedestrian network, whose role is to guide pedestrians efficiently, comfortably, and safely from any place in the city to any other place within it. The pedestrian network is supported by other important urban elements that complement and enhance it - such as paths between buildings, in gardens and open spaces, squares and plazas, auxiliary facilities like escalators and elevators, and so on - all of which integrate into a complex system of means for guiding pedestrians in the urban space. 

The geometric basis of the urban pedestrian network, like any geometric network, consists of 'arms' and 'connectors.' The arms of the network are the walking strips along the city streets, as well as the paths and passages within the fabric and in open areas. The connectors are the intersections and junctions that link the walking strips, as well as plazas, expansions, squares, activity areas, and so forth.

Planning principles
Pedestrian movement is the basic and essential component of the street and can be the main or even the sole component (unlike a road, which is primarily intended for motor vehicle traffic). Pedestrian movement occurs along the street and must be continuous, comfortable, and free of obstacles (pedestrian movement 1918 and detours, in accordance with the requirements of the Israeli accessibility standard (T.I. 1918)). It is meant to serve the buildings and uses along the street and its active facades, and therefore, complete accessibility to entrances of homes and active facades must be maintained. For this purpose, a walking strip will be installed on every street and urban road, designated solely for pedestrian movement along the street. (Exceptions to this are special and local solutions of 'shared movement strips' and alleys as detailed in the street space planning guidelines book.)

Guidelines for Street Planning in Cities - Pedestrian Traffic / Combined Auxiliary Lane with Parking Lane  
In existing or planned streets that are particularly narrow, where the width is insufficient for all intended functions, it is advisable to consider merging the auxiliary lane on the sidewalk with the parking lane on the road. Both lanes are generally designed close to each other, and both are intended for stationary objects (infrastructure and vehicles). Merging them into one lane allows for the complete elimination of the auxiliary lane and the installation of most stationary objects within the parking lane, as described in the diagram.  
This situation has several distinct disadvantages, such as:  
- Giving up some parking spaces for the installation of stationary objects;  
- Greater complexity of the curb line;  
- Exposure of stationary objects to the traffic of parked vehicles (or the need to protect them from damage with special protective measures);  
- The need to adjust the location of stationary objects considering parking modules.  
Despite the disadvantages of merging the parking lane and the auxiliary lane, in many cases, this is a preferable solution over harming the traffic lanes of street users - the walking lanes, bicycle lanes, and roadways.

Arcades Along the Street  
Arcades along the street are a good solution for protecting pedestrians from weather conditions and also for encouraging the presence and activity of pedestrians on the street. In addition, arcades have a clear design significance that affects the structure and character of the street. The area of the arcade can be integrated into the sidewalk structure as defined in this chapter - the arcade area can serve as a buffer zone and a protected walking area, or alternatively as a buffer zone and an activity space, and so on. It is important to ensure that the arcade area integrates with the sidewalk and is accessible to pedestrians. An arcade along a street is particularly suitable for streets with active facades (commercial and similar). Parallel use of pergolas is also possible.  
However, it should be emphasized that designing an arcade beneath the floors of the buildings themselves requires an appropriate property solution that allows for open public passage within private property, or another legal solution that ensures reasonable functionality for the arcade.  
Designing a street with an arcade requires consistency and patience over a long period - until the street is realized in the planned format. Partial implementation of an arcade, or a change in policy in sections of the street, may create functional hazards.

Path in Open Space  
The urban public space includes, in addition to the city streets, a network of open spaces primarily serving pedestrians - gardens, parks, squares, plazas, and the like. These areas have many roles such as providing comfort and relaxation for the community, green lungs, playgrounds for young children and youth, and a venue for sports, cultural activities, and more.  
Among other roles, open spaces also constitute part of the pedestrian movement system in the city. Pedestrians use the paths in open spaces as part of their daily movements. In planning urban open spaces, it is necessary to define the paths that are part of the urban pedestrian movement network. These paths should be designed according to the planning variables of the walking strips (Section 4.3 on the sidewalk), considering the expected traffic volume and its characteristics.  
Due to the desire to avoid congestion and crowding in the open space as much as possible and to allow for more relaxed movement of pedestrians, it is recommended to widen the dimensions of the path beyond the detailed requirements for the walking strip.  
It is important to emphasize that garden furniture, lighting, benches, or other fixed accessories are installed outside the walking strip.

To allow for a more relaxed movement of pedestrians, it is recommended to expand the dimensions of the path beyond the requirements specified for the walking strip. It should be emphasized that garden furniture, lighting, benches, or other stationary accessories are installed outside the walking strip. If necessary, the path includes an auxiliary strip for furniture and stationary objects.

Passage Path
The movement arrangement for pedestrians also includes passage paths that are not part of open space and are not urban streets. Their main role is solely for pedestrian (and bicycle) movement, and they do not have main entrances to construction sites along the side or any distinct additional activity. 

The width of the walking strip of passage paths that are not intended for bicycle movement shall not be less than 4 meters. The walking strip should be supplemented according to the nature of the planning with a landscaping strip and/or an auxiliary strip of 4 meters for infrastructure and above-ground stationary objects. Therefore, it is recommended that the minimum width of a secondary path be 6 meters. When the path is shared by pedestrians and bicycles (a configuration that is not recommended), it should be widened for safety separation between users, as detailed in section 4.9 of the bicycle movement guidelines.

Introduction  
Bus stations are a significant component of the quality and efficiency of public transportation services, and their quality is essential for encouraging usage. However, bus stations are a major consumer of street space, both on the road for bus stops and on the sidewalk for pedestrians waiting for and boarding buses. Where the station is located, a "bottleneck" is expected for all street users, necessitating preparation and planning, with a broad and balanced view of the needs of all street users.  
The guidelines published by the Ministry of Transportation so far mainly address the traffic aspects of public transport stations and their location in relation to the road, such as their location and the number of stopping positions required for buses at the station, dimensions and geometry of the bus stopping area, signage, etc., as well as accessibility issues in Section 1918 of the technical specifications for waiting shelters. Within the framework of the Israeli standard for the built environment for people with disabilities, and the Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Regulations (Public Transport Accessibility Regulation), there are mandatory definitions regarding ensuring maximum accessibility for persons with disabilities to and from a bus station.  
The planning guidelines of the section

Women with disabilities, and in the regulations for equal rights for people with disabilities (accessibility arrangements for public transportation), there are mandatory definitions regarding the assurance of maximum accessibility for individuals with disabilities to and from a bus station. The planning guidelines of the current section are added to others, integrating them in terms of the sidewalk, and propose a system of rules and conditions for the integration of public transportation stations into the street, aiming to balance the needs of the station and its users with the needs of other street users. The guidelines include both recommendations and optimal dimensions for the planning of new streets, as well as solutions and minimal dimensions for forced situations in existing streets. The role of the guidelines is to assist in the planning and design of the station from the statutory planning stage and the determination of right-of-way and street and intersection space, to the detailed planning level of the station and its surroundings. For planning for high-capacity public transportation systems (BRT, light rail), see the specific guidelines for these systems.

The design of the public transport station and the integration of its components into the street will be based on two fundamental principles: ensuring the proper functionality of the station and ensuring the proper functionality of the walking strip.
A. Ensuring the Functionality of the Station
Every station will include, in any case, the essential functional components for its operation (Group A) as mentioned in section 4.11.2 above.
It is desirable that every station includes a waiting shelter, provided that its integration into the street ensures the proper functioning of the walking strip as detailed below. Introduction  
An intersection of streets is primarily a meeting place - a meeting of streets, of movements, of people and activities.  
The intersection in the city has a distinct urban, spatial, and functional significance. The connection between the streets and the various traffic lanes often makes the intersection a focal point and a landmark for orientation. Some intersections in the city have been developed into wide urban squares, rich in activity and holding special cultural and social significance for the city's residents.  
At the intersection, pedestrian movements from different streets and public transportation stations (located at the intersections and nearby) converge. Typically, road crossing occurs at the intersection, creating a concentration of waiting pedestrians. This concentration of pedestrians at the intersection encourages additional activities - commerce, street vending, advertising and marketing, guidance, information dissemination, and more. All of these are significant space consumers and require the allocation of suitable space. Therefore, a larger area is needed at the intersection for pedestrians and service facilities than along the streets leading to the intersection.  
Just as the spatial demands of pedestrians at the intersection increase, so do the spatial demands of other users on the street. The intersection serves as a bottleneck for the flow of traffic.

The intersection serves as a bottleneck for motor traffic due to the convergence of movements, the need for space for turns, and the slowing of traffic. B. Safety Function of All Movements in the Street  
A busy intersection poses a risk to all users. The higher the speed of the approaching motor vehicle, the larger the space required to be free of obstacles in order to ensure visibility, clarity, and to prevent surprises and safety risks.  
C. Urban and Design Function  
The intersection is an urban activity hub, as well as a means of orientation and a component in the city's design. The urban activity taking place at the intersection, as well as design considerations for street junctions, require additional spaces within the street corner area. (For example, the design of corner lots at the intersection is a fundamental component in shaping the urban fabric. Rounded, chamfered corners, and similar features influence the design language of the intersection and the entire fabric.)  
The three different functions of the street corner are allocated three different spaces accordingly: a space for visibility and clarity, a visibility space for pedestrian movement, and the street corner for pedestrian activities at the intersection and design considerations, as detailed below.

Guidelines for Maximum Expansion of the Street Corner  
Introduction  
In planning the intersection, efforts should be made to expand the street corner beyond the minimum required space by increasing the activity and auxiliary areas. To this end, it is recommended to adopt several measures:  
- Unifying sidewalk strips (and sometimes also the parking strip) into a continuous area for pedestrians (details in section 5.4.2).  
- Reducing the curb radius between the sidewalk and the road, subject to traffic guidelines (details in section 5.4.3).  
- Expanding the 'right of way' by setbacks in the corner lots of the intersection (details in section 5.4.4).  
- Unifying sidewalk strips and incorporating the parking strip into the street corner (ears).  
The need for maximum expansion of the street corner requires the removal of any non-essential use and its allocation for pedestrian traffic and activity. To this end, the longitudinal division of the street within the street corner changes (service strip, walking strip, edge strip, parking strip, etc.). All strips are unified into a continuous area from the curb to the street edge line, as described in diagram 5.6.  
The greatest contribution to the expansion of the street corner is the inclusion of the parking strip area from the road (which is not used for parking in the intersection area).

All the strips are unified into one continuous area from the curb to the street edge, as described in diagram 5.6. The greatest contribution to the expansion of the street curb is the addition of parking strip area from the road domain (which is not used for parking in the intersection area). The area of the added parking strips greatly facilitates pedestrians' waiting before crossing the street curb, as described in diagram 5.6, shortens crossing distances, and allows for the creation of good accessibility slopes to the road crossing level.

Introduction  
Along the city streets, exclusive traffic lanes are allocated for pedestrians and other street users (motor vehicles, bicycles, public transportation, light rail, etc.) as much as possible. In certain places, the traffic lanes for pedestrians intersect with the traffic lanes of other street users. These places are crosswalks.  
A crosswalk, therefore, is any location determined by the planner where there will be an intersection of pedestrian movements with other users.  
The classification of crosswalks, their adaptation to different types of streets, and detailed guidelines for planning crosswalks are the subject of this chapter.  
Considerations for Determining Crosswalk Locations in Urban Areas  
Introduction  
Planning crosswalks in the city requires initial decisions in the following areas:  
- Location of the crosswalk - where to establish crosswalks at intersections and along street segments between intersections, subject to the flow of pedestrian traffic and their specific needs.  
- Type of crosswalk - what type of crosswalk to choose to ensure maximum safety and efficiency, subject to the speed and intensity of motor traffic at the crosswalk.

B. Crosswalks on Street or Road Segments  
Crosswalks on street and road segments are an integral part of the pedestrian traffic system in the city. The location of crosswalks on street/road segments is based on the following assumptions:  
1) A pedestrian's tendency is to choose the shortest and most convenient path in their movement.

3) It is preferable to allow as many pedestrians as possible to cross under good and safe crossing conditions whenever possible.

Unmarked Crossing  
A. General Description  
An unmarked crossing is primarily installed on local streets where motor traffic volume is low and numerous pedestrian crossings between the sides of the street are required. An unmarked crossing can be installed without signage and markings that emphasize it.  
B. Justifications and Conditions  
Unmarked crossings are possible in the following locations:

Location of Crossings at Intersections  
The planning characteristics related to a crossing at an intersection differ between street intersections and road junctions, as detailed below.  
A. Location of Crossings at Street Intersections  
Crossings at street intersections are determined in a way that facilitates pedestrian movement as much as possible, while strictly maintaining their safety. The crossings are located between the corners of the street, continuing directly and seamlessly to the walking strip along the street. The crossing axis shall not be shifted from the walking strip axis by more than 6.6 meters, as described in Diagram 2, except in exceptional cases where continuity cannot be maintained.  
Several examples of correct and incorrect installations of crossings at intersections (whether marked or unmarked) are provided in Diagram 6.  
B. Location of Crossings at Road Junctions  
At road junctions, characteristics related to vehicle flow, junction capacity, and the level of service for vehicles are generally preferred over the comfort and continuity of pedestrian movement. Therefore, no special planning characteristics are established for determining the location of crossings at road junctions.

Crossing Length (Crossing Distance/Crossing Duration)  
The duration of the crossing, resulting from the length of the crossing, is a significant component related to pedestrian safety. Crossing the road requires the pedestrian to perform fairly difficult assessment actions to estimate the speed of the approaching vehicle and the distance between the vehicle and the crossing point, and based on that, analyze their chances of safely crossing the road.  
Some of the pedestrian population (children, youth, and the elderly) struggle with this estimation and make incorrect decisions (avoiding crossing the street when it is safe to do so, and hastily crossing the street when conditions are not suitable). The shorter the distance that needs to be crossed on the street, the greater the ability to make the correct decision. Therefore, efforts should be made to minimize the crossing distance as much as possible.

Warning Signs Indicating Pedestrian Traffic  
In the signage board, there are warning signs (135, 136) indicating pedestrian traffic in their vicinity. Generally, drivers do not notice or take these signs seriously as required. It is recommended to use these signs in rare cases and to place them only as assistance and as a complement to additional measures.  
The practice of increasing warning signs, such as 150 or 439, does not contribute to the safety of pedestrian traffic. On the contrary, the more these signs are placed, the more they lead to a devaluation regarding drivers' attention to them. In many cases, the placement of these signs, which has minimal cost, is done instead of other safety measures that are effective and contribute to safety, even if their cost is much higher. The explicit recommendation on this issue is to minimize these signs as much as possible and to prefer physical/safety arrangements, as explained in section 6.

Planning for Pedestrians at Signalized Intersections
During the planning of a signalized intersection, the planner must remember that, in addition to vehicles, pedestrians also cross the intersection. The design of the signalized intersection should fully and accurately reflect the needs of the crossing pedestrians. The planner must internalize the fact that crosswalks at the intersection are areas shared by pedestrians and vehicles, and that pedestrians are entitled to appropriate consideration of their basic needs. To this end, the following recommendations are provided:
A. At a signalized intersection, crosswalks should be established at all sides of the intersection. Crosswalks should not be omitted for reasons related to the capacity and level of service of vehicles at the intersection. Omission of a crosswalk should only occur when the geometric structure of the intersection or the right-of-way data do not allow for a crosswalk to be established at one of the intersection's legs. At urban road intersections, or at intercity intersections that do not serve as a focal point for pedestrians due to land uses designated for them, such as a public transport terminal, a crosswalk may be omitted on one arm only if it has a significant impact on the operation of the intersection, and no alternative solution can be found, such as the use of push buttons (see guidelines for traffic signal design).
At street intersections, right-turning movements should be limited as much as possible (recommendation B regarding...).

D. The crossing times for pedestrians at traffic lights are sometimes the leftover time remaining after planning the times for vehicle displays. During the planning of the intersection timings, pedestrian crossing data must be taken into account, and it is not sufficient to set a crossing time of six seconds if the volume of pedestrians is high, or when the crossing is located near a shopping center or central station.  
E. The design of multi-lane intersections requires pedestrians to cross the intersection in three stages and sometimes even more. In streets, it is preferable to design the traffic light so that the crossing can be done in a continuous manner as much as possible, and in any case, a suitable waiting area must be ensured in medians/islands for pedestrians who need to wait.  
F. At pedestrian traffic lights, a sound signal should be integrated to allow visually impaired individuals to cross the intersection safely.  
Safety Barriers and Fences for Pedestrians  
Introduction  
Safety barriers for pedestrians (not included in the traffic sign table) are placed on the sidewalk and are intended to prevent pedestrians from falling onto the road. Safety fences are placed in medians, in places where pedestrian traffic or road crossing endangers pedestrians, or

Safety Barriers for Pedestrians  
Due to the fact that safety railings and fences have various aspects that include points of merit and points of obligation for their installation, there are no fixed justifications for their installation, and the decision should be left to the planning teams and local authorities.  
On divided roads, a fence in the median is preferable to a safety railing for pedestrians along sidewalks, as a means of preventing crossings and directing walking paths. Both the fence and the railing should

They should be designed and positioned so that any impact on them does not pose a danger to road users - that they do not break apart and fly away, and that there is no need for protection against them.  
Below are some guidelines for the installation of railings and safety fences:  
A. It is advisable to positively consider placing these devices on urban roads and at road intersections.  
B. In streets and at street intersections, the placement of devices should be considered only where the need for their installation is very essential.  
C. In traffic calming areas, the installation of railings and fences should be avoided as much as possible.  
D. Railings and fences should be installed in places where pedestrian crossing is dangerous, must be prevented, and there are no other means to prevent it.  
E. The installation of railings should be considered in the areas of school gates, kindergartens, community centers, and similar public institutions, and at the intersection of pedestrian paths with roads, to prevent pedestrians from bursting onto the road.  
F. In no case should a blanket rule be applied to all intersections and streets for or against the placement of devices, and each street, each segment of a street, and each intersection should be considered on its own merits.

Guidelines for the placement of railings and safety fences for pedestrians
Separation fence
A separation fence will generally be installed in the center of the separator; however, when there are lighting poles, signs, or trees in the separator, it will be shifted aside, to a minimum distance of 0.50 meters from the curb. Near intersections and before crosswalks, it is recommended to install the fence next to the edge of the island on the side where the obstruction to the field of vision will be minimal (diagrams 7.2, 7.3). In edge segments where the fence obstructs the field of vision, primarily at a height of 1.00 meters to 1.10 meters, the height will be lowered to 0.80 meters near crosswalks.
Safety railing for pedestrians
A safety railing will be installed on the sidewalk as close as possible to the curb. It must be ensured that the railing does not obstruct the view at the intersection for drivers and pedestrians. In edge segments where the railing obstructs the field of vision, the height of the railing will be lowered from 1.00 meters to 1.10 meters to 0.80 meters.
General
No overlap should be created between safety railings for pedestrians and fences in separators along segments of the road to prevent overlap of 20 to 30 meters. In intersection and junction areas, overlap can be created along a diagonal crosswalk.
A safety railing for pedestrians should not be installed separating a parking bay from the adjacent sidewalk.

Between barriers in medians along segments of 20 to 30 meters to prevent diagonal crossing. In intersection and meeting areas, overlapping can be created along a diagonal length. 
A safety railing should not be installed for pedestrians that separates a parking bay from the adjacent sidewalk.

Guidelines for Street Planning in Cities - Objects and Vegetation  
The urban street accommodates many users, including pedestrians, cyclists, public transport passengers, and private vehicle drivers. These users have different needs and designated areas. This is the focus of the series of guidelines for street planning in cities, prepared in recent years by the Ministry of Transport, together with the Ministry of Construction and Housing.  
This document serves as a new volume added to the series, complementing previous volumes that focused on the proper characterization of street areas according to their function, and discusses the placement of objects on the street, such as traffic signs and lighting, street furniture, and overhead infrastructure on one hand, and trees and vegetation that contribute to the urban landscape and improve environmental quality on the other.  
The roles of objects and vegetation are diverse; some are intended to provide guidance and instructions to users on the road, while others are meant to serve pedestrians on the sidewalk and provide a high-quality and attractive urban environment.  
These guidelines establish rules and instructions designed to enable the optimal integration of objects within the street space, without interference and contradictions between them and street users or other objects, while considering the positive contribution of vegetation, greenery, and landscape to the quality of life in the city and ensuring the safety of various users.  
We hope that this document will contribute to the improvement of urban environments.

Introduction

In the street space, stationary elements are placed, including objects such as street furniture, traffic signs, and road accessories, as well as overhead infrastructure and various types of trees and vegetation. The arrangement of these objects and vegetation is of great importance for the proper functioning of the street, especially for the pedestrian space, since most of the objects are located on the sidewalks. These elements play a significant role in creating an accessible, spacious, pleasant, and inviting urban environment. Increasing the amount of vegetation and trees is an essential component both visually and in terms of environmental quality. All of this is done while creating an urban environment that is as safe as possible.

The guidelines for street planning in cities (under the "Green Arrangement") are divided into several volumes: the first volume, the street space, relates to the overall planning of the right of way and defines the basic principles for street planning in cities. The other volumes each focus on a specific aspect of street planning: pedestrian movement, bicycle movement, motor vehicle movement, and traffic at intersections.

This volume serves as an additional layer within the guidelines for street planning in cities, focusing on the design of the strips and areas in the street where objects and vegetation are placed, and is based on the terminology of the "Green Arrangement," with further details on relevant topics. Introduction  
The treatment of objects and vegetation is primarily influenced by the distinction between "urban street" and "urban road." The determination that the planned urban space is a "street" means that high accessibility to the uses on both sides is required. Streets are divided into two main types: local and collector. The determination that the planned urban space is an "urban road" emphasizes the conditions that allow for the transfer of traffic between one part of the city and another at relatively high volumes and speeds.  
To balance the needs for accessibility and safety with the flow of motor traffic, three designated speeds have been established: 30 km/h for local streets, 50 km/h for collector streets, and 70 km/h for arterial roads. In most streets, the designated speed will be 30 km/h, 50 km/h, or 70 km/h, depending on the extent of activity on the street and the need to maintain user safety. On collector streets and in traffic calming areas, the designated speed will be 30-50 km/h. On arterial roads, a designated speed of 50 km/h will be allowed if these roads cross residential and activity areas.  
The above characteristics form the basis for planning the placement of objects and vegetation in the street and influence the approach to the principles of design.

In arterial roads, a designated speed of 50 km/h will be allowed if it concerns arteries crossing residential and activity areas. The above characteristics form the basis for planning the placement of objects and vegetation in the street and influence the approach to planning principles. This chapter details the considerations that must be taken into account when planning objects and vegetation in the five areas where planning principles have been defined: safety, accessibility, urban design, sustainability, and the planning process.

Safety Aspect
Distance or protection from objects
To allow a vehicle that has veered off to return to the lane without colliding with any object, it is necessary to provide a safety clearance from objects at the edge of the road. This clearance increases according to the speed of traffic, which directly affects the severity of the accident in the event of a lane deviation. The determination of the clearance rule is guided by two basic documents: the guidelines for street planning in cities and the guidelines for the selection and placement of safety devices in urban roads. 1. The minimum distance of hard objects from the curb in streets serves as a basis for determining the need for protection against collisions with hard objects in the urban environment. 
In applying the distancing rule, a distinction must be made between streets where the allowed speed is up to 70 km/h and roads where the speed is higher (usually up to 50 km/h). 
The separation between traffic lanes and the walking area in streets is achieved by the height difference using the curb, as well as by a basic safety margin. This margin also provides flexibility during parking maneuvers when a vehicle's bumper rises onto the sidewalk, as well as a minimal safety margin for a vehicle that has mounted the sidewalk to return to the traffic lanes. 
The guidelines for street planning in cities stipulate that a minimum distance must be maintained between the surface of the stationary object (the outer plane of its protruding part) and the edges of the traffic lane adjacent to the object. This safety margin applies to both sidewalks and medians, as shown in the diagram. 
As a rule, the traffic sign will be placed on the sidewalk at a distance of 30 cm from the curb, referring to the closest point of the sign to the curb, and not otherwise.

In traffic adjacent to the object, this safety margin applies to both sidewalks and medians. Generally, the sign will be placed on the sidewalk at a distance of 30 cm from the curb. (This refers to the closest point of the sign to the curb, and not necessarily the location of the pole holding the sign). 

The guidelines for the selection and placement of road safety devices in urban areas state that in streets with a maximum permitted speed of 50 km/h, the installation of protective measures against rigid objects, such as safety barriers and energy absorbers, is not necessary and not justified. Street lighting is a central component of the street cross-section. Considerations for placing lighting in the street: Proper lighting allows various road users to see and be seen, and to move safely and securely during dark hours. Lighting also plays a significant role in the vitality of the urban space and in transforming it into an aesthetic and pleasant environment. The planning of lighting on roads is guided by two documents: the lighting guidelines for roads (T.I. 13201 and T.I. 1996, basis: guidelines for road lighting planning) from the Ministry of Transportation (2010, Roads) and the Standards Institute.  
The guidelines for road lighting stipulate that there is an obligation to install lighting on all city streets. As part of this obligation, special emphasis should be placed on illuminating intersections, pedestrian crossings, and bus stops. Highlighting these areas with additional lighting encourages drivers to act as required and encourages pedestrians to use the marked crossing.  
However, lighting can also become a nuisance if not well planned. For example, during the day, lighting poles can obscure movements in the street and also create a visual nuisance. At night, street lighting can cause "light pollution," which includes interference with adjacent land uses, glare, and negative impacts on environmental quality.

The perception of surface runoff as a resource with economic and environmental potential aims to replace the traditional drainage planning approach, which mainly addresses flood risks and focuses on the rapid removal of runoff water. The stormwater management method focuses on finding optimal solutions and making as much intelligent use of runoff water as possible, such as: irrigation, storing runoff water for further treatment as drinking water or for irrigation, infiltrating it into groundwater, and more.

Infiltrating rainwater into the growth medium has an additional advantage, as it channels water to deeper soil layers and prevents its removal through drainage and sewage systems outside the city. Good drainage of the growth medium must be ensured to prevent excess water and damage to the growth conditions of the trees. 

Designing a drainage system in the street that takes environmental considerations into account will preserve rainwater and direct excess water to "green" areas within the city. In these areas, settling ponds will be created to retain water in the garden/park area for the benefit of garden vegetation and the infiltration of rainwater into the root zone.

A debt that takes environmental considerations into account will preserve rainwater and lead excess water to "green" areas within the city. In these areas, settling ponds will be created to retain water in the garden/park area for the benefit of the garden's vegetation and the infiltration of rainwater into the ground in areas where there is an active aquifer.

Planning Process
In order for objects and vegetation to be installed without mutual interference and without disrupting the functioning of traffic lanes, a high level of coordination among those involved in the planning is required. Street planning brings together various disciplines, such as building and landscape architecture, traffic and road engineering, agronomic aspects, infrastructure engineering, lighting engineering, accessibility, and more. The final outputs of the planning include a variety of plans such as building plans, positioning and spaces, traffic, landscape development, and infrastructure coordination. 
To improve the level of coordination regarding the placement of objects and vegetation in streets, three principles have been defined in these guidelines for the planning process: integrative planning, inclusion of trees in infrastructure coordination, and local guidelines.
Integrative Planning
To enable optimal coordination among the various planning entities at each stage of the planning process, it is essential to ensure that all principles are implemented from the conceptual planning stage. One way to improve coordination is to prepare a "superposition" (multi-layered) plan of all street components (above and below ground) in the design, which serves as a basic tool for coordination among the different entities. One way to improve coordination is to prepare a "superposition" plan (multi-layered) of all street components (above and below ground) in the design, which serves as a basic tool for coordination among the various stakeholders. A superposition plan is a plan that integrates programs from different fields, aimed at ensuring there are no conflicts between them and allowing for feedback and coordination among the planners. A superposition plan for streets should include several layers, the main ones being traffic plans, landscape development plans, particularly regarding plantings, and plans for coordinating above-ground and underground infrastructures. The plan should be prepared for both ground level and sub-ground level. The plan must be clear and allow for a clear view of the different systems, with the goal of providing optimization between traffic and safety considerations and landscape and accessibility considerations, as well as identifying potential conflicts between these areas. In this plan, it is recommended to also include street furniture. Coordination is required among all objects in the sidewalks and curbs, in conjunction with the required sight distances at intersections, segments, and pedestrian visibility. As part of the traffic plan, sight lines at intersections should also be added, which represent areas with development restrictions, as well as the placement of objects and tree plantings. Inclusion of trees in infrastructure coordination
Infrastructure coordination is a necessary step in preparing a plan for a street or neighborhood. Currently, this process does not give sufficient weight to the issue of existing and planned trees. In order for infrastructure planners to take into account the dimensions of the root zone and to prevent conflicts between tree roots and underground infrastructure, the infrastructure coordination process must include the location of trees and indicate the boundaries of the root zone along with other infrastructures.

According to the Non-Ionizing Radiation Law (2006), the electrical cabinet must be located at a distance of 1.0–3.0 meters from inhabited structures, depending on the type of cabinet. This distance requires the removal of people. In practice, this distancing is currently achieved by placing the cabinet in concrete niches. Planning a buffer strip that includes trees and/or other vegetation requires addressing the issue of increasing the amount of runoff captured in pits, in the landscaping strip, and in the flower beds. Designing the slope of the pavement in the walking and buffer strip towards the protective surface. This solution can incorporate a shallow channel in the buffer strip with engineered surface, which will direct the water to a pit or to flower beds.

Introduction  
The median is an elevated strip within the street that separates different vehicle movements and opposing directions of traffic. The median has various roles, including traffic and landscape functions. From a traffic perspective, the roles of the median include separating travel lanes, providing optional space for special left-turn lanes, and serving as a refuge area for pedestrians and cyclists crossing the street.  
In addition to its traffic and safety functions, the median serves as an important space in the street for landscape development, complementing the city's green areas and allowing for an increase in the number of trees. Sometimes, medians are designed wider than necessary for traffic purposes to enable diverse landscape development in accordance with the dimensions of the street. Since medians are located on main streets, they have a significant impact on the city's appearance.  
The median allows for the coordinated placement of trees along with lighting, and the creation of layers of shrubs and seasonal flowers along the segment, in combination with the landscape development on the sidewalk. The median's surface varies and includes different coverings, vegetation, and design landscape elements. Due to the landscape development and vegetation, ongoing maintenance activities are required, including pruning and watering.

Seasonal vegetation along the section, combined with landscape development on the sidewalk. The median cover varies and includes different cladding, vegetation, and design landscape elements. Due to the landscape development and vegetation, regular maintenance activities are required, including pruning and irrigation. The vegetation in the median must be pruned so that it does not encroach into the roadway. Additionally, care must be taken with irrigation methods to ensure that water does not leak onto the roadway and pose a danger to road users and waste water. 

Two main factors influence the planning of objects and vegetation in the median: the speed of travel, where there is no requirement for safety devices at speeds of 50 km/h, and the width of the median. In medians on streets with a designated speed of 70 km/h, it is required to keep rigid objects away from the edge of the curb, or alternatively to protect against them using safety barriers or to place forgiving objects. The second most important factor in determining objects and vegetation in the median is the width of the median, which affects the options for tree placement, type of cover, and the need for protective devices on roads.

Tree Planting
Planting trees in the median requires consideration of safety aspects, alongside urban considerations, provision of habitat, and prevention of the tree's canopy encroaching into the roadway area. At an intersection, different traffic flows from adjacent streets converge, and it is where road crossing occurs, creating a concentration of waiting pedestrians. Intersections between main streets in the city serve as landmarks for orientation, meeting places, and points of interest. The activities occurring at the intersection consume space and require the allocation of suitable areas, all according to the level of activity. The intersection presents a potential for conflicts between flow and objects. First and foremost, it is necessary to ensure the needs of pedestrians, which include connecting walking strips on sidewalks with each other and with crosswalks. Therefore, a larger area is required for pedestrians at the intersection than along street segments. Additionally, for vehicle movement, the intersection serves as a place for turns and merging. Signs in the intersection space  
The intersection is an area where many movements meet, and there is a need to create priority orders among the intersecting movements through signs placed at the street corner that serve various roles.  
For traffic control purposes, essential signs for the functioning of the intersection are placed, including "Yield" and "Stop" signs, the choice of which mainly depends on visibility considerations.  
In addition to control signs, other signs such as no entry, parking, one-way, speed, traffic calming area, urban area, truck entry restrictions, bus lanes, bike paths, crosswalks, and more are also placed at the street corner.  
The guiding approach to placing signs at the street corner is the "minimum necessary" approach, and therefore the number of signs at the intersection should be minimized as much as possible.  
The placement of signs on the street will be according to the "Regulations and Guidelines for Sign Placement" updated by the Ministry of Transportation.

The placement of traffic signs at the intersection of the street follows a "minimum necessary" approach, and therefore, the number of signs at the intersection should be minimized as much as possible. The manner of placing the signs on the street will be in accordance with the "Regulations and Guidelines for the Placement of Traffic Signs" updated by the Ministry of Transportation. It should be noted that at a signalized intersection, "default" signs are placed in case of a traffic light failure, positioned on some of the arms. These signs are mounted on the appropriate traffic light poles.

The rules for placing signs at the intersection of the street include:
Signs that can be placed on a road segment should not be placed at the intersection. 
Duplications or excessive information should be avoided. The number of poles should be minimized as much as possible to improve the readability of the intersection, reduce visual clutter, and prevent the obstruction of pedestrians. Other poles should be utilized for placing the signs, such as lighting poles or traffic light poles. 

Obstruction of other signs and/or street name signs should be avoided. The reduction of the number of poles is achieved by consolidating signs on a shared pole. The guidelines for the arrangement of the signs should be followed.

Poles, such as lighting poles or traffic light poles. It is necessary to prevent the obstruction of other signs and/or street name signs. At a forced street corner, there is a challenge in preventing the pole from intruding into the walking space. As mentioned in previous sections, there is a need to place poles that carry lighting fixtures, traffic lights, and road signs at intersections. Poor planning can create a situation of a "forest of poles" at the corner of the street, which increases the visual clutter of the intersection and reduces its readability, creates additional safety risks, and makes it difficult for the driver to notice waiting pedestrians. To avoid this situation, it is recommended to carry out "comprehensive pole planning at the intersection," which includes an analysis of the pole locations, aiming to minimize the number of poles as much as possible by integrating devices onto a single pole. Pole integration is a common solution implemented both in the country and worldwide. An example of a "Pole Integration Plan" is presented in Diagram 49.  
It should be noted that the prevalence of the "forest of poles" problem increases over time, with the addition of new devices at an existing intersection, when there is not necessarily coordination in the placement and removal of the various poles. For this purpose, whenever work is done at an existing intersection, the "Pole Integration Plan" should be re-evaluated, as mentioned above.

Marking the locations of necessary poles at the intersection, according to the guidelines specified. The principle that only essential devices should be left at the corner of the street must be applied.

This chapter focuses on the placement of street furniture and several additional road accessories, positioned as required according to various criteria of function, layout, type of street, and more. 
The first section of the chapter outlines various considerations for integrating street furniture. Following that, a functional analysis of the placement of objects in the street is presented. Due to the importance of planning bus stop areas, a separate section is dedicated to this topic, discussing the placement of objects at stops. The final section of the chapter provides detailed guidelines for several selected objects, including: bollards, benches, trash bins, recycling facilities, driver guidance signage, and mail distribution centers. 
Integration of Street Furniture 
Street furniture is a concept that refers to the collection of facilities placed in public spaces, whose main purpose is to serve the entire population of the city and provide essential services on the street. Objects included in this category consist of: benches, drinking fountains, trash bins, recycling facilities, bulletin boards, information and advertising boards, public telephones, mailboxes, and street sculptures.

When placing street furniture, attention must be given to the accessibility of the facility, the safety and security of various users in the street, the location that meets the needs of pedestrians, and the required maintenance. The impact of objects on the walking area
A central component of these guidelines is the interaction between the auxiliary and edge strips and the walking strip. The auxiliary and edge strips are indeed intended for placing objects and vegetation, but they are not "sterile" strips from pedestrians. On the contrary, in many cases, the auxiliary and edge strips serve pedestrians and complement the walking strip (in fact, the auxiliary and edge strips are the "margins" of the walking strip). The auxiliary and edge strips are used by pedestrians for stopping and sitting, and also allow pedestrians to flow through. Hence, their importance in creating public space on the sidewalk.
The guidelines for street planning in cities provide comfortable dimensions for the width of the walking strips, as determined according to the intensity of pedestrian traffic (Table 4 in the sidewalk planning chapter). However, pedestrians will often have to "flow" into the auxiliary or edge strips for passage, as pedestrians sometimes move in pairs, with strollers, with children, or walking dogs. These activities sometimes require the full width of the strip.

Pedestrians will often have to "glide" to the auxiliary or edge strips for passage, as pedestrians sometimes move in pairs, with strollers, with children, or walking a dog. These activities sometimes require the full width of the walking strip, and a pedestrian coming from the opposite direction is forced to glide to the auxiliary strip or stop and allow them to pass. Examples of visual clutter  
When the auxiliary strip allows for crossing, care must be taken regarding the minimum spacing between objects in the auxiliary strip, in order to allow pedestrian passage for crossing the street or access to the parking strip.  
Certain objects require a passage beyond the minimum spacing. For example, the minimum spacing between bollards is 1.3 meters.  
On the street side, adjacent to a wall or fence, there is no objection to placing objects next to each other, unless there is a functional conflict that requires distancing. For example, it is not possible to place an infrastructure cabinet 30-40 cm next to hydrants, as hydrants require functional clearances around them, and additionally, distancing is required between water and electrical infrastructures.  
Reducing visual clutter  
Visual clutter is the accumulation of objects in the street that create a "visual disorder," causing a sense of overload and making street reading difficult, and at times may harm accessibility and safety for users. Visual clutter can be caused by several circumstances: excessive placement of objects in the street, lack of coordination and planning between different authorities responsible for placing objects and infrastructures, placing objects at a later stage than the initial planning due to specific considerations not included in a comprehensive planning process, excess advertising space in the street area, broken objects.

Lack of coordination and planning between different authorities within their areas of responsibility. The placement of objects and infrastructure, the placement of objects at a later stage than the initial planning due to specific considerations that are not part of a comprehensive planning process, excessive advertising spaces in the street environment, broken or damaged objects that have not been removed or repaired, and so on. The placement of objects based on ad-hoc decisions, rather than comprehensive planning, can lead to an increase in visual clutter and unnecessary duplication of objects. This conflict is particularly significant in urban renewal projects, where new elements are placed in the street, and in this situation, a decision must be made regarding which existing objects are necessary and which unnecessary ones should be removed as part of the urban renewal. 

The objects that create visual clutter can be classified into four main types: unnecessary objects, essential objects located in the walking strip, essential objects that are not properly designed or improperly located, and temporary objects that can be removed or relocated. Trash Bins
Trash bins are relatively small waste containers located on main streets and near activity centers and public transport stations, and they are part of the street maintenance system. Their role is to assist in keeping the street clean, but at the same time, without proper maintenance and frequent emptying, they may lead to the opposite result from what they are intended for.

Placement of Waste Bins Together with Other Objects  
The capacity of the waste bin should be in accordance with the emptying rate and the level of usage.  
A waste bin should not be installed without a proper collection and maintenance plan.  
In residential areas, waste bins should be placed according to the garbage collection route.  
Easy access for emptying the waste bins and for various users must be ensured.  
The main consideration for determining the dimensions of the waste bin is the volume required according to the evacuation plan, which is determined based on the filling rate of the waste bin. The dimensions of the waste bin should allow access for maintenance personnel and the public using the waste bin.  
In central areas, the average dimensions of a waste bin are 70 cm in height and 40 cm in diameter. In areas where the holding volume is insufficient, larger waste bins are sometimes placed.  
In areas with security sensitivity, waste bins designed to absorb the force of an explosion are sometimes used.  
Additionally, in residential areas, it is recommended to place a waste bin for every 100 meters in areas with high pedestrian activity, such as in central streets, near activity centers, close to public parks, and near central bus stations. Waste bins should be added as needed based on expected demand.

To place waste bins according to the distribution of bins:  
Where there is significant pedestrian activity, such as in main streets, near activity centers, close to public parks, and near central bus stations, additional waste bins should be added as needed and based on expected demand.  
In order to reduce visual clutter and optimize space usage, it is possible to integrate the location of the waste bin with a "combined pole." Otherwise, it is preferable to place the waste bin near a pole or in seating areas and corners, but not too close, due to potential odor nuisance. In any case, the waste bin should be positioned outside the walking path.

Mail distribution centers  
A mail distribution center serves as a facility with mailboxes provided for the use of residents in the distribution area. The use of mail distribution centers is increasing due to efficiency in mail delivery.  
Adequate accessibility to the mail distribution facility must be ensured for both pedestrians and private vehicle users. Therefore, it is recommended to locate the mail distribution center near parking and stopping areas to allow for safe exit from the vehicle.

Efficiency in Mail Distribution.
Adequate accessibility to the mail distribution facility must be ensured, both for pedestrians and private vehicle users. Therefore, it is recommended to locate the mail distribution center near parking and stopping areas, in order to allow safe exit from the vehicle, collection of mail, and continuation of travel. It is not advisable to place a mail distribution facility at the street corner or anywhere where stopping would cause a nuisance or risk. Recommended locations for placing a mail distribution center include: near the local post office, in the neighborhood shopping center, or in a public space facing the right-of-way. In any case, the activity at the facility should not obstruct the walking path, including the structure itself and any queue that may form near the facility.

Recycling Facilities and Recycling Centers
The Ministry of Environmental Protection, in collaboration with many cities in Israel, promotes recycling as part of the overall agenda. As part of the recycling system in the city, many authorities are establishing new recycling centers to continue handling and recycling waste. Recycling facilities are designated containers for collecting sorted waste for further treatment and recycling. Common types of facilities include: bottles, paper, plastic, glass, clothing, metals, disks, and batteries. A recycling center is a collection of recycling facilities grouped together, providing centralized service for waste management.

The sorted materials are intended for continued treatment and recycling. The common types of facilities are: bottles, paper, plastic, glass, clothing, metals, discs, and batteries. A recycling center is a collection of recycling facilities grouped together, providing centralized service to the neighborhood. The dimensions of recycling facilities vary according to the model of the facility and its function. The common factor among the facilities is their relative size compared to other objects on the street. A table presents examples of typical dimensions of recycling facilities. As of the time of writing these guidelines, a uniform standard has not been applied to recycling facilities, and recycling facilities in different authorities have varying dimensions and designs. Coordinating the design of recycling facilities may create a common language that will improve the accessibility of the facilities and reduce visual nuisances.

The population lives in cities, and therefore the street, which is the artery of life, culture, and the economy of the city, occupies a central and irreplaceable space in the daily existence of most citizens of the state. In light of this, and due to the special importance given to the street among all those engaged in the fields of engineering, behavioral sciences, and the humanities, an innovative system of guidelines for street planning was prepared about a decade ago, which combined the best knowledge in Israel with the best global knowledge accumulated in the field of urban development and architecture, integrated with the transportation sector. This was done after the government policy for land conservation and mixed-use, prioritization of public transportation, safety, and quality of life was also incorporated into the books. The urban structure, which combines residential, employment, education, culture, and commercial uses, inherently generates significant movement of diverse populations for various purposes and between different places. The Ministry of Transportation's policy generally states that walking is the preferred means of transportation that should be encouraged as much as possible as an alternative to motorized travel, followed by a preference for public transportation and bicycle use. October 2020 / Guidelines for Street Planning in Cities - Bicycle Traffic  
The transportation system in Israel has so far been largely based on private and public motorized traffic. In recent years, awareness of personal transportation means, such as walking and cycling, has entered the public consciousness and that of authorities around the world and in Israel. In recent years, bicycles, including electric ones, as well as various types of scooters, have become more popular in Israel, including rental services. These means play an important role in the urban transportation system - their strengthening and encouragement are also part of a policy developed for transportation in Israel, as part of the 21st century.  
In cities, primarily from the aspects of capacity and service level for private vehicles, the perception that related to motorized traffic has been replaced in developed countries by a new perception that emphasizes quality of life and safety, along with a redistribution of public space. The new urban planning reduces the area allocated for private vehicles in favor of space for public transportation, soft movements (bicycles), and for protective areas and permeable surfaces for stormwater.  
In the new worldview, there is also a notable increase in listening and attention to the public's desires. Experience from around the world shows that public opinion has changed.

Public transportation, soft movements (bicycles), and for the benefit of protected areas and permeable surfaces for rainwater drainage. Pedestrians are also highlighted in the new worldview, with greater listening and attention to the public's desires. Experience around the world shows that public opinion has changed, and people are willing to give up some advantages of private vehicles for the sake of improving their quality of life. The central issues that have become part of an ongoing dialogue with the public include more safety, less traffic flow, less noise and air pollution, less space for private vehicle movement, and more space for gardening, playing, walking, and cycling. In many places in the Western world, bicycles are increasingly taking part in the transportation system as an alternative to private and public motorized traffic, or in combination with it. This phenomenon has recently been noticeable in Israel as well, especially in flat cities like Tel Aviv-Jaffa. The shift to bicycles as a means of transportation is not only due to difficulties in motorized traffic; cycling saves space in urban areas, allows direct contact with the environment and community, and the physical activity involved provides added value, giving the cyclist a feeling of implementing positive values along with personal enjoyment. Riding a bicycle means adopting a lifestyle that aligns with the values of the twenty-first century.

The environment and the community, along with the physical activity involved, provide added value, giving the cyclist a sense of implementing positive values combined with personal enjoyment. Cycling means adopting a lifestyle that aligns with the values of the twenty-first century. Furthermore, cycling has proven to be the most efficient and fastest mode of transport for short distances in urban areas, especially for completing the 'last mile.' Within this new perception, developing infrastructure for bicycles makes them an even more efficient mode of transport that can compete with motor vehicles, especially if this is done alongside imposing restrictions on private vehicle traffic, and together with the improvement and strengthening of public transportation, including its connectivity with bicycles, which will ensure cyclists a continuity of means. These guidelines are part of the new set of guidelines "Guidelines for Bicycle Traffic Planning" from the Ministry of "Green Regulation" and are applicable from March 1 for street planning in cities, detailed in the transportation section. The Green Regulation guidelines emphasize prioritizing safety, quality of life, and consideration of residents' and community desires at the top of the priority list in planning transportation infrastructure and the urban environment. They are based on the experience accumulated worldwide and in Israel, for the use of decision-makers and planners from all fields of sustainable planning and on principles of planning domains.

Purpose of the Guidelines
The basic purpose of the planning guidelines is to create a guiding framework for conducting an orderly, systematic, and clear planning process, through which the policy for developing public space can be implemented, as proposed in the guideline books. The guidelines are a multidisciplinary document that provides policymakers with tools for decision-making regarding the planning, establishment, and maintenance of the street space in general, and bicycle infrastructure in particular. The guidelines present the needs of cyclists, the policy behind the allocation of bicycle infrastructure, the perception, and the various planning components. The guidelines also address education and awareness, enforcement, and parking.

From Israel, these guidelines are based on the latest guidelines and findings from those countries where experience in developing bicycle infrastructure has already been accumulated, while adapting them to the legal framework and transportation planning policy in Israel. The guidelines present the planner with the options available to them. However, the guidelines are not intended to limit the planner's solutions but to define a framework on one hand and to broaden their horizons on the other hand, in order to assist them in dealing with non-standard issues.

A. Guidelines for Street Space Planning
This book is the foundational master book and the overarching framework of the guideline system, in which the fundamental guidelines for street planning are consolidated. The book details the foundational concept of the guideline system, which places the individual and their well-being at the center of the public space.

In the book, a significant distinction is made between 'urban street' and 'urban road,' which serves as a basic benchmark for planning the public space, as detailed below:

Urban Street - A space in the city that serves all urban activities (traffic, housing, commerce), where the important traffic component is accessibility.

Urban Road - An urban space primarily used for passage between parts of the city, where the important traffic component is mobility.

Historical and Cultural Background  
Understanding the historical and cultural background of cycling, which also encompasses the traffic habits of cyclists, serves as a foundation for planning the bicycle traffic system, as will be presented and detailed in this chapter and the following chapters.  
Until World War II, bicycles were a common means of transportation in many countries around the world, particularly in Western Europe. After the war, with the steep rise in living standards, the flourishing of suburbs, and the decrease in car prices, a convenient and efficient road system was developed, daily travel distances increased, and the car replaced the bicycle. Apart from a few countries (such as the Netherlands and Denmark), where bicycles remained a common and accepted means of transportation, motor vehicles pushed bicycles aside, and their use for daily commuting became marginal.  
In the early 1980s, a significant change emerged in the approach of authorities and policymakers towards the transportation system in the city (and especially in the city center), as it became understood that the car not only contributes to quality of life but also, to no lesser extent, harms it—the need to provide more and more capacity for traffic (lanes and parking) in cities at the expense of sidewalks, boulevards, and public spaces.

Policy Principles
The policy of densification of existing cities, adopted by the Government of Israel, and the internalization of the approach that it is not possible to provide the required capacity and maintain existing parking standards for the arrival of commuters by private vehicle to every point in the dense city, has led to thinking about alternative transportation solutions for urban movement. 
These solutions belong to two main groups of means:

Since in most cases - especially in existing urban fabrics - it is not possible to widen the right of way to allocate space for additional lanes, the recommended solution is to integrate all transportation means within the existing public space, through reallocation. This reallocation must be done with a holistic view, emphasizing the quality of urban life and the well-being of residents.

Design Principles for Bike Paths
There are two basic design characteristics related to the design of the bike path: its location in the right of way (on the road, on the sidewalk, or in a separate area), and the traffic regime (one-way or two-way).

In Israel, bike paths are regulated in various options - in new streets, in existing streets, on roads, in public open spaces, and in open areas.

A. Traffic Regime
Unlike the bike lane, which is always intended for one-way traffic only, a bike path can be one-way or two-way. 

There is still a debate involving both planners and users about what the optimal arrangement is. A two-way path requires a smaller allocation of right of way than two one-way paths, but it is...

Bicycles can be one-way or two-way. There is still a debate among both planners and users about what the optimal arrangement is. A two-way path requires a smaller allocation of right-of-way than two one-way paths, but it requires more complex solutions at intersections. A one-way path, on the other hand, facilitates traffic management at intersections, but in the absence of enforcement and a tradition of bicycle path usage, it happens that cyclists ride in both directions, causing mutual disruption and risking the safety of cyclists and other users. Additionally, one-way paths create a symmetrical cross-section of the street and provide access to both sides of the street, while a two-way path serves only one side.

Rarely, the divider (in a divided street) will be removed, and the street will become one-lane with a two-way bicycle lane on one side. - Safety consideration - bicycles pose a danger to pedestrians.
- Convenience consideration - pedestrians interfere with the movement of cyclists.
- Encouragement of walking - maintaining space for pedestrians.

Bicycle Lanes on Existing Streets  
Introduction  
The planning guidelines for implementing bicycle lanes on the street, as presented in the previous chapter, lead to a clear conceptual line indicating that integrating bicycle lanes at sidewalk level is not recommended. This planning approach, which differs from the one previously accepted among planners, raises questions regarding its application on existing streets, where the ability for expression and implementation is more limited than on new streets.  
It is important to emphasize again that creating infrastructure for bicycle traffic in the city, although important in itself, is intended to serve broader and significant additional purposes - creating an alternative to private vehicles and reducing their movement in the city streets, improving the quality of the urban space to promote pedestrian activity, encouraging the use of public transportation, and more. Therefore, it is appropriate to examine every solution for pedestrians in relation to its suitability for all the intended goals for developing bicycle traffic on existing urban streets.  
In general, it can be clarified that allocating a lane for bicycle traffic from the space designated for pedestrian activity does not align with these goals and, to a large extent, contradicts them. Such allocation is recommended only if the planner is convinced that there is sufficient space for activity and movement.

Such an allocation is recommended only if the planner is convinced that there is sufficient space for pedestrian activity and movement, and that this activity will not be harmed at all, or that its impact will be proportional in relation to the impact on all users of the street.

Promoting bicycle traffic in existing streets is particularly important, and it is necessary to act decisively to implement it despite the many difficulties. This goal often requires a comprehensive examination of how the street functions, and a programmatic examination in the form of a 'street portrait' as detailed in the guidelines book.

It should be emphasized that the guiding lines presented in Chapter 3 regarding the maximum separation of bicycle and pedestrian traffic are also applicable in existing streets, as well as the levels of separation between bicycles and motor vehicles as detailed in this chapter.

4.3.4 Bicycle Lane on Sidewalk  
The installation of a bicycle lane at sidewalk level will only be carried out when it is determined that the following four parameters are positive:  
A. The location of the bicycle lane on the sidewalk is determined as part of the process of examining the street profile and distributing the street space in a balanced manner among its users.  
B. The width of the pedestrian traffic lane is not less than the minimum width required for this lane according to the guidelines for pedestrian traffic.  
C. The width of the bicycle traffic lane is not less than the minimum width required for this lane according to the guidelines for bicycle traffic.  
D. The planner is convinced that implementing the bicycle lane at sidewalk level in this street is preferable to implementing the bicycle lane at road level.  
Specifically, it is advisable to consider the installation of a bicycle lane at sidewalk level on collector and arterial streets in cases where all the following conditions are met:  
A. Collector Street  
The street data requires complete separation at level G between bicycles and motor vehicles, meaning that the installation of a path physically separated from motor traffic is mandatory (see section 4.2.4).

A main street that is urbanly active, along which there is intensive pedestrian activity such as commerce, public services, etc. There is a large amount of pedestrian crossing expected or existing on the street, active pedestrian traffic along the street, public transport stations, and so on.

Level crossing is based on the principle of complete separation between intersecting traffic at an intersection, by moving one or more of the traffic flows to a different level at the intersection.  
In principle, level separation ensures maximum safety and efficiency for intersecting traffic; however, level separation has several fundamental disadvantages.  
It requires at least one of the traffic flows (usually pedestrians and bicycles) to disconnect from street level and move locally to another level. This requirement contradicts the essence of the urban street planning guidelines, which are based on strengthening the connection between pedestrians and the street space.

Introduction and Principles  
Bicycles, pedestrians, and motor vehicles move along streets and roads parallel to each other. When bicycles reach an intersection and encounter pedestrians, near public transportation stations, the movements intersect and conflicts arise between movements with different characteristics, speeds, and intensities. Optimal management of these conflicts will help reduce safety risks for various users and improve the functionality of the intersection.  
General guidelines for planning intersections are detailed in the guidelines for urban intersection planning within the street planning guidelines, and they also apply to bicycle movements at intersections. The main points are:  
- Speed reduction of approaching traffic - It must be ensured that all movements approaching the intersection, including bicycle traffic, slow down (to the point of stopping if necessary) to notice other movements and allow other movements to perceive what is happening at the intersection.  
- Reducing the area of conflicting movements - The areas where different and intersecting movements occur should be minimized as much as possible to reduce the conflict space.  
- Simplifying traffic arrangements - It must be ensured that the traffic arrangements at the intersection are...

Reduction of conflicting movement areas - It is necessary to minimize as much as possible the areas where different and intersecting movements occur, in order to reduce the conflict zones as much as possible.  
Simplification of traffic arrangements - It must be ensured that the traffic arrangements at the intersection are clear and simple for all movements approaching the intersection.  
Visibility and clarity - The intersection should be designed to ensure mutual visibility of all movements present at the intersection, so that they can notice each other already at the approaches to the intersection.

The following are the design principles for intersections and junctions with an emphasis on bicycle traffic:  
At intersections and junctions, as well as along the entire street, separation between bicycle traffic and pedestrian traffic is desired.

The design components of bicycle movements at intersections  
Integrating bicycle movement at intersections requires consideration of three layers of design components: the level of separation of the bicycle movement arriving at the intersection, the directions of bicycle movement at the intersection, and the level of control of the intersection, as detailed below:  
A. Levels of separation  
Bicycle movement arrives at the intersection at one of the levels of separation: Level A - integrated with motorized traffic; Level B - when there is no free right turn for cars - in a separate lane from motorized traffic, and also when right turns are allowed only for bicycles; Level C - on a separate path as independent movement. Crossing the intersection by bicycles can be done at a different level of separation than that along the route leading to the intersection. In many cases, the crossing of the intersection will be planned at a lower level of separation than in the segment, based on the slow traffic speeds at the intersection and the need to simplify traffic arrangements. In other cases, where the functionality of the intersection and the safety of the riders will require it, the design will be adjusted accordingly.

In many cases, the intersection crossing will be planned at a lower level of separation than in the segment, based on the slow traffic speeds at the intersection and the need to simplify traffic arrangements. In other cases, where the functioning of the intersection and the safety of cyclists will require it, the level of separation for bicycles will be maintained according to its level along the corridor and even at a higher level, as will be detailed later.
