Bicycle Traffic in Roundabouts  
A bicycle lane can be continuous, meaning it integrates into a roundabout as a lane; alternatively, it can reach up to the stop line or stop before it, as detailed in Table 20-5.1 m before it. A bicycle path can bypass the roundabout and cross the arms of the intersection at a crosswalk; alternatively, when right-of-way does not allow this, or for planning considerations, it will connect to the roundabout as an arm. A one-way path can become a lane before the roundabout and integrate into it as a lane. The larger the roundabout, the less efficient and convenient it becomes.

When road rights do not allow this, or for planning reasons, it will connect to the roundabout as a branch. A one-way path can become a lane before the roundabout and merge into it as a lane. The larger the roundabout, the more it detracts from the efficiency and comfort of bicycle traffic.

Interaction Between Bicycles and Bus Stops  
The bicycle lane is usually located between the traffic lanes and the sidewalk. At bus stops, the bus pulls up to the curb, creating a conflict between bicycle traffic and passengers waiting at the stop, or between the bus stopping on the bicycle lane or crossing it. There are several solutions for bicycle passage in the area of bus stops.  
A. Bicycle Lanes  
In the area of the bus bay, the bicycle lane continues uninterrupted parallel to the bay. The bus entering the bay crosses the bicycle lane but does not block it during the stop in the bay. In this case, the departing bus must yield to bicycles entering and exiting the bay. When there is no bus bay and the stop is located in an 'anti-bay' or on the side of the street, the bicycle lane is interrupted in the area of the stop. When a bus stops at the station, bicycles either overtake it or wait behind it until it leaves the stop.  
B. Bicycle Path

Bicycle intersection with rapid bus transit lanes (BRT)
The bicycle intersection with rapid bus transit lanes will be based on the guidelines for rapid bus transit. This chapter's guidelines for bicycle traffic at signalized intersections, and on the chapter in case there is a crosswalk for bicycles at an intersection with rapid bus transit, should avoid as much as possible a stepped crossing, which may create a conflict between pedestrians and cyclists.
Bicycle intersection with light rail
The bicycle intersection with light rail will be based on the guidelines of this chapter for bicycle traffic at intersections "crosswalks" in the regulations manual.

Bicycle interaction with light rail  
The interaction of bicycles with light rail will be based on the guidelines of this section for bicycle traffic at intersections "Crosswalks" in the guiding rules for integrating public transport systems, and on the section for public transport traffic lights.  
In case of a contradiction between planning issues (for example, determining the width of a separator), a section will be established in the rules for the public transport system.  
Bicycle interaction with heavy rail  
It is advisable to avoid planning bicycle lane crossings with heavy rail tracks as much as possible and to implement grade separation for bicycles. If it is not possible to avoid the crossing, reliance should be placed on the "Guidelines for Planning Railway Crossings" from the Ministry of Transport, and to adopt solutions as detailed in the "Guidelines for Planning Pedestrian Crossings at Railway Crossings," which also refer to bicycles.  
Bicycle lane in front of entrances to yards and parking lots  
When a vehicle exits from yards and parking lots, the driver may be surprised by an encounter with bicycles, unlike a possible encounter with pedestrians and cars, which the driver is accustomed to in the past. To improve safety in areas where bicycles and vehicles meet at exits from yards and parking lots, appropriate sight lines should be ensured and the bicycle lane should be marked.

Bicycle Path Intersection with Crosswalk  
When the bicycle path is at the same level as the road between the sidewalk and the parking lane, a continuous crosswalk that crosses both the bicycle path and the parking lane may be long. To shorten it and make it safer, it will be divided into two segments - one segment crossing the bicycle path, and a crosswalk crossing the traffic lane, with a paved strip (at least 5.39 m) between them at road level and width.  
Bicycle Path Intersection with Disabled Parking  
The separation strip between the bicycle path and the parking lane blocks access to the sidewalk. Therefore, in the section where disabled parking is designated, there will be no separation strip, and accessibility details on the sidewalk will be maintained. It is recommended that the section of the path near the disabled parking be paved with Trento or another material that distinguishes it from the asphalt and warns the cyclist of crossing pedestrians.

Introduction and Legal Framework
General
This chapter is intended to present the recommended way to use markings and traffic signs to define for road users the various arrangements presented in the previous chapters, and to regulate their use. The main terms and their definitions are according to their use in the book. Since the guidelines for bicycle traffic were published in October 2009, the traffic signs and regulations have been updated several times, thus providing answers to the various arrangements existing in the integration of bicycles in public space.
Table 6.1 presents the types of unlicensed personal vehicles that are allowed to move on roads without a license and insurance, and the main rules that apply to them. In addition, there are also various types of roller skates that are not intended for movement on roads but for designated areas. According to the definitions in the Traffic Ordinance, bicycles are vehicles, and in the absence of a designated path or lane, they are required to move on the road and not on the sidewalk. The traffic regulations stipulate, among other things, "a bicycle path has been allocated on the road and marked with a traffic sign."

Dedicated paths. According to the definitions in the Traffic Ordinance, bicycles are vehicles, and in the absence of a dedicated path or lane, they are required to move on the road and not on the sidewalk. The traffic regulations state, among other things, "If a bicycle path has been allocated on the road and marked with appropriate signage, a cyclist shall not ride in any other part of the road except for the bicycle path," meaning that wherever there is a special path for bicycles (or lane), bicycles are required to move only on them. Furthermore, only standard electric bicycles, which comply with the requirements of standard 15194, referred to as "bicycles with auxiliary motors" according to regulation 25, are allowed to move on bicycle lanes and paths. The electric motor, with a power of 250 watts, is activated only while pedaling and stops functioning at 25 km/h. Other two-wheeled vehicles that do not meet the standard requirements are considered motorcycles and are permitted for use only on the road.

Signage and Marking for Various Arrangements in the Section  
General  
This section will present the signage and marking of the various arrangements as they are adapted to the levels of separation defined in Chapter 4. In this chapter, we will use the term "exclusive arrangements for bicycles" (lanes and paths).  
In addition to the required marking and signage as detailed below, the bicycle lane surface will be in green in areas of conflict with other road users (motor vehicles and pedestrians), and it is also possible to use color differentiation along the lane - see Section 6.2.2 below.  
Color Differentiation  
In areas of conflict, it is mandatory to paint the bicycle lane in green. Conflict areas are road sections at intersections, crosswalks, bus stops, large entrances to yards or parking lots, or large pedestrian entrances, etc. The color differentiation will be carried out with materials approved according to the "Specification for Green Color Material for Paths and Bicycle Lanes" of the Inter-Ministerial Committee for Examining Traffic and Safety Devices, which also refers to the relevant requirements from Israeli standards. The marking will cover the entire width of the lane.

Approval will be granted according to the "Specification for Green Guidance Material for Paths and Bicycle Lanes" of the inter-ministerial committee for examining traffic and safety devices, which also refers to the relevant requirements from Israeli standards. The marking will cover the entire width of the strip. 

Regarding the above, for details on marking lanes, paths, crosswalks, and traffic signs, see the diagrams in section 6.17-6.14, 6.11, 6.9-6.1. It is important to avoid using any other shade to create a uniform language throughout the country. 

Bicycle traffic without a separate lane (Level of Separation A) 
As vehicles, bicycles move along with motorized traffic and must comply with the signage intended for all vehicles. Even in sections where there is no special arrangement for bicycles, point arrangements using calming measures and at intersections are possible, aimed at facilitating bicycle movement. Such arrangements are accepted in traffic calming areas, but not only there, and they are marked and signposted accordingly - see "Guidelines for Traffic Calming Areas."

Bicycle traffic in the direction of traffic or on a path (Levels of Separation B, C) 
In a section where there is a separate lane for bicycles (lane or path), bicycles must travel in it, and they are prohibited from moving in motorized traffic lanes, let alone in pedestrian strips (except at intersections). The bicycle strip...

In a section where there is a separate lane for bicycles (path or trail), bicycles must move within it, and they are prohibited from moving in motor vehicle lanes, let alone in pedestrian areas (except at intersections). The bicycle lane is marked and indicated on the road to clarify to all users that this lane is reserved for cyclists only. At the beginning of every bicycle arrangement, a sign or appropriate marking must be placed, and it should be renewed after every intersection. 

Bicycle paths must be physically separated from pedestrian and motor vehicle traffic according to one of the following options:
A. The path is at a lower level than the pedestrian lane by 10 cm.
B. The path is separated from the pedestrian lane by an overhead infrastructure strip or street furniture (light poles, trees, benches), and if that is not possible, at least by a separation strip of at least 0.50 m (for example, rough and distinguishable material). 

A path that meets conditions A or B or both will be marked accordingly. A shared path for bicycles and pedestrians is marked with a specific sign, which is less recommended according to the guidelines, but is not prohibited.

Determining the Location of Bicycle Parking Areas  
The location of bicycle parking areas is extremely important and should be examined in relation to potential users, the destinations that cyclists aim for, and according to the duration of parking, as detailed below.  
A. Parking in High-Activity Concentrations  
In high-activity concentrations, such as public transport terminals, mass transit stations, commercial centers, sports centers, schools, higher education institutions, etc., it is recommended to allocate suitable parking areas where bicycle parking concentrations will be located.  
It is essential that the parking is close to the entrance. It is advisable that the parking be covered and protected from wind, rain, and sun; however, it should be avoided that the covering obscures the bicycles, unless the parking is in a regulated area with supervision, like in a regular parking lot.  
B. Parking in Public Space  
In public spaces (streets, parks, etc.), designated parking spaces for bicycles should be allocated. Without such designated spaces, every signpost, every railing, and every street furniture may be used for tying bicycles.  
In streets where the main uses are employment or commercial, it is preferable to install locking facilities for every pair of bicycles. The appropriate location is in the strip of the street.

The exit from such places may cause every traffic sign, every railing, and every street furniture to be used for tying bicycles. In streets where the main uses are occupational or commercial, it is advisable to install tying facilities for every pair of bicycles. The appropriate location is in the service strip of the sidewalk, 5-10 meters from the traffic lane (and in no case within the pedestrian traffic lane). In the absence of space, it is recommended to confiscate a parking space for vehicles for this purpose. 

The preferred location for installing bicycle facilities within the roadway is in the parking strip near intersections and crosswalks. Indirectly, such installation will contribute to traffic safety at the intersection, as the field of vision between different users will increase. 

C. Parking in Residential Buildings
In residential buildings, a closed and locked space should be allocated for the residents' bicycle parking. It should be ensured that the parking space is as accessible as possible to the street, without stairs. In places where bicycle parking is offered in a parking basement, the bicycle parking should be designated in the upper basement, as close as possible to the entrance. In places where a guard is stationed, it is appropriate to install the bicycle parking close to the guard and under their direct supervision. 

Next to each building, it is advisable to allocate a tying space for bicycles for guests or for short-term parking by residents. 

D. Parking in Public Buildings and Employment Buildings

It is advisable to install the bicycle parking close to the guard and under his direct supervision. Next to each building, it is preferable to allocate a place for tying bicycles for guests or for short-term parking of residents. 

D. Parking in Public Buildings and Employment Buildings
Next to every public building and every employment building, a bicycle parking area with tying facilities should be allocated. In places where a guard or security personnel is responsible for vehicle parking, it is preferable to locate the bicycle parking close to them.

Types of Bicycle Parking
The most common and effective bicycle parking in public spaces are in parking bays, in the service strip on the sidewalk, in open parking lots, etc. These parking areas, which include a facility for tying the bicycle frame and wheels, are inexpensive, accessible, and safe. These parking areas can be upgraded by adding a cover to protect them from weather damage, but it is important that the cover does not obscure the bicycles from their surroundings. Efficient and inexpensive facilities can be installed next to walls, with bicycles parked parallel and close to the wall, or hanging parallel to the wall with the front wheel hanging up. Protected (locked) and reserved (supervised) parking.

Bicycles can be parked efficiently (in place) and cheaply next to walls, with the bicycles parked parallel and close to the wall, or hanging parallel to the wall with the front wheel suspended upwards. Protected (locked) and reserved (electronically monitored and/or with cameras) parking provides better protection for bicycles but at a higher cost. To further enhance the protection of bicycles, "lockers" can be used. To accommodate more pairs of bicycles in a limited space, double-decker (or even triple-decker) facilities can be utilized. Facilities that allow only the locking of the wheel are not recommended, although they can be used in areas where the risk of theft is low.

Introduction  
Bicycle lanes are generally located within the roadway area, and their implementation is derived from the other components of the road.  
The bicycle lane is part of the road surface, and therefore it is part of the shared surface with the vehicle lanes alongside it.  
A bicycle path located within the right-of-way is separated from the vehicle traffic lanes and pedestrian traffic lanes, and therefore can have a separate structure.  
This chapter will provide the basic tools for optimal handling of bicycle traffic lanes, so that they are as comfortable, pleasant, and safe for riding as possible.

Urban Landscape and Design
Bicycle paths and lanes generally do not constitute an independent component in the open public space but are part of a designed and planned system of public streets, public parks, urban roads, etc. Therefore, they contribute to this system while simultaneously being an integral part of it. The physical design of the bicycle path must be part of the overall design thinking of the street concerning finishing materials, planting along the path, accompanying street furniture, parking facilities, lighting, etc. 

Decisions regarding each of these components must be made as part of the design decision for the entire street (or for all public open spaces in the case of bicycle paths within public areas), with a systemic view of all street users, their needs, and the balance between them (see the guidelines book for street space planning).

Lighting  
The lighting should provide good visibility conditions during dark hours. Lighting plays a major role in instilling a sense of security for the cyclist. However, lighting also has architectural aesthetic importance as it is part of the "toolbox" of street furniture, forming a complete system that constitutes the public space.  
In addition to enhancing the sense of safety and security for street users, proper lighting can strengthen the sense of order and organization in the street, and visually highlight important elements in the context of the entire street.  
Bicycle lanes within the street can utilize street lighting for illumination, or alternatively, pedestrians can receive independent lighting aimed at illuminating the bicycle path and the sidewalk. In built urban areas, it is appropriate to establish "service centers" in places where bicycles are concentrated (central stations, shopping malls, educational institutions, sports and recreation complexes, etc.), where public services, drinking facilities, and resting points will be established as part of the services required for all residents. Maintenance of bicycle lanes 
Regular and frequent maintenance of bicycle lanes is essential for ensuring the safety of cycling. Ongoing maintenance should include repairing defects in the pavement (flooring, asphalt, gravel, etc.), cleaning the pavement from sand, mud, and other nuisances, trimming tree branches, ensuring proper lighting, addressing resting area corners, and maintaining service facilities, etc.

During the implementation of changes or maintenance of streets and intersections, care should be taken when preparing temporary traffic arrangements to also consider bicycle traffic. 
Clearances 
Similar to the movement of other users on the street, bicycle traffic must also maintain horizontal and vertical clearances free of obstacles in the bicycle lane area (path or lane). The vertical clearance is intended to prevent injuries to the upper body of the rider (up to the height at which the rider pedals while standing), and the horizontal clearance is meant to allow the bicycle to deviate to the edge of the path without coming into contact with obstacles. 
Horizontal Clearance 
Maintaining a horizontal clearance free of obstacles to the edge of the bicycle lane is intended to allow horizontal deviation of the bicycle and enable the rider to stay close to the edge of the path, for example, when overtaking or stopping. 
The width of the upper body of the rider and the handlebars is wider than the area of the pedals and wheels. Therefore, a different clearance must be maintained between low and high obstacles. Care should be taken to ensure the required clearance both for a single obstacle such as a pole, and for a continuous obstacle such as a fence. Introduction  
The purpose of this guideline book is to regulate and establish the rules for bicycle traffic in the urban space, and to present to those involved in the planning work, decision-makers, and planners, a systematic process for planning an urban bicycle network. However, given that the field of cycling in Israel is still in its infancy relative to the potential it holds, and in comparison to existing models around the world, there is significant importance to supportive activities needed to expand the circle of users. Experience in European countries has shown that the phenomenon of cycling has gained momentum in many cases as a result of user pressure, rather than national intent. In order for the number of bicycle users to increase, it is necessary to allow cyclists to exercise their right to move safely in the urban space, while simultaneously educating and guiding as broad a population as possible about the benefits of cycling, thereby increasing the circle of users. The purpose of this chapter is to address these complementary issues.

Enforcement
Dedicated bike paths are one of the basic conditions for expanding the circle of cyclists. A comprehensive, convenient, and safe urban network free from hazards may encourage additional users, as well as encourage parents to allow their children to ride. In the current reality, however, there are many phenomena where there is a devaluation of the approach to bicycle infrastructure: the presence of cars and motorcycles in bike lanes, parking of vehicles within these lanes, and pedestrian movement within them instead of in their designated lanes.
Unauthorized motor vehicles, especially two-wheeled vehicles, pose a danger to cyclists. Pedestrians walking on bike paths hinder cyclists, causing them to deviate from the path and risking injury. A vehicle parked on the path blocks it and forces cyclists to veer off the path. A vehicle that crosses the stop line and waits for the green light in the area designated for bicycles endangers cyclists, whose balance is not stable. All these phenomena must be prevented as a basic condition, alongside the promotion of additional plans for bike paths. Effective and consistent education and enforcement are required to prevent them; without these, cyclists may avoid using the paths.

Public Awareness and Education
Bicycles are considered by some in the public as an inferior means of transportation suitable for young people and those without resources, for children, and for those who are crazy about it. Some of the public may see riding a bicycle as a loss of dignity, while others view a woman riding a bicycle as a negative and immodest phenomenon. Transforming bicycles into a means of transportation suitable for everyone is a long process of changing perceptions, and it must be accompanied by public awareness and encouragement from the authorities. The Ministry of Transportation, the Ministry of Tourism, the Ministry of Environmental Protection, the Ministry of Education, and local authorities can and should encourage the use of bicycles as a daily means of transportation.

The use of bicycles can be encouraged by providing incentives in salaries for those who commute by bicycle. An employee who arrives by bicycle, instead of by car, saves the employer parking space and is presumably a healthier employee who utilizes their commute as exercise. Planning Stages  
The project planning is carried out according to a defined program for each project and each planning stage. Inputs from the landscape architect and building architect, planning outputs, and their contents are detailed in the "Planning Task Guide." Therefore, the instructions in this guide should be read together with the planning task guide, with an emphasis on the document of mutuality between the professions, which aims to coordinate and divide the planning tasks among the planning team. The guide and instructions refer to the planning stages according to the main characteristics of each stage as follows:  
In the initial planning stage, alternatives for the project design are examined. The space and the activities within it are studied, the landscape and environmental sensitivity of the area are defined, and a comparison between the alternatives is conducted based on criteria that reflect the degree of sensitivity of the space. At the end of this stage, the chosen alternative is proposed by the planning team, and after evaluation, the company decides on the alternative that will be recommended for advancement in the statutory process.  
In the early planning stage, additional alternatives for the design are examined, as required by the planning institution. Subsequently, the planning team develops the chosen alternative and prepares its statutory planning documents. The landscape architect and building architect write the chapters on landscape and architecture in the environmental impact assessment or in the document.

The landscape architect and the building architect write the chapters on landscape and architecture in the environmental impact assessment or in the environmental document and prepare the guiding documents of the statutory plan in their field. At the end of the preliminary planning stage, after the plan is validated by the planning institution and the government, the completion of the preliminary planning documents is carried out. The update is conducted according to the decisions of the planning institution, with reference from the landscape and architecture planners to the proposed development and implementation stages for the realization of the project. Judgment 2 summarizes the preliminary planning stage and establishes the principles for continuing the planning in the detailed planning stage, including the type of tender. 

After Judgment 2, the detailed planning for implementation is carried out, according to the principles of the preliminary planning and the binding and guiding documents of the statutory plan. 1.3 Preliminary Analysis of Views  
The purpose of the views analysis is to characterize the visual impact of the project on the space where it will be established.  
The analysis will include references to the subject of views from various focal points in the space towards the project in each of the planning alternatives and the views of different landscape units in the space from the project.  
The views analysis will be conducted using the following means:  
1) Photography of views from typical vantage points. The photography points must be marked on a key map and not rely solely on verbal description.  
2) A view diagram from and towards the project from selected points, distinguishing between near and far views. The angles of view will be marked on the diagram.  
3) Cross-sections, prepared based on photogrammetric measurements of the space, will express the morphology of the space (flat areas, mountainous, built areas) and the location of the proposed road in each of the planning alternatives. The standard scale for the cross-sections is 1:500 to 1:1000. The cross-sections must be marked on the view diagram.

1.2. Objective  
The main objective is to regulate the issue of improving the appearance of the city in local authorities in Israel so that the role of the unit, its subordination, interfaces with various entities within and outside the authority, the comprehensive vision, and its areas of responsibility will be clear. All this is to raise the level of service to residents and optimize the use of the authority's resources. From a sample of about 62 local authorities, it can be seen that the organizational structure in local authorities is not uniform and that there is not necessarily a unit for improving the city's appearance in every authority. In many cases, the main areas of activity of the city appearance improvement unit are dispersed among other various municipal bodies, and in some cases, the field of environmental quality is subordinate to other units such as the operations department. Of all the authorities that participated in the sample, it was found that in 53%.

The main areas of activity of the Urban Improvement Unit are dispersed among various municipal bodies, and in certain cases, the field of urban improvement is subordinate to other units such as the Operations Department. Among the authorities that participated in the sample, it was found that 53% of them have an Urban Improvement Unit. On average, the number of areas subordinate to urban improvement is between 4-5, with a significant gap between the authorities, and there is no correlation to the municipal status of the authority or its population size.

2. Case Studies from Around the World
To compare the situation of the Urban Improvement Unit in Israel with that of other countries, we surveyed two cities: the first, Somerville in Massachusetts, USA, and the second, Cambridge in England. From the review, it can be seen that in these cities, as in the situation in some local authorities in Israel, the roles of the Urban Improvement Unit are divided among different departments in the city. 

Somerville, located northwest of Boston in Massachusetts, has a population of about 75,000 residents and is one of the most densely populated cities in the USA. The city has won several times the title of Best Run City in Massachusetts and even in the entire USA. The responsibility of the Urban Improvement Department, as practiced in Israel, is divided among several different departments in the Somerville City Hall.

1.1 Introduction  
The first part of the guidelines for street planning in cities deals with the geometric design of urban road intersections, while the second part of these guidelines addresses the topic of urban roads (at a single level). As a natural continuation, the third part of these guidelines is dedicated to the presentation and detailing of the guidelines related to the structural elements of the transportation infrastructure, which includes roads, squares, and sidewalks.  
The significance of the term structural elements is comprehensive and includes all the geometric and structural elements related to road paving, earthworks, slope stability, excavation (or quarrying) stability, the structure of the element, the quality of materials, and the durability of various elements over time under the harmful effects of time, climate changes, and traffic loads.  
The guidelines presented in the following chapters of this part are primarily based on local Israeli experience in local authorities and the Ministry of Construction and Housing, but they also draw from other sources such as: the American Federal Highway Administration, the Public Works Department (M.A.T.Z.) in Israel, and similar departments in Australia, South Africa, etc., the American Corps of Engineers, the British Road and Transport Laboratory, the Technion Institute for Transportation Research, and so on.

2.1 General  
The purpose of the roadway is to serve the movement of vehicles as exclusive users. Therefore, understanding the nature of traffic variables is essential for roadway planning. Traffic variables are highly complex and include all the information related to the loads of vehicles exerted on the roadway. The following subsections summarize the traffic information required for planning, while comparing the traffic variables to the planning:  
A. Axle loads and their distribution (nature of mixed traffic).  
B. The configuration of the wheels or axles of the vehicles.  
C. Contact pressure (tire pressure) of the various vehicle wheels.  
D. Volume and distribution of truck traffic over a month and year.  
E. Speed of vehicles.  
F. Lateral distribution (lanes) of truck traffic on the road.  
G. Nature of the load (static, dynamic, stopping, or accelerating).  
Traffic variables are numerous and diverse, and most of them depend on people, laws, technology, and time. Almost infinite. Therefore, each variable is highly complex in itself, and the combinations between them make it impossible to quantitatively generalize all these variables separately in the planning system, thus requiring simplification methods to generalize and unify the number of variables into an overall planning factor.  
The following sections present practical methods used for generalization and...

It is impossible to quantitatively generalize all these variables separately in the planning system, and therefore simplification methods are required to generalize and unify the number of variables into an overall planning factor. 2.3 Axle Loads and Their Distribution

The maximum permissible load in the country is 13 tons for a single axle and 21 tons for a tandem axle. 4.1 Introduction  
The first stage in the paving process to achieve the "road shape" (subgrade surface) is earthworks. Earthworks in road and surface infrastructure consist of excavation and filling activities. In most cases, slopes are paved without support. When support is required, it is usually permanent (not temporary during paving) and mainly consists of retaining walls for fill embankments, rock slopes, base layers, etc. Protective measures for unstable excavated slopes, such as armor for the excavated slopes, are also included. This section primarily discusses the design and stability of unsupported excavation and fill slopes intended for a relatively long lifespan. For this purpose, it is also recommended to refer to the Israeli standard T.I. 940, "Foundation of Structures."

5.4 Structure of Embankments on Expansive Clays  
The structure of embankments on expansive clays is determined more by the activity strength of the clay than by the strength of its resistance to the destructive actions derived from the effects of traffic. To overcome the potential swelling or shrinkage of the clay, the following measures are commonly adopted:  
A. Maintaining a minimum structural thickness for the conventional structure (including road shoulders) that restrains swelling up to a value of 3.0 cm, with or without sealing membranes covering the embankment base.  
B. Covering the road shoulders or sidewalks with a sealing layer in sections where there is no subsurface drainage.  
C. Installing surface drainage for the rapid removal of surface water to minimize, as much as possible, the amount of water penetrating the base.  
D. Installing subsurface drainage to efficiently remove water reaching the base from outside the road area through the granular embankment layers.  
E. Processing the base under optimal conditions that reduce the potential for swelling and protecting the base with sealing membranes extending beyond the edges of the road or sidewalks, in areas where subsurface drainage systems do not interfere with covering the area with the aforementioned membranes.

id: segment_doc_78_היתרים ואישורים בנושא אחזקת כבישים עיירית ירושלים_9_c0
english_text:
1. Land leveling must be ensured; excess excavation after land leveling will be removed as approved by the municipality.
2. All crossings, including public crossings, will be designed and executed by the developer at their expense and will include access for strollers and disabled individuals, as well as lighting that is pre-approved by the lighting department. The width of public crossings that require the installation of T.K. systems along their length shall not be less than 8 meters.
3. Handrails must be installed on every flight of stairs (starting from 3 steps and above).
4. A safety railing must be installed wherever there is a height difference of 90 cm or more (the height of the railing shall not be less than 100 cm).
5. A lowered curb must be installed at the sidewalk entrances - the height of the step is 2 cm.
6. All infrastructure systems will be underground (Bezeq, electricity, telecommunications, etc.).
7. It is advisable to coordinate and prepare necessary infrastructure for mailboxes, public phones, and the like, in order to prevent unnecessary excavations in the future.
8. The road must be paved in 3 layers, with the top layer being basalt, according to the technical specifications for road paving of the Jerusalem municipality.
9. The surfacing of sidewalks/public crossings and traffic islands will be done with materials that are approved by the maintenance department.
10. Blind pipes (sleeves) must be laid for all infrastructure systems for plots/areas where construction will be delayed to prevent unnecessary excavations in the future.

english_text:
1. Coordination and integration of excavation works by various infrastructure entities to minimize road/sidewalk openings in the city.
2. Shortening the duration of the excavation approval process.
3. Issuing a quality excavation permit that consolidates all conditions and requirements of stakeholders.
4. Enforcement and supervision of all conditions and requirements stated in the permit.
5. Reducing the inconvenience to city residents and visitors caused by transportation restrictions, noise, dust, and safety risks that may arise during the execution of work in the field.

7. Stage B - Execution of the excavation, while adhering to the technical specifications and daily supervision, meeting safety standards, and not disrupting traffic.
8. Stage C - Restoring the surface to its original state and rehabilitating the entire site.
